10085-moorish-literature-comprising-roma:
This 1901 collection, translated into English for the first time with an introduction by René Basset of the University of France, gathers the literature of the Moors. Basset explains that the region from Egypt to the Atlantic, and from the Mediterranean to the Niger, was inhabited by the Berbers.

Inside are Moorish ballads and romances, the story of Sidi Brahim of Massat, five Berber stories, poems of the Maghreb, popular tales of the Berbers and Kabyles, and Fatima's love. Readers get North African storytelling in English at last: heroic, romantic, and rooted in a long oral tradition.
10386-thoughts-on-the-necessity-of-impro:
Thomas Clarkson published this essay in 1823, arguing for better treatment of enslaved people in British colonies as a road to final emancipation. Clarkson, a leading abolitionist, first printed the piece in The Inquirer, then reissued it with a candid note that he had overrated recent improvement. His tone is reasoned and humane.

Clarkson shows that emancipation, proposed even by a friend of planters in 1792, is neither new nor wild. He weighs safety, practicality, and advantage, urging gradual reform toward freedom. Readers get a key abolitionist argument, clear on why slavery must end and how it might end well.
10589-turkish-prisoners-in-egypt-a-repor:
Delegates of the International Committee of the Red Cross wrote this report in 1917, on Turkish prisoners in Egypt during the First World War. The delegates visited camps in December 1916 and January 1917, after sailing from Marseilles on the liner Morea to Port Said. Their account is official, careful, and humane.

At Cairo, General Murray put them in touch with Brigadier General Casson, director of prisoners, and Colonel Simpson helped plan visits. A motor car, permission to photograph, gifts, and free talk with prisoners aided their work. Readers get a primary, wartime record of prison camps, inspected by neutral eyes.
10609-english-literature-its-history-and:
William J. Long wrote English Literature as a school textbook tracing the whole story of English writing. It opens by asking what literature is and why it matters, then moves from Anglo-Saxon poems such as Beowulf, through Chaucer and Shakespeare, to modern writers. Each chapter ends with a summary, questions, dates, and books for further reading.

Long stresses the life behind the books: the speech, faith, and history of the English-speaking world. His style is clear and direct, meant for classroom use. Students still find it a helpful road map, and general readers can use it to place famous authors in their periods.
10703-the-history-of-rome-book-iii-from-:
Theodor Mommsen's Book III of his History of Rome runs from the union of Italy to the subjugation of Carthage and the Greek states. Dickson's sanctioned translation follows Rome as it turns from an Italian power into a Mediterranean empire, through the Punic Wars and the conquest of the Greek east. The narrative weighs armies, treaties, and the strain of empire on Roman life.

Mommsen shows how victory abroad changed politics at home, setting up the crises of the later books. His scholarship and storytelling carry the reader through complex campaigns with clarity. Readers get the middle republic at its height, in a work that defined Roman history for a century.
10779-happy-little-edward-and-his-pleasa:
Happy Little Edward, published in 1850, is a picture book for small children about a four-year-old boy's country visit. Edward Jones lives in a Connecticut city with his parents, brothers, sisters, and a kind aunt who cares for him. One spring morning the family sets out to visit his mother's sister, a farmer's wife in Massachusetts.

The book follows Edward's carriage ride and rambles in verse and pictures, urging little readers to wake and follow him to the country. Its tone is sweet and instructive, typical of early American children's books. Modern readers get a charming glimpse of how the 1850s taught city children about farm life.
10810-the-young-trail-hunters-or-the-wil:
Samuel Woodworth Cozzens published The Young Trail Hunters in 1877, telling the veritable adventures of Hal Hyde and Ned Brown across the great plains of the Southwest. Cozzens, who traveled with the boys, says no book fascinated him from youth like travel among Indians, where danger attends every step. A prairie on fire fronts the book.

The narrative records hair-breadth escapes and, from personal observation, the habits and customs of plains tribes Cozzens calls fast vanishing. Its tone is that of a guide turned storyteller. Readers get a firsthand-flavored Western adventure, with the plains and their peoples at its center.
11564-an-essay-on-war-in-blank-verse-hon:
Nathaniel Bloomfield's 1803 poems open with an essay on war in blank verse, followed by Honington Green, a ballad, The Culprit, an elegy, and other poems on various subjects. The preface recalls his brother George and their younger brother Robert, the Farmer's Boy, whom the two elder brothers helped to raise.

War poems look at gunpowder, soldiers, and shepherd boys sleeping on hills that hide warriors' tombs. The verse is plain and moral, written by a working poet for readers who knew the countryside and the cost of fighting at first hand.
11941-the-winning-of-the-west-volume-1-f:
Volume 1 of Theodore Roosevelt's Winning of the West, from the Alleghanies to the Mississippi, 1769 to 1776, with a map, opens the Presidential Edition's frontier history. Dedicated with permission to Francis Parkman, it carries an epigraph on a strange new world whose youth was wrung from it by gripping need.

Roosevelt follows the first settlers across the mountains into Kentucky and Tennessee country, where hunters, land speculators. Native peoples met in a contest for the West. The volume sets the pattern for the series: vigorous narrative, attention to individuals and battles. An argument that the frontier shaped American character as surely as the eastern seaboard did.
11942-the-winning-of-the-west-volume-2-f:
Theodore Roosevelt's second volume of The Winning of the West, in the Presidential Edition, covers the years 1777 to 1783, from the Alleghanies to the Mississippi, with maps. Dedicated to Francis Parkman, it follows the frontier war in the Northwest and George Rogers Clark's conquest of the Illinois country in 1778.

Roosevelt treats the western war as part of the Revolution itself, not a sideshow, with settlers, soldiers, and Native peoples contesting the same ground. Chapters on the war in the Northwest and Clark's campaign show how a thinly held frontier shaped the later boundaries of the United States.
12039-beaumont-and-fletcher-s-works-vol-:
Volume 1 of Beaumont and Fletcher's works presents The Custom of the Country, with its persons represented. Count Clodio is governour and a dishonourable pursuer of Zenocia. Manuel du Sosa is governour of Lisbon and brother to Guiomar, and Arnoldo is a gentleman contracted to Zenocia.

Rutilio, a merry gentleman and brother to Arnoldo, Charino, father to Zenocia, Duarte, son to Guiomar and a gentleman well qualified but vain glorious, and Alonzo, a young gentleman, complete the cast. The play's custom, a lord's claimed right over a bride, drives a Jacobean plot of pursuit, honor, and escape, in the frank, theatrical manner of its authors.
12272-the-history-of-puerto-rico-from-th:
R. A. Van Middeldyk wrote this history of Puerto Rico from Spanish discovery to American occupation, published in 1903 and edited by Martin G. Brumbaugh, first commissioner of education for Puerto Rico. The book belongs to the Expansion of the Republic series.

Van Middeldyk traces the island from Columbus landing in 1493 through Spanish rule, slavery, trade, and revolt, to the American occupation of 1898. Brumbaugh preface notes that the newest American possession was also the oldest in European occupation. The history is written from an American administrative view, praising order and education. Modern readers will read it against Puerto Rican accounts, but it remains a clear early survey of four centuries.
12363-the-botanist-s-companion-volume-ii:
William Salisbury, of the Botanic Garden of Sloane Street, wrote The Botanist Companion, volume two, as an introduction to practical botany and the uses of plants. The volume covers plants growing wild in Great Britain or cultivated for agriculture, medicine, rural economy, or the arts.

Contents treat plants useful in agriculture, with observations on saving grass seeds and the use of British grasses. Later entries describe mullein, whose flowers have a honeylike sweetness, and vervain, used as an emollient and held in esteem in consumptions. Salisbury writes for farmers, gardeners, and apothecaries who need to know a plant by sight and use. The book is a practical Georgian herbal, plain and methodical.
12440-d-ri-and-i-a-tale-of-daring-deeds-:
Irving Bacheller's 1901 tale, D'Ri and I, gives the memoirs of Colonel Ramon Bell in the second war with Britain. A letter from Captain Darius Hawkins introduces young Bell to the Comte de Chaumont, and illustrations show Louise, D'Ri, a pretty prisoner, an old brig and two girls Bell cannot choose between.

Daring deeds follow: fighting, capture, escape and loyalty tested under fire. Bacheller, author of Eben Holden, writes in a warm, anecdotal voice, mixing humour with war story. The novel offers a popular, patriotic romance of 1812, told as remembered adventure rather than formal history, with friendship at its heart.
12522-an-account-of-the-extraordinary-me:
Matthew Turner, surgeon in Liverpool, published this short account of aether, an extraordinary medicinal fluid, around 1761. Turner had prepared and used it in private practice for several years, and now sought to extend its utility by making it public. No one, he says, had published its medicinal virtues, offered it in perfection, or given criteria to tell genuine from spurious.

The pamphlet explains the fluid, its uses and its tests, in the plain language of an eighteenth-century practitioner. It belongs to a time when new remedies circulated by reputation and by print, and quack copies followed success. The account survives as a small document of medical history, and of a surgeon defending his preparation against imitation.
1281-tom-swift-and-his-aerial-warship-or:
Victor Appleton sends Tom Swift to sea and sky with a new aerial warship, a flying craft armed for naval war, which spies and enemy agents try to steal. The tale moves through test flights, sea chases, and a battle above the waves, with Tom's inventions deciding the day.

The book, written as naval arms races filled the news, mixes boy's adventure with dreams of air power. Tom's pluck and his machines carry a brisk plot. It suits young readers who like Swift's formula of invention, danger, and triumph. Swift's flying warship yarn suits young readers who love machines and danger.
13906-conception-control-and-its-effects:
Florence E. Barrett, a London surgeon and president of the Federation of Medical Women, wrote this 1922 study of birth control. A foreword by the Archbishop of Canterbury fronts the volume. Chapters cover the problem of today, the demand for knowledge, methods, and effects on national efficiency. A summary of conclusions closes the argument.

Barrett traces debate from the late 1870s, when Besant and Bradlaugh republished The Fruits of Philosophy. She warns against teaching people to postpone childbearing lightly, noting gynaecologists see many who later cannot conceive. Her tone is medical and cautious, not polemical. The book records early twentieth-century professional views on a contested subject.
14126-the-marriage-of-william-ashe:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1905 novel follows William Ashe and Lady Kitty Bristol through acquaintance, three years after, development, storm, and requiescat. Kitty, slim in white at the far end of a large room, dazzles a world of politics, art, and society talk. Cliffe, a treasury official's friend, debates old passions with her, while she laughs that modern people have lost the power to feel as old poems felt.

Illness reshapes the story. Kitty's collapse on a terrace moves even Lord Parham to near-cordial kindness, and Lady Tranmore nurses her night and day beside a paralyzed husband. Lord Grosville offers Grosville Park for convalescence, and a dean travels repeatedly from his cathedral town to sit with her. Eddie Helston's flowers arrive with the rest. Ward writes society fiction with moral weight, tracing a marriage through charm, scandal, suffering, and slow amendment.
14150-the-light-in-the-clearing-a-tale-o:
Irving Bacheller's 1917 novel of upstate New York follows a boy growing up in the time of Silas Wright. Set in the north country, it mixes school days, farm work, and political talk. A silent woman points, a new suit causes careful worry at dinner, and a girl's invitation to school plants a hope that grows through the book. Arthur I. Keller's pictures add to the period charm.

Public life gives the tale its spine. A teacher's five counsels urge modesty, honesty, and putting subject before self, with the good of all the people as the aim. Wright's 1834 Senate speech on public money serves as the model: he voiced his state's wishes and cast himself aside. Bacheller, author of Eben Holden, writes warmly about democracy learned young, in schoolrooms, dooryards, and town meetings.
14237-the-christian-home-as-it-is-in-the:
Rev. S. Philips published The Christian Home in 1865, showing the mission, duties, influences, habits, and responsibilities of home, with education, government, and discipline. Hints on match making and parents' relation to children's marriage choices join a study of tests for selecting a companion. A verse motto praises home's smile and mutual look, when hearts are sure of each other.

Baptism draws sharp criticism. Many parents, Philips writes, treat christening as mere name-giving, choosing fashionable novel names that recall love-sick tales or the burning of Rome, then thinking no more of dedication. Legacy and work receive equal care: a child left wealth without a pursuit may squander inheritance by dissipation faster than parents amassed it by industry. Sickness and adversity may sweep funds away, leaving an idle heir helpless. Earnest, old-fashioned, and practical, the book urges families to train character before fortune.
14369-the-young-engineers-on-the-gulf-or:
H. Irving Hancock wrote this boys' adventure of young engineers at work on a million-dollar breakwater in the Gulf. Tom Reade and his friends face night explosions, vanished men, and plotters who strike in the dark. Mr. Bascomb, their chief, grows peevish as trouble piles up. Divers, lamps, and concrete work fill the days. The tale is told for boys who love machines, teamwork, and a straight fight.

A man named Hazelton vanishes, and Tom will not believe him dead while no body is found. The engineers walk the breakwater wall toward the scene of two night blasts, watched by a sulky Bascomb. Later a prisoner slips his cords: Sambo Ebony snaps them and flees with a little Mexican. Tom groans at his own folly, then takes a magneto and sets out on the trail. The book keeps its mystery tight and its heroes plucky.
14460-faust-a-tragedy-part-1-translated-:
Charles T. Brooks translated Goethe's Faust, Part One, into English verse, and this seventh edition, published in Boston in 1868, carries his notes. Brooks apologized for adding yet another version of a much-translated poem.

The tragedy follows the scholar Faust, who bargains with Mephistopheles, seduces Gretchen, and curses love, faith, and hope in despair, while a chorus of spirits answers his ruin. Brooks keeps Goethe's varied meters in English. The translation introduced many American readers to the German classic, and its notes explain the folklore and philosophy behind the drama.
14626-the-boy-allies-with-the-victorious:
Ensign Robert L. Drake's Boy Allies novel sends Frank and Jack with the victorious fleets to witness the fall of the German navy at the end of the Great War. A. L. Burt published the boys' series volume.

Lord Hastings explains that enemy submarines, cut off from bases, may still prey on merchant ships for food and fuel, snaring a victim every few days. The boys sail aboard the Plymouth, rescue sailors, and chase U-boats. The story is brisk boys' adventure, patriotic and sea-minded, in the long-running Boy Allies series.
14889-the-meadow-brook-girls-under-canva:
Janet Aldridge sends the Meadow-Brook Girls to summer camp in this girls' adventure, subtitled fun and frolic in the summer camp. Crazy Jane's wild drive and what happened to Tommy open the story, before the trail leads to Camp Wau-Wau in the heart of the forest.

Troubles multiply, a first degree is taken, Tommy has a nightmare, and a day ends with excitement and a general alarm. Around the council fire, tried by flames, Harriet turns the tables, the camp gets a surprise, and the ghost of Wau-Wau is laid. Aldridge writes camp life with energy: tents, trails, pranks and friendship, in a series made for young readers.
15011-the-spirit-and-the-word-a-treatise:
Z. T. Sweeney's treatise, published by the Gospel Advocate Company in Nashville, studies the Holy Spirit in light of a rational interpretation of the word of truth. Its contents move from Old Testament and New Testament through personality and divinity of the Spirit.

John the Baptist, Jesus, the apostles and the apostolic church follow, with the Spirit and the world, the Spirit and Christians, and a parting word. Sweeney notes the Old Testament gives less prominence to the Spirit than the New, since the former deals largely with material things. The book is a plain, argumentative work of Restoration theology, meant to be tested by Scripture.
15106-origin-of-the-anglo-boer-war-revea:
C. H. Thomas, a former burgher of the Transvaal, published this second edition in London in 1900 to argue a partisan case about the Anglo-Boer War. He claims the war sprang from a long Afrikaner Bond plot to push Britain out of South Africa, not from British aggression. His notice says he meant the book for South Africa in 1899.

Thomas writes as an insider turned critic, naming the men and groups he holds guilty and urging peace between Boer and Briton once the truth is known. The argument is fierce and one-sided, which is itself part of its value. Historians read it as evidence of wartime feeling, not as a neutral record of causes.
15260-a-portraiture-of-quakerism-volume-:
Thomas Clarkson's first volume on Quakerism, dated 1806, studies moral education among the Society of Friends. Chapters divide amusements into useful and hurtful, with the hurtful forbidden, and games of chance condemned as below human dignity and Christian character. Excitement of passions and gaming habits draw censure.

Clarkson, an abolitionist admirer of Quakers, writes with care for their discipline and reasons. The volume sets the ground for later books on manners, economy, and tenets. Students of Quaker history will find it a detailed, sympathetic guide to early Friends' moral life. It remains a useful window onto early Quaker discipline.
15261-a-portraiture-of-quakerism-volume-:
Thomas Clarkson's second volume on Quakerism, published at New York in 1806, studies the Society of Friends through education, discipline, manners, and economy. Peculiar customs open the book, with marriage rules from George Fox onward, disownment for marrying out, and terms for restoration to membership. More women than men faced disownment.

Later chapters treat social manners, civil life, and religious character, with Clarkson's careful, sympathetic eye. As an abolitionist, he admired Quaker witness, and his portrait is fair-minded. Students of American religion will find the volume a detailed, humane guide to early Quaker life.
15304-a-portraiture-of-quakerism-volume-:
Thomas Clarkson's third volume on Quakerism treats the great tenets of the Society of Friends. Chapters open with civil government: rulers must not meddle in religion, and the governed must suffer penalties rather than resist by arms. Oaths, war, and other tenets follow in careful order.

Clarkson writes with sympathy and precision, drawing on Quaker discipline and practice. His portrait shows a people who refuse oaths and war on scriptural grounds, yet obey law where conscience allows. Students of religion and peace history will find the volume clear, fair, and deeply informative.
15723-the-rover-boys-on-treasure-isle-or:
The thirteenth Rover Boys book, by Edward Stratemeyer, issued in 1909. Stratemeyer, creator of the series, calls it a complete tale in itself. The Rover brothers leave school tales behind for a steam yacht and a treasure hunt. Ten years of Rover books had built a loyal boy audience, and this volume feeds it well.

A strange cruise carries the boys toward Treasure Isle, where gold, rivals, and hidden clues await. Storms, chases, and narrow escapes test their courage and their teamwork. Old friends help, old enemies plot, and the treasure stays just out of reach. The book delights as pure boys' adventure: clean fun, quick action, and brothers who never quit.
15752-personal-reminiscences-of-early-da:
Reminiscences of early California by Stephen J. Field, later a justice of the United States Supreme Court. A stenographer took the sketches down in San Francisco in the summer of 1877, from Field's own narrative. Printed for a few friends in 1893, the book was not published for sale. George C. Gorham adds the story of Field's attempted assassination.

Field recalls gold-rush law, courts, and politics in a raw new state, with vivid portraits of judges and miners. Gorham's addition tells how a former associate on the state supreme bench tried to kill him. The two parts join to form a rare record: law made on the frontier, by a man who lived it. Historians still prize the book for its firsthand voice.
15883-the-london-bawd-with-her-character:
A Restoration pamphlet on London vice, third edition, printed for John Gwillim in Bishopsgate Street in 1705, at three shillings. The London Bawd promises her character and life, with the various and subtle intrigues of lewd women. Its tone is satirical and moral, in the manner of the age. Chapters anatomise a trade London loved to condemn and to use.

The first chapter defines a bawd as the refuse of an old whore, who, burnt herself, sets greener wood on fire. Later chapters trace her tricks, her girls, and her clients through town. The prose is coarse, vivid, and learned in street slang. The pamphlet fascinates as social history: London's underworld, drawn by a writer who knew it well.
16290-the-bible-book-by-book-a-manual-fo:
This manual for the outline study of the Bible by books opens with Genesis, whose name means beginning, origin, or creation. Its leading thought is creation. Students should seek everything whose beginning Genesis records. The world God created, man as God's creature, and sin entering through disobedience come first. Redemption in promises and types and the chosen family follows. Condemnation in the punishment of individuals, cities, and the world closes the list.

The purpose of Genesis, the manual says, is religious history, showing how God, after man's fall, began to give him a religion and unfold a plan of salvation. God appears as Creator, Preserver, Law-Giver, Judge, and Merciful Sovereign. Book by book, the manual guides readers through the whole Bible in outline form.
16724-the-campaign-of-1760-in-canada-a-n:
This 1887 Quebec narrative of the campaign of 1760 in Canada is attributed to Chevalier Johnstone and issued under the Literary and Historical Society of Quebec. It opens with a meditation on hope, which never leaves the distressed, not even the dying man or the prisoner due to die next day. Hope, it says, dwells in prisons and in agony alike.

The narrative then follows the last campaign for Canada, as French hopes fade and British force closes in. It mixes personal reflection with marches, sieges, and loss. Readers of Canadian history will find a rare, first-hand voice from the losing side, full of feeling and of the hard facts of a war's end.
16975-the-haunted-house-a-true-ghost-sto:
Walter Hubbell wrote this 1879 true ghost story of the Great Amherst Mystery, issued by the Daily News steam office in Saint John, New Brunswick. It tells of strange events in the presence of Esther Cox, a young girl said to be possessed of devils and known through the Dominion. Hubbell says he lived in the house and saw the wonders himself.

Hubbell's introduction says the events began a year before, no one could find their cause, and men of science from Canada and the United States probed them in vain. Some blamed electricity, some mesmerism, others the devil, which Hubbell calls the most plausible. Readers who like ghost lore will find a vivid, period account, best read as a tale of its time, not as proof.
17002-history-and-ecclesiastical-relatio:
The Rev. J. V. N. Talmage, missionary of the Protestant Reformed Dutch Church, wrote this 1863 history of the churches of the presbyterial order at Amoy, China, printed in New York by Wynkoop, Hallenbeck and Thomas. His preface to ministers, elders, and members says the importance of church order in heathen lands justifies the paper, even where readers differ on its views.

Talmage asks how churches gathered from non-Christian folk should be ordered, when few have yet grown enough for practical rules. He weighs Dutch, Presbyterian, and local needs with care. The paper gives a rare, early view of mission church polity in China, useful for church historians and for readers of mission history.
1710-la-grande-breteche:
A shuttered house in Touraine called La Grande Bretèche has stood empty for years, and a visiting doctor learns why from local gossip and a servant's memory. The house has stood empty for years. The doctor learns why from a local story: a husband who came home early, a hidden lover, and a wall built in haste.

Balzac tells the horror sideways, through gossip, a servant's memory, and a room that no one will open. The tale is brief but it lingers, because its cruelty is so quiet: no murder is shown, only a door sealed and a woman left behind it. The reader is left to imagine what the silence inside that room must have meant.
17149-creative-chemistry-descriptive-of-:
Edwin E. Slosson's 1919 book grew from articles in The Independent meant to interest plain readers in new chemical work. Chapters cover nitrogen, soil food, coal-tar dyes, scents and flavors, cellulose, plastics, rubber, sugars, corn goods, and metals old and new. War steel, fumes, and the electric furnace get their own turns.

Slosson writes with cheer and clear examples, linking lab work to farms, shops, and homes. The book captures a moment when chemistry seemed able to make almost anything from air, coal, and plants. For readers keen on science history, it is a lively, plain guide to the industries that shaped the early 1900s.
17321-history-of-egypt-chaldea-syria-bab:
L. W. King and H. R. Hall, both of the British Museum's department of Egyptian and Assyrian antiquities, wrote this history in the light of recent discovery, published in 1906 with over twelve hundred plates and pictures. The authors had visited many of the sites themselves and took many of the photographs, so the book rests on first-hand digging as well as reading.

Chapters run from prehistoric Egypt and Abydos through Memphis and the pyramids. They cover early Babylonian life, the temples and tombs of Thebes, and the Assyrian and neo-Babylonian empires, ending with the last days of ancient Egypt. Readers get a survey of Egypt and Mesopotamia as scholars understood them just after a decade of fresh finds. Its plates still make it a handsome introduction to the ancient Near East.
17369-the-fifth-leicestershire-a-record-:
Captain J. D. Hills, holder of the Military Cross and the Croix de Guerre, wrote this record of the 1/5th Battalion of the Leicestershire Regiment, Territorial Force, during the war of 1914 to 1919. Lieutenant-Colonel C. H. Jones supplied an introduction. The battalion's story runs from training and embarkation through the Western Front campaigns to demobilisation.

Hills writes as a battalion officer, naming actions, places, and men with a soldier's care for detail. Readers get a unit history of the kind that regiments published after the Great War, valuable for families, local historians, and students of the Territorial Army. Its value lies in its closeness to events rather than in grand strategy.
17440-amadis-of-gaul-an-opera-as-it-is-p:
Printed in London in 1715 for Jacob Tonson, this libretto gives the words of Amadis of Gaul as performed at the King's Theatre in the Haymarket. The dedication to Richard, Earl of Burlington, praises his support for stage music and notes that the opera was composed in his own family. That courtly frame fits an age when opera in London lived on noble patronage.

Readers get the sung text of an early English opera, drawn from the old romance of the knight Amadis. The spelling and stage directions keep the flavour of the 1715 theatre, where Italianate opera was still a fresh import. It serves students of opera, of early modern print, and of how chivalric romance was refashioned for the London stage.
17749-the-mystic-will-a-method-of-develo:
Charles G. Leland wrote The Mystic Will as a guide to training the mind through the will, in a plain process open to any person of fair sense. The American edition came from the Progress Company in Chicago, after Leland's death in 1903.

Chapters teach care, self-talk, forethought, will and character, recall, and the shaping powers of the mind. Leland claims that a willed thought, held with care, can steer habit and mood. Modern readers may take it as period self-help, earnest and odd by turns, and a window on how Victorians thought the mind could be schooled.
18643-the-first-landing-on-wrangel-islan:
Irving C. Rosse, a navy surgeon, wrote this account of the United States revenue steamer Corwin's 1881 Arctic cruise from San Francisco. The ship sought two missing whalers and news of the exploring yacht Jeannette, sailing to Alaska and the northwest Arctic. After storms, hail, and a blind landfall among Aleutian cliffs, the Corwin pressed toward Herald and Wrangel islands.

Wrangel, reported by Russian Admiral Wrangel from native tales and glimpsed by Captain Kellett in 1849, had come to seem a myth after failed tries. Rosse tells how the Corwin at last made the first landing there, with notes on northern peoples. The pamphlet is a vivid record of Arctic search and discovery.
18941-the-fight-for-a-free-sea-a-chronic:
Ralph D. Paine's 1920 chronicle The Fight for a Free Sea tells the story of the War of 1812 as a struggle for American rights on the ocean. It is a volume of the Chronicles of America series. The book opens with the ill-fated drive on Canada, then turns to the naval war that forms its heart, from Lake Erie and Lake Champlain to frigate duels on the open sea.

Chapters follow Perry's victory on Lake Erie, the ebb and flow on the northern frontier, the matchless frigates and their single-ship actions. The cry of don't give up the ship, the last cruise of the Essex, and the final victory on Lake Champlain close the book, with peace with honor. Illustrated with images including the frigate Constitution, the volume offers a readable, patriotic narrative history of a war fought as much for freedom of the seas as for territory.
18973-day-symbols-of-the-maya-year-sixte:
Cyrus Thomas contributed this paper to the Sixteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, published in Washington in 1897. It studies the day symbols of the Maya year: the names, signs, and meanings attached to each day in the Maya calendar. Thomas works through the days in order, from the first to the twentieth, with illustrations of glyphs.

The paper draws on Maya codices and inscriptions, comparing day signs and their forms, including copies of glyphs and a shell bearing Maya glyphs. Thomas asks what each symbol meant and how the calendar ordered time. Readers get a pioneering work of Maya scholarship, detailed and technical, that helped later scholars read Maya dates and texts.
18979-narrative-of-a-journey-to-the-shor:
John Franklin wrote this first volume of his account of the Arctic expedition of 1819 to 1822, traveling to the shores of the Polar Sea. The volume opens with departure from England, transactions at Stromness, and a perilous passage through Davis' Straits to the coast of Labrador. From York Factory, the party prepares for the journey into the interior.

Later chapters follow rivers and lakes inland: Hayes River, Swampy Lake, Lake Winnipeg, and the long water route toward the north. Franklin records native peoples, weather, and the hard logistics of moving men and stores. Readers get a classic of Arctic exploration, plain in style and rich in firsthand detail about a journey that tested its party to the limit.
18985-narrative-of-a-journey-to-the-shor:
John Franklin wrote this second volume of his account of the Arctic expedition of 1819 to 1822. It opens at Fort Enterprise, with Mr. Back's narrative of his journey to Chipewyan and back, and an account of the Copper Indians. Preparations follow for the journey northward, the hard core of the expedition.

Later chapters trace the Copper-Mine River, a visit to the Copper Mountain, and meetings with Inuit groups. The party then navigates the Polar Sea itself in two canoes, as far as Cape Turnagain and beyond. Hunger, cold, and loss mark the return. Readers get the grimmer half of a famous exploration narrative, notable for its restraint and its record of endurance.
1903-everybody-s-guide-to-money-matters-:
William Cotton, Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, writes a plain guide to money matters for ordinary readers, explaining banks, interest, stocks, and household finance in clear terms. The book aims to help people manage money well. Cotton, a banker and antiquary, wrote for readers with no training in finance.

Cotton describes savings, investments, and the pitfalls of speculation, with examples from Victorian commerce. The guide serves as a readable introduction to nineteenth-century finance, and as a period piece on thrift. His guide explains interest, shares, and wills in language a shopkeeper could follow.
19084-in-the-yule-log-glow-book-ii-chris:
Harrison S. Morris edited this second book of Christmas tales from round the world, published in 1900 with an 1891 copyright. It gathers stories for winter firesides, from Christmas with the Baron to tales by Daudet, Ewing, and Repplier, plus a picture of the Nativity by Fra Filippo Lippi. The motto quotes Scott on tales told at a winter hearth.

A baron's fire burns hollow, tumbles in, and blazes again while smoke curls to a carved ceiling and old oak panels seem to nod in the light. Such scenes set the book's mood. Readers get warm, varied Christmas stories from many lands, made for reading aloud by the fire.
19659-the-elements-of-general-method-bas:
Charles A. McMurry wrote this study of teaching method based on the principles of Herbart, published in Illinois in the early eighteen nineties in a second edition. The Herbart school, strong in Germany for thirty years, sought a clear leading purpose for schooling and a set of linked principles.

McMurry stresses interest as a spur to mental vigor and as a test for choosing what children should study at each age. His book helped bring German pedagogy to American teachers, and it remains a clear statement of method before progressive reform reshaped the field.
19753-the-youth-of-goethe:
P. Hume Brown wrote this life of Goethe's youth, published in London in the early nineteen teens and dedicated to Viscount Haldane, who prompted the book. It opens in Frankfurt, with Goethe's birthplace, father, mother, sister, friends, and schooling.

Later chapters cover religious influences, the Seven Years' War, and the French occupation of Frankfurt, which shaped the boy's mind. Brown's study follows Goethe from a point that slowly opens into a circle, and at last enfolds the world. Brown follows Goethe from Frankfurt boyhood toward wide world fame. The opening chapter also notes Goethe's first love, before he was destined for the study of law.
19767-george-borrow-and-his-circle-where:
George Borrow wrote Lavengro and The Bible in Spain, two singular Victorian books. George Borrow and His Circle gathers facts about the man and his friends. One figure is William Ireland Knapp, a scholar of modern languages. Knapp held chairs at Vassar, Yale, and Chicago. He spent eleven years in Spain and wrote Borrow's life. He died in Paris in 1908, aged seventy-four.

Borrow biographies attract odd, devoted scholars like Knapp. Clement King Shorter assembled this circle of lives around Borrow. Gypsies, languages, and Spain run through all of them. The book serves readers who finish Lavengro wanting the real man. It also preserves a vanished scholarly world. Borrow's circle was nearly as strange as Borrow.
20811-two-decades-a-history-of-the-first:
Histories, says Frances W. Graham, wake lost memories and bare hidden events. Two Decades traces the first twenty years of a New York reform group's work. Its shuttle of memory weaves fact and incident into one full cloth.

The Woman's Christian Temperance Union fought drink as a threat to homes. Graham records its New York campaigns, leaders, and wins across two decades. Petitions, meetings, and laws mark the slow grind of reform. The book keeps the voice of those who did the work, proud of ground gained and clear-eyed about how much ground still lay ahead.
21112-the-causes-of-the-corruption-of-th:
John William Burgon, Dean of Chichester, left this defence of the traditional text of the Gospels unfinished at his death. Edward Miller arranged, completed, and edited it for publication in London in 1896 as a sequel to Burgon's Traditional Text of the Holy Gospels. Burgon distrusted the new critical Greek texts of his day.

He argues that errors crept into Gospel copies through careless scribes, deliberate changes, and other causes he sorts one by one. A long section attacks Dr Hort's theory of confluence and the so-called Neutral Text. Indexes of subjects and passages make it a working reference for textual critics.
21240-the-lone-ranche:
Captain Mayne Reid set this tale of the Staked Plain around Chihuahua, a city he says calls up strange records of frontier life. Early cowboy and Indian fiction is what readers get: rough speech, Spanish and Mexican words, and hard riding on the border plains. Reid's characters speak in dialects that fill the pages with non-dictionary words.

The Lone Ranche of the title stands at the centre of the action on the dry Staked Plain of Texas and the Mexican border. Reid helped invent the Western adventure novel, writing from his own years in America. Frontier memory, raids, and ranch life give the tale its colour and pace.
21592-the-art-of-making-whiskey-so-as-to:
Anthony Boucherie of Lexington, Kentucky, promises better whiskey in The Art of Making Whiskey, printed there in 1819. His full title pledges a purer, cheaper spirit, and more of it, from the same grain. A second art turns that spirit into gin, after the Dutch method.

The work was translated from Boucherie's French by a hand masked as C. M. It was entered at law in December 1818, in the district of Kentucky. Copies survive only in poor shape, and the editors kept the printer's errors marked. Early American distilling gets a rare, close record in these pages.
22207-the-romance-of-giovanni-calvotti-f:
The Romance of Giovanni Calvotti comes from David Christie Murray's story set Coals of Fire. Calvotti introduces himself with unusual candour. He is an Italian and a gentleman, aged thirty. His main fault, he says, is being able to do much in too many directions. Music, verse in four languages, and composition all show his great undeveloped talent.

Murray lets the man's vanity narrate its own undoing. Calvotti's romance tests whether brilliance without ballast can win or keep love. The tale is part character study, part cautionary comedy. Among the Coals of Fire stories it shows Murray's lighter, more ironic touch.
22547-the-rover-boys-on-treasure-isle-or:
The Rover Boys on Treasure Isle sends three brothers on a strange cruise. The subtitle names the steam yacht that carries them south. In his preface, the author recalls the series' long run with readers.

Years ago the first three volumes began the Rover Boys' adventures. They were The Rover Boys at School and On the Ocean. The Rover Boys in the Jungle completed that first trio. At that time, he thought to end with a fourth volume. Readers wanted more, so the brothers kept sailing onward. Treasure Isle promises buried wealth and a curious voyage together. The Rovers remained models of pluck for American boys. This cruise delivers sea adventure in the series' brisk style.
23003-the-new-minister-s-great-opportuni:
A villager prices sermons in The New Minister's Great Opportunity, a story by Heman White Chaplin first published in a magazine. I don't see much job in that, the man says. A pastor already owes two sermons a week, the man reckons, with an endless supply behind them. One extra sermon costs nothing, since the stock is free. It's like wheeling gravel from the pit.

That dry arithmetic frames the minister's chance when it comes. Chaplin's coastal people test their new pastor with the same plain sense they apply to fish and freight. Faith, in his stories, must survive the store's counter talk. The humor is dry as salt cod. Readers get a small, perfect specimen of his village manner.
23029-ohio-arbor-day-1913-arbor-and-bird:
Ohio's governor signs off in the Ohio Arbor Day 1913 manual. The proclamation closes in full legal form. At Columbus in mid-January 1913, the governor signs his name and orders the state's Great Seal attached.

The manual that follows arms teachers for Arbor and Bird Day. Programs, poems, tree-planting directions, and bird lore fill it, all meant for schoolrooms across the state. Ohio took the holiday seriously, and print like this carried the observance into one-room schools. The booklet preserves a whole civic ritual of the Progressive Era. Trees, birds, children, and the state seal share its pages in perfect confidence.
23320-the-deaf-their-position-in-society:
This study examines the position of deaf people in society and the provision made for their education and care. It weighs how schools, work, and public life treat deaf citizens, and what better provision might look like.

Written when deaf education was a live public question, the book argues from facts and cases rather than pity. It remains a useful record of how Victorian reformers thought about disability, schooling, and a fair place in society. The study weighs schools, work, and public life for deaf citizens alike. The study notes the Convention of American Instructors, oldest of the bodies meeting for deaf education.
2390-the-conquest-of-the-old-southwest-t:
Archibald Henderson tells the romantic story of the Old Southwest: the Carolinas, Tennessee, and Kentucky from 1740 to 1790, when pioneers crossed the mountains into a contested land. The Conquest of the Old Southwest follows Boone, Robertson, and Sevier through wars with Native peoples, land hunger, and the founding of new settlements. Henderson writes with the sweep of a popular historian.

The book's older view of frontier heroism now needs balancing with Native perspectives, but its narrative energy endures. It preserves the pioneer legends as Americans once told them. Readers of frontier history will find a vivid account.
24080-the-stewardship-of-the-soil-baccal:
John Henry Worst, president of North Dakota Agricultural College, gave this baccalaureate address at the college commencement in Fargo on June 6, 1915. He spoke to graduates of a young farming state whose wealth lay not in mines or forests but in millions of fertile acres. His theme was stewardship: the care of the soil as a trust held for others.

Worst argued that no trust carries heavier duties than the farmer's care of the land, since harvests feed the whole nation. He urged graduates to treat farming as service to society, not merely as a way to make a living. The address still reads as a plain statement of why good farming matters far beyond the farm gate.
2476-the-circus-boys-in-dixie-land-or-wi:
The Circus Boys take their show to Dixie Land in this volume, winning plaudits from Southern crowds as they perform under new skies. Edgar B. P. Darlington follows the young aerialists through Southern towns, with fresh rivals, mishaps, and the particular color of the road in the South. The circus itself remains the hero.

The story's travelogue flavor adds to its adventure, as the boys learn new audiences and new tricks. Series readers will enjoy the change of scene. It is a cheerful, fast-moving boys' book. Darlington's series ran to many volumes following the same young performers.
24800-darwin-and-after-darwin-volumes-1-:
George John Romanes wrote Darwin and After Darwin to lay out Darwin's theory and then weigh the questions that came after Darwin. This volume joins the first part, on the Darwinian theory itself, with the third, on post-Darwinian questions. Romanes, a Cambridge fellow and friend of Darwin, writes with care and full command of the science of his day.

Chapters trace how organs shrink and vanish, using the tail of the ancient bird Archaeopteryx beside the tail of a modern bird. Pictures and diagrams back the argument at each step. The book gives a clear, early statement of evolution by natural selection and of the debates it raised among Darwin's heirs.
25056-the-brothers-in-law-a-tale-of-the-:
Louis Becke's 1901 tale, from 'The Tapu of Banderah' and published by C. Arthur Pearson, opens with Tâvita the teacher pointing his paddle at a narrow peninsula in a shallow lagoon, where a battle was fought. A village of thirty houses once stood there; now people come to gather cocoanuts. The White Man, the one trader living in Peru, lands with Tâvita to rest and smoke under cocoa palms until the sun loses its fierceness.

Tâvita, a Samoan counted among the Pacific's oldest and bravest missionaries, has dwelt twenty years among Peru's warlike people. Undaunted courage, genial disposition, integrity, and skill as fisherman and carpenter preserved him, rather than preaching alone. As the two watch silvery mullet disporting on the glassy lagoon, the trader asks who the white men were who fought in the battle. Tâvita refills his pipe and begins the tale.
25143-the-curlytops-and-their-playmates-:
Howard R. Garis's CurlyTops and Their Playmates, published in 1922, follows Ted, Jan, and baby Trouble Martin through jolly times across the holidays. Garis, creator of the Uncle Wiggily stories, writes for young readers who like snow, pets, and mild mischief.

Chapters bring a postman's whistle, a trip to the country, a stalled train in a storm, and new playmates at Crystal Lake. The children build a toboggan slide and a snow house, lose a pet named Skyrocket, and find Trouble missing before a happy reunion. The book is cheerful, old-fashioned family fare.
25407-the-merrie-tales-of-jacques-tourne:
Anatole France's Merrie Tales of Jacques Tournebroche, published by John Lane in 1919, opens with Olivier's Brag. Charlemagne and his twelve peers, on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, visit King Hugo at Constantinople, where ruby birds sing in emerald bushes beneath a golden dome.

At table they eat stags, boars, cranes, wild geese, and peacocks served in pepper, drinking Greek and Asian wines from ox-horns. Later, Brother Joconde preaches beans to the people, meaning charitable works to sow before Judgment comes quickly. France retells medieval tales with wit, learning, and gentle irony.
25589-he:
He answers H. Rider Haggard's romance She with a comic companion volume, published in London by Longmans in 1887. Its author is billed only as the author of It, King Solomon's Wives, Bess, Much Darker Days, and other romances, leaving the joke in the byline itself.

A dedicatory verse addressed to Haggard denies that Ayesha still lingers in waste, swamp, and lagoon, in mysterious Kor with lonely towers beneath the moon. The world, it says, is disenchanted, and Europe will send spies through all the land. Hearts brooding over buried loves supply the real romance now.
25802-ruth-fielding-on-the-st-lawrence-o:
Alice B. Emerson writes Ruth Fielding on the St. Lawrence, or The Queer Old Man of the Thousand Islands. Cupples and Leon published the book with pictures. Cameras whir in a front picture while a barge pushes close into shore. That picture hints at Ruth's moving picture work.

Chapters open with here comes the bride, as organ peals sound joyously. A rift in Tom Cameron's lute follows. Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill and Ruth Fielding in the Great Northwest. She sends Ruth to the Thousand Islands. An old man, river life, and film making mix into a girls' adventure.
25998-the-riflemen-of-the-ohio-a-story-o:
Joseph A. Altsheler continues the fortunes of Henry Ware, Paul Cotter, and their friends in The Riflemen of the Ohio, printed by Appleton in 1922 from a 1910 copyright. The tale, complete in itself, follows heroes of The Young Trailers, The Forest Runners, The Keepers of the Trail, The Eyes of the Woods, and The Free Rangers. Chapters open with the eye of the fleet and the Wyandot chief, then the song of the leaves and a forest village.

Play and council, the gantlet, and alone in the wilderness follow, with a shadow in the water and the gathering of the five. One night scene finds Henry and Major Braithwaite on a ledge inside the palisade, gazing at a clearing in heavy gloom. A faint sliding sound reaches Henry's ear, though the major sees nothing. Altsheler writes of the Ohio frontier with pace and care.
26035-religion-and-theology-a-sermon-for:
John Tulloch, principal of St. Mary's College, St. Andrews, preaches on religion and theology in a sermon for the times, given at Crathie parish church on September 5 and at the College Church, St. Andrews. Second edition printed by Blackwood in 1875, the sermon weighs faith against systems, and the life of religion against the study of it. Tulloch, known for his history of rational theology, writes with large minded, lively thought.

The sermon runs through figures of faith. Peter and Andrew are taken from boats, Matthew sits at custom, the good Samaritan, the devout centurion, curious Zaccheus, and the repentant prodigal appear. James speaks on justification by works and not faith only. Apollos, mighty in Scripture yet knowing only John's baptism, and disciples at Ephesus close the roll. Tulloch asks how belief lives in deed as well as doctrine.
26837-love-marriage-birth-control-being-:
A speech delivered at the Church Congress at Birmingham in October 1921, with a foreword by Lord Dawson of Penn, published by Nisbet of London in January 1922. Its sections run from an imperious instinct and the church and marriage to the facts of life and the allegiance of the young. They close with passion as a worthy possession, birth control, and the way of happiness. The speaker divides middle-aged people into three classes: those still young, those who forgot they were young, and those never young.

Sex love, the speech argues, is a clamant force that cannot be suppressed, only guided into healthy channels. Marriage best secures the union of body, mind, and spirit joined to love of children. The speech then disputes the view that intercourse is right only for procreation, calling sexual union as an end in itself a condemnation that would leave most couples celibate.
27455-the-radio-boys-at-the-sending-stat:
Allen Chapman, author of The Radio Boys' First Wireless and Ralph of the Roundhouse, wrote this boys' adventure with a foreword by Jack Binns. It was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York with illustrations. It is the third Radio Boys book, after the Ferberton Prize story and the Ocean Point message that saved a ship.

Here the boys work at a sending station and try to make good in the wireless room. Later volumes promise a midnight call at Mountain Pass and a wireless mystery to trail. One illustration shows the time come for Joe to give his recitations. Young readers interested in early radio will find adventure mixed with the new wireless craft.
27502-sketch-of-handel-and-beethoven-two:
The Rev. T. Hanly Ball, curate and lecturer of St. Mary's, Wimbledon, delivered these two lectures in the lecture hall of the Wimbledon Village Club on Monday evening, 14 December 1863, and Monday evening, 11 January 1864. Charles J. Skeet published them in London in 1864, at the request and expense of a parishioner.

Ball dedicates the lectures to John A. Beaumont of Wimbledon Park House, praising him in Seneca's terms as a judicious benefactor. The sketches introduce Handel and Beethoven, their lives and music, to a general village audience. The booklet gives a charming mid-Victorian view of two composers already counted among the great.
28157-a-student-s-history-of-england-v-1:
Samuel R. Gardiner's A Student's History of England, volume one, covers B.C. 55 to A.D. 1509, from Caesar's landing to the end of Henry VII's reign. Gardiner, late fellow of Merton College, Oxford, wrote for school pupils, with 173 pictures and maps in this 1916 reissue. Longmans, Green, and Company published the volume.

Chapters move from Roman Britain through Saxon kings, Norman conquest, and medieval parliaments to the Tudor dawn. Gardiner stresses clear narrative, dates, and causes over legend. The book remains a solid school history of early England, plain enough for students and useful for general readers.
28183-shadow-and-light-an-autobiography-:
Mifflin Wistar Gibbs wrote Shadow and Light in Washington in 1902, with an introduction by Booker T. Washington. Gibbs, born fatherless, worked as carpenter, contractor, anti-slavery lecturer, merchant, railroad builder, mine superintendent, lawyer, judge, and United States consul to Madagascar. His autobiography spans the last and present centuries.

Gibbs says he wrote to help young readers eager for advancement through hard study. Portraits of noted men fill the book, as models living and dead. His life, from slavery's shadow to public office, offers a striking record of Black achievement in nineteenth-century America.
28248-the-testimony-of-the-rocks-or-geol:
Hugh Miller's The Testimony of the Rocks, published in Boston by Gould and Lincoln, treats geology in its bearings on natural and revealed theology. Miller, author of The Old Red Sandstone and Footprints of the Creator, argues that rocks, fossils, and ancient seas speak for a Creator, and that geology need not fight Scripture. Louis Agassiz praised his powers of description.

The book moves through old fields, seas, and strata with vivid, clear prose, aimed at general readers. Miller writes as a working geologist and a believer, not as a pulpit scold. It remains a landmark of Victorian science writing, where faith and geology meet on friendly terms.
28472-patrician-and-plebeian-or-the-orig:
Thomas J. Wertenbaker's Patrician and Plebeian in Virginia, copyrighted in 1910, traces how the social classes of the Old Dominion took shape. Wertenbaker argues that the great Virginia families, the Carters, Ludwells, Burwells, Custises, Lees, and Washingtons, grew up inside the colony. They were not an English upper class simply moved across the sea.

Old letters back him up. Governor Berkeley was struck by Nathaniel Bacon's fine quality, while Governor Nicholson mocked the planters' claims of high birth. Plain planters, Nicholson wrote, knew full well where the great Dons came from. The book remains a classic study of how Virginia's elite truly formed.
28481-history-of-company-f-1st-regiment-:
Charles H. Clarke, a member of Company F, wrote its history from the daily journal he kept during service, publishing it at Newport, Rhode Island, in 1891. Company F, 1st Regiment, Rhode Island Volunteers, was the first company to leave Newport, on April 17, 1861, under the Stars and Stripes.

Clarke begins with Fort Sumter, fired on April 12, and Lincoln's call on April 15 for seventy-five thousand troops to defend Washington. Governor Sprague offered a regiment and a battery, and Colonel George W. Tew recruited his Newport Artillery company from fifty to one hundred men, armed with Springfield rifles and French-pattern sabres. The brief history follows their spring and summer of 1861.
28884-a-history-of-england-from-early-ti:
David Widger edited this linked index to David Hume's History of England, with continuations by Tobias Smollett, E. Farr, and E. H. Nolan. The index covers volume one in six parts. They run from early times to King John, then Henry III to Richard III, Henry VII to Mary, Elizabeth to James I, Charles I to Cromwell, and Charles II to James II. Volumes two and three run from William and Mary to George II, and from George III to Victoria.

The first part lists the Britons, the Romans, the Saxons, and the seven kingdoms, then Egbert, Alfred, Canute, and William the Conqueror. The index gives every chapter and picture, from Boadicea haranguing the Britons to Alfred before the Danish general. Readers get a guide to Hume's classic history and its continuations, spanning Britain from ancient times to Victoria.
29004-english-translations-of-works-of-e:
David Widger edited this index to the English translations of Emile Zola's works, covering the novelist who lived from 1840 to 1902. The index lists the Three Cities trilogy complete, Lourdes, Rome, and Paris, with Fruitfulness, A Zola Dictionary, and the Fête at Coqueville. His masterpiece, The Downfall, The Fortune of the Rougons, and The Fat and the Thin follow.

Later entries include Thérèse Raquin, L'Assommoir, The Dream, Nana, Doctor Pascal, and Abbe Mouret's Transgression. The Lourdes chapters alone run through five days, from pilgrims and patients to Marie's cure and the death of Bernadette. Readers get a map to Zola's great naturalist shelf in English, novel by novel and chapter by chapter.
29215-some-observations-on-the-ethnograp:
Samuel George Morton, author of Crania Americana, published these observations in 1846, extracted from the American Journal of Science. Morton writes about the ethnography and archaeology of the American Aborigines, as Native peoples were then called in scholarship. He opens by praising recent discoveries in American archaeology as monuments of art and contributions to science.

Morton singles out Stephens and Norman for their extraordinary revelations about ancient American peoples. The paper reflects the science of its day, including its now-discredited racial theories, and should be read as a historical document. Readers get a mid-nineteenth-century survey of what explorers and scholars then thought they knew about the continent's first peoples.
29263-the-autobiography-of-sergeant-will:
Sergeant William Lawrence tells his own life in this autobiography, edited by George Nugent Bankes and published in London in 1886. Lawrence, a hero of the Peninsular and Waterloo campaigns, served in the wars against Napoleon. Bankes, author of A Day of My Life at Eton, prepared the soldier's account for print.

Lawrence died at Studland, the preface notes, and his story runs through the campaigns in Spain and Portugal to Waterloo. The book gives a rank-and-file view of war: marching, fighting, and survival, told without an officer's polish. Readers get a soldier's memoir from the Napoleonic wars, direct and unadorned, valuable for its ground-level picture of famous battles.
29324-a-poetical-review-of-the-literary-:
John Courtenay published this poetical review in 1786, on the literary and moral character of the late Samuel Johnson. This Augustan Reprint Society volume, number 133, reprints Courtenay's poem with an introduction by Robert E. Kelley, published by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library in 1969.

Courtenay writes in verse about Johnson the lexicographer, critic, and moralist, weighing his writings and his character together. The poem belongs to the age of Johnson's own friends and rivals, who debated his fame while it was fresh. Readers get an eighteenth-century verse portrait of Johnson, useful for seeing how his contemporaries judged the man behind the Dictionary.
29811-the-two-story-mittens-and-the-litt:
Aunt Fanny, whose real name was Fanny Barrow, printed this book in New York in 1867 as the fourth book of her series. It holds two stories and one little play, told to children as they knit mittens. Twelve pairs were done during the third book, and more were on the way. Some evenings Aunt Fanny could send no story, and the little mother read a book or talked with her children instead.

The contents give More About the Mittens, The Party Lillie Gave for Miss Florence, The Fairy Benevolence, and Master Edward's Trial. George writes delightful letters from camp, read aloud again and again to his eager sisters and brothers. The book mixes homely craft, family talk, and moral tales in the style young readers of the 1860s knew well.
29972-the-fathers-of-confederation-a-chr:
A. H. U. Colquhoun wrote The Fathers of Confederation, a chronicle of the birth of the Dominion, printed in Toronto in 1916. A frontispiece after Robert Harris's painting shows the fathers themselves. Colquhoun dedicates the book to Colonel George T. Denison, whose life-work proves, he says, that loyalty to the Empire is fidelity to Canada. Fourteen chapters carry the story from dawn to dominion.

The dawn of the movement and obstacles to union lead to the eve of confederation, the hour and the men, and the Charlottetown Conference. The Quebec Conference, its results, and the debates of 1865 follow, with rocks in the channel and the battle of union. The framing of the bill, the first Dominion ministry, and the road from sea to sea close a short, clear history for Canadian readers.
30001-on-the-origin-of-clockwork-perpetu:
Derek J. de Solla Price wrote On the Origin of Clockwork, Perpetual Motion Devices and the Compass as paper six in the Contributions from the Museum of History and Technology. Five sections order it: power and motion gearing, mechanical clocks, mechanized astronomical models, perpetual motion and the clock before de Dondi, and the magnetic compass as a fellow-traveler from China.

The clock's ancestor, some have thought, was the sundial. Price argues otherwise: sundial and clock are two different approaches to time-keeping. The clock's true ancestor lies among astronomical machines of great complexity, built since Hellenic times to show the relative motions of the heavenly bodies. Preparing a new hall for the museum on the history of time-keeping would draw on the study's findings, tracing this ancestry back across two thousand years of history on three continents.
3003-wild-flowers-an-aid-to-knowledge-of:
Neltje Blanchan wrote Wild Flowers, also published as Nature's Garden, as a guide to knowing North American wildflowers in the field. The book describes each flower by family, color, season, and habit, so a walker can name what grows beside the path. Entries give size, scent, and leaf shape in plain language rather than technical keys alone.

A trailing arbutus entry, for example, notes pink flowers fading to nearly white, very fragrant, about half an inch across, in few or many clusters. Another describes a straggling bush lower than lambkill, blooming in June with deep rose or lilac clusters. The book remains a friendly introduction to flower study, written for readers who walk and look.
30192-chips-from-a-german-workshop-volum:
F. Max Müller gathers essays chiefly on the science of language in volume 4 of Chips from a German Workshop, published by Scribner's Sons in 1881. An inaugural lecture at Oxford in 1868 defends comparative philology as a branch of academic study, while Rede lectures at Cambridge treat the stratification of language and Curtius on Indo-Germanic chronology. Notes on Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin forms support the arguments in detail.

Later lectures follow the migration of fables from India westward, the results of language science at Strassburg in 1872, and missions preached at Westminster Abbey in 1873. An index to volumes 3 and 4 closes the book, which Müller dedicates to Arthur Penrhyn Stanley, Dean of Westminster. The volume suits readers who want Victorian philology in the voice of its most famous popularizer.
30377-the-adventurers-of-england-on-huds:
Agnes C. Laut writes volume seventeen of the Chronicles of Canada series, The Adventurers of England on Hudson Bay, edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton. The thirty-two volume series moves from first European visitors and the rise of New France through the English invasion, American invasions, and Indigenous peoples in Canada.

Laut's volume centers on the English adventurers who pushed into Hudson Bay country, trading, exploring, and founding a northern enterprise. It fits a national chronicle meant for general readers, pairing short narrative history with illustrations. The book gives a clear, story-driven account of how Hudson Bay became a key stage in Canada's early trade and rivalry.
30758-communism-and-christianism-analyze:
Bishop William Montgomery Brown and his wife set out this short, fiery booklet in Galion, Ohio, with new editions in 1920 and 1921. Brown, once the fifth Bishop of Arkansas, had left the old church path and now praised the ideas of Marx and Engels as a gospel for wage workers. The booklet's sales note calls lying supernaturalism finished, robbing capitalism falling, and saving laborism rising.

Across its pages Brown sets communism and Christian faith side by side, argues that workers face body and soul harm under wage labor, and urges readers to spread the booklet among neighbors. It is frank propaganda, not a calm study, and it shows how one American churchman turned to radical politics after the First World War. Historians of religion and labor will find it a sharp, if one-sided, voice from that moment.
30847-compound-words-a-study-of-the-prin:
Frederick W. Hamilton, educational director of the United Typothetae of America, wrote this 1918 study for apprentices, number thirty-six in the Typographic Technical Series, part six. Its subject is compound words: the principles of compounding, the components of compounds, and the use of the hyphen. Hamilton writes for printers who must decide, line by line, when words join and when they stay apart.

Contents cover an introduction, general principles, accent in compounding, formation and components of compounds, and rules for the hyphen, with supplementary reading and review questions. Hamilton cites three general principles from F. Horace Teall, and shows how a hyphen can mark a special meaning, as in a saw for cutting iron as against a saw made of iron. It is a short, practical guide to a small but fiddly part of English.
30969-the-big-five-motorcycle-boys-on-th:
Ralph Marlow wrote this 1916 boys' war adventure for A. L. Burt in New York, subtitled With the Allies in France. Marlow had already sent the Big Five Motorcycle Boys under fire, to the front, on a swift road chase, through Tennessee wilds, by wireless, and on Florida trails. Here the five boys ride in the country of the Great War, and a picture shows Josh ducking his head at a sudden spiteful crack from the rear.

Chapter one, On the Streets of Antwerp, opens with farewells to Elmer and Rooster. The boys must hurry home and break up their combination just when they have had royal good times in wartime country. A cable message tells Elmer he must go. Marlow mixes motorcycling, comradeship, and war work in the wholesome adventure style of his day, for young readers who love a crew that sticks together.
31172-old-english-poems-translated-into-:
Cosette Faust and Stith Thompson's 1918 volume, published by Scott, Foresman, translates Old English poems into their original meter and adds short selections of Old English prose. Pagan poetry comes first, with Widsith, Deor's Lament, Waldhere, the Fight at Finnsburg, charms, riddles, and Exeter gnomes. Its elegies include The Wanderer, The Seafarer, The Wife's Lament, and The Ruin.

Christian poetry follows, with Caedmon's Hymn, Bede's Death Song, selections from Genesis and Exodus, and the school of Cynewulf, before poems from the Chronicle close the verse. For students, the book offers the earliest English verse in readable, rhythm-faithful form, with prose to show the language beyond poetry.
31563-walladmor-vol-1-of-2-freely-transl:
Walladmor, volume one, presents itself as freely translated into German from the English of Sir Walter Scott. It is now freely translated from the German into English, in two volumes, printed in London for Taylor and Hessey. An epigraph quoted from Massinger speaks of a desolate branch, trampled down, that might have propped a ruined house as a column. The volume's chapters run from chapter one through chapter nine.

The edition's notes explain the real history behind the title page: the three-volume German original was fictitiously attributed to Scott, but was actually written by G. W. H. Häring under the pseudonym of Willibald Alexis, and was freely adapted into English by Thomas De Quincey. Readers thus get a double translation and a literary hoax in one. The novel itself is a romance of Wales and rebellion, in Scott's manner if not by his hand.
31568-walladmor-vol-2-of-2-freely-transl:
Walladmor, volume two, continues the romance presented as freely translated into German from the English of Sir Walter Scott. It is now freely translated from the German into English, printed in London for Taylor and Hessey. Where volume one closed at chapter nine, volume two runs from chapter ten through chapter twenty-one, carrying the story to its close. The same Massinger epigraph, of a desolate branch that might have been a column, heads the volume.

The edition's notes explain, as in volume one, that the German original was fictitiously attributed to Scott, but was actually written by G. W. H. Häring under the pseudonym of Willibald Alexis, and freely adapted into English by Thomas De Quincey. Readers finishing the novel get the second half of a Welsh romance of rebellion and identity.
31618-silver-links-a-collection-of-salut:
W. L. Mason compiled Silver Links. It is a collection of salutatory, valedictory, and other addresses. They were delivered at the first five commencements of the Female Stenographic and Typewriting Class of the General Society of Mechanics and Tradesmen of New York. Albert B. King published it at New York in 1892. Mason inscribes the little volume to Isaac Pitman, the father of phonography, as the compiler respectfully puts it.

The addresses mark the graduations of young women trained in shorthand and typewriting, a new skilled trade for women in the eighteen nineties. Silver Links preserves their public words, salutatory and valedictory alike, as a record of a class finding its voice.
31810-the-everett-massacre-a-history-of-:
Walker C. Smith's history of the Everett Massacre tells the class struggle in the lumber industry of the Pacific Northwest, from the point of view of the Industrial Workers of the World. It is dedicated to the men murdered on the steamer Verona at Everett, Washington, on Sunday, November 5, 1916, in the struggle for free speech, free assembly, and the right to organize.

The opening chapter rejects tales of self-made lumber barons and instead describes theft of public lands, bribery of officials, sabotage of competitors, and coercion of workers through company stores and murder. Readers get a partisan labor history, vivid and angry, that treats Everett as one fragment of a larger industrial war.
32250-american-red-cross-text-book-on-ho:
The American Red Cross Text-Book on Home Hygiene and Care of the Sick, by Jane A. Delano and revised and rewritten by Anne Hervey Strong, was published in Philadelphia by P. Blakiston's Son and Company in 1918. Delano was chairman of the National Committee of the Red Cross Nursing Service and director of its Department of Nursing. She had served as superintendent of the Nurse Corps of the United States Army and of training schools at Bellevue Hospital and the University of Pennsylvania.

Strong, professor of public health nursing at Simmons College in Boston, revised the second edition of Delano and Isabel McIsaac's hygiene text. It was prepared for and endorsed by the American Red Cross. Its first chapter treats causes and prevention of sickness, including communicable diseases, micro-organisms and bacteria, and parasites. Readers get a home-nursing manual, for families caring for the sick at home.
32458-after-two-nights-of-the-ear-ache: Francis Hard's short poem, printed in Weird Tales in October 1937, addresses Sleep after two nights of ear-ache. The speaker has wooed Sleep in vain, since Sleep will not come to banish racking pain. Hard defines Sleep as life in stone bound fast, and as oblivion of the present, the future, and the past, a rest that pain keeps just out of reach.
32608-some-war-time-lessons-the-soldier-:
Frederick Paul Keppel, third assistant secretary of war, gathers three essays on lessons from the Great War, published by Columbia University Press in 1920. The first weighs the conduct of the American soldier, the second tests American scholarship in wartime, and the third asks what the nation has learned.

Keppel treats the army of nearly four million men as a cross-section of American manhood, shaped by a moral purpose and by high standards for drink, disease, and discipline. He then shows scholars solving scores of war problems, from airplane instruments to camouflage detection, and closes by asking what such effort means for peace. Keppel writes as an insider, not a distant critic. His tone is earnest and practical throughout.
32650-some-personal-reminiscences-of-ser:
Colonel Hampton S. Thomas recalls four years as a cavalryman with the Army of the Potomac. He joined the First Pennsylvania Cavalry after a short spell on foot. He writes from his own part in marches, camps, and fights.

The memoir opens at Dranesville in late 1861, where his regiment first met heavy fire. It follows later rides, scouts, and clashes through the war. Thomas keeps the focus on what he saw and did, from raw recruits learning the trade to hard days under fire in the field. His plain account gives weight to small details, such as horses, roads, and orders, that larger histories pass over.
32761-caxton-s-book-a-collection-of-essa:
W. H. Rhodes, known as Caxton, left essays, poems, tales, and sketches that Daniel O'Connell collected after his death, published in San Francisco by A. L. Bancroft and Company in 1876. Rhodes had meant to gather his newspaper and periodical pieces himself, but died before he could.

Many pieces were written for the monthly gatherings of the Bohemian Club, where friends thronged to hear Caxton's wit, keen and sparkling, without malice. Anecdotes that began in absurdity often closed in pathos. The Case of Summerfield, praised for the originality of its plan, was widely copied. Other pieces tell of a burning steamer and a calm judge, and sing St. Patrick, who gave Erin back to God.
32806-christopher-crayon-s-recollections:
James Ewing Ritchie, writing as Christopher Crayon, tells his own life and times, published in London by James Clarke and Company in 1898. Seventeen chapters run from East Anglia in 1837 through village life, college, London long ago, and his literary career to Cardiff, Exeter Hall, men he has known, and a bank gone.

In 1837 Lord Melbourne, the handsomest and most courteous gentleman of the court, guided a young queen, while the Whigs held office but not power. Ritchie recalls a Poor-Law Bill, a peer who called the Bible Society a damned good society, Norfolk daughters swearing in the hunting field, and a Norwich election fought with bribery and drunkenness. Later he recalls college, freehold land societies, and James Taylor of Birmingham.
33113-the-divorce-of-catherine-of-aragon:
J. A. Froude's Divorce of Catherine of Aragon supplements Froude's History of England with a close account of a royal marriage's end. It is subtitled the story as told by the imperial ambassadors resident at the court of Henry VIII and published in New York in 1891. Its first chapter lays out a disputed succession, various claimants, Catherine's inability to have further children, the irregularity of her marriage, papal dispensations, and the first mention of divorce. It also covers the situation of the papacy, Charles V, Wolsey's policy, and an Anglo-French alliance.

Froude builds the narrative from ambassadors' dispatches, letting diplomats who watched Henry's court report intrigue, law, and conscience in their own terms. The result is a history of a divorce that split England from Rome. For students of Tudor history, it remains a source-based study, showing how a personal and dynastic crisis became a European event.
33287-hints-on-the-use-and-handling-of-f:
Lieut. H. Onslow Curling's hints, published in London in 1885, teach the use and handling of firearms in general and the revolver in particular. Curling writes after the National Rifle Association took up military revolver practice in July 1885, a subject long felt to need attention. His motto, never unready, sums up his aim: to make shooters safe, steady, and sure.

The book covers care, loading, aim, and practice, with advice for both service and civilian use. Its tone is practical and plain, aimed at men who would carry a revolver well rather than merely own one. For readers of military history and old shooting manuals, it is a clear window on Victorian ideas of skill, safety, and readiness.
33638-constitution-of-the-state-of-north:
Issued from the North Carolina Secretary of State's office at Raleigh in 1914, this pamphlet prints the Constitution of the State of North Carolina as it then stood. It also prints a copy of the General Assembly act amending it, chapter 81 of the public laws of the extra session of 1913. By direction of the General Assembly, the pamphlet was furnished for distribution to citizens, with proposed amendments and a copy of the official ballot shown from page 39 onward.

The text opens with a preamble. In it the people of North Carolina, thankful that the American Union survived and that their civil, political, and religious freedoms endure, ordain and establish their constitution. A declaration of rights follows. Additional copies could be had from the county clerk of court or the Secretary of State. The pamphlet is a useful primary source for North Carolina constitutional history.
33672-the-essential-faith-of-the-univers:
Harriet Martineau argues for the essential faith of the universal church from the sacred records in this 1833 Boston volume. The book grew from a premium offered in March 1830 by the British and Foreign Unitarian Association for three tracts promoting Christian Unitarianism among Roman Catholics, Jews, and Muslims. Martineau won all three prizes, submitting her essays under sealed names opened only after the decision.

Her epigraph declares that religion is closed to no one and invites all, choosing neither house nor wealth but content with the naked human being. The American edition's advertisement praises her grasp, vigor, felicitous style, and fairness, without asperity.
