The book remains an important early statement of liberal Unitarian theology and of Martineau's powers as a religious writer.
33768-the-middle-english-poem-erthe-upon:
This volume presents the Middle English poem Erthe upon Erthe, a meditation on earth, death, and human vanity, in a scholarly edition with glossary, notes, and variant readings. The poem's refrain returns again and again to earth upon earth, reminding readers that all flesh returns to dust, whatever its rank or wealth. The edition unpacks the poem's difficult Middle English, with yogh, Tironian ampersand, long vowels, and expanded abbreviations explained for modern readers.

Editorial material gives two versions, marked A and B, with line references, footnotes, and a glossary keyed to page and line, so students can follow the text closely. The poem belongs to the tradition of contempt for the world, plain, stern, and memorable. Medievalists and poetry readers will value an accessible, careful edition of a short work that speaks across six centuries with undiminished force.
33858-the-adventurous-simplicissimus-bei:
Hans Jacob Christoph von Grimmelshausen's Adventurous Simplicissimus appears here in its first English edition, limited to one thousand copies, published by William Heinemann in 1912. The facsimile title page of the first German edition, printed at Monpelgart in 1669, presents the description of the life of a strange vagabond named Melchior Sternfels von Fuchshaim. These include how he came into the world, what he saw, learned, experienced, and suffered, and why he willingly quit it.

Grimmelshausen's hero wanders through the Thirty Years' War, from peasant simplicity to courts, camps, and hermitage, in a picaresque tale at once comic and grim. This English version opens the great German novel of the seventeenth century to new readers. Lovers of classic picaresque fiction will find a sprawling, vivid chronicle of war, fortune, folly, and repentance.
34060-prisoners-of-poverty-women-wage-wo:
Helen Campbell wrote this study of women wage-workers, their trades and their lives, published in Boston in 1900 by Little, Brown, with copyright in 1887. Campbell, author of Mrs. Herndon's Income and Miss Melinda's Opportunity, built the chapters from papers for the Sunday New York Tribune, based on minute personal research into the conditions she describes.

Verse epigraphs on giants, light, chains, and freedom open the volume, but the body is plain reporting on women's work and pay. Campbell writes with care for working women and their daily struggle. The book remains a sharp early study of women's labor and poverty.
34187-a-new-banking-system-the-needful-c:
Lysander Spooner wrote this banking tract, printed at Boston in 1873 and sold by A Williams and Company. Its full aim stands in the title: a new banking system to supply the capital needed to rebuild the burnt district. Chapters treat specie payments, price inflation, and the security of the plan.

Spooner argues that real estate can back a vast loanable capital. He puts it at more than twelve times the capital of all the national banks in Massachusetts. He also sets it near the whole paper currency of the United States, greenbacks and national bank notes together. A chapter weighs the true character of the national system, and one prints Amasa Walker's opinion of Spooner's plan. The close urges the system's worth to Massachusetts.
34209-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, volume two, slice seven, is a part-issue of the famous dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. This slice runs from Arundel, Thomas to Athens. Its transcriber's notes explain the typography: numbers following letters were printed as subscripts, and characters after a caret were superscripts. Side-notes were moved to serve as titles of their paragraphs.

The articles listed include Arundel the town, the Arval Brothers, the Aryan article, Asa, Asafetida, and Asbestos. Asbjörnsen the tale-collector, Assam and Assamese, Assassin and Assaying fill the later columns. A second list preserved in the copy runs on: Ascension, Assisi, Roger Ascham, Association of Ideas, Asclepiades the Greek physician, and Assumpsit. The eleventh edition of 1910 and 1911 was the Britannica at its scholarly height, written by named experts.
3430-the-suitors-of-yvonne-being-a-porti:
Rafael Sabatini presents this romance as part of the memoirs of a French adventurer in the age of Cardinal Mazarin. The chapter titles tell the shape of the plot: a boy drinks too much wine, a fight breaks out in the horse market, fair rescuers intervene, and Mazarin himself turns matchmaker. Love sickness, a whip used as argument, and a rescue follow.

At the center stands Yvonne, courted by rival suitors while her family and the Cardinal maneuver around her. The narrator's fortunes rise and fall with duels, disguises, and sudden reversals. Sabatini writes with speed and color, and the book suits readers who like cloak and sword romance set among real figures of seventeenth century France.
34333-captain-ted-a-boy-s-adventures-amo:
Captain Ted: A Boy's Adventures Among Hiding Slackers in the Great Georgia Swamp, by Louis Pendleton, was published by D Appleton and Company at New York in 1918. Pendleton, who also wrote King Tom and the Runaways, inscribes the story to the fighting youth of America.

The illustrations promise hand-to-hand combat and creatures closing in each other's grip, drawing nearer. Ted and his friend Hubert open the tale, which sends a brave and devoted boy among the draft evaders hiding in the swamp. A wild cry and a jump that comes too late mark the climax pictured at page 270.
34350-a-manual-of-elementary-geology-or-:
Sir Charles Lyell wrote a Manual of Elementary Geology, or the ancient changes of the earth and its inhabitants as illustrated by geological monuments. John Murray in London issued a fourth and entirely revised edition in eighteen fifty two. Five hundred woodcuts aid the text. A front plate shows strata of red sandstone resting on vertical schist at Siccar Point. A Playfair line on Hutton heads the plate, on the abyss of time.

Lyell had earlier written Principles of Geology and Travels in North America. It is a philosophy which never rests, its law is progress, an Edinburgh Review line heads the book. The manual teaches strata, fossils, volcanoes, and the slow shaping of the earth for beginners. Chapters move from rocks and minerals to the ages of life. Students get the classic uniformitarian textbook in one volume.
34531-the-pilgrim-s-shell-or-fergan-the-:
Eugene Sue wrote The Pilgrim's Shell, or Fergan the Quarryman. Daniel De Leon translated it from the French for a labor press. The Labor News company at New York put it out in 1904. Its tale is from the feudal times, the title page says. The translator's preface places the book in a vast series.

Sue wrote in French a monumental work, the Mysteries of the People. It is a work of fiction, yet the best universal history extant, De Leon holds. It traces the systems of class-rule in their succession. The struggle between the contending classes fills its episodes, he adds. Law and religion serve each tyrant class in turn. The mistakes of the toilers in their struggles stand recorded there. Fergan the quarryman is one of that majestic series of novels. Sue gives a feudal tale of the people's long fight.
34613-woman-s-work-in-english-fiction-fr:
Woman's Work in English Fiction is a literary history by Clara Whitmore, published by Putnam of New York and London in 1910. It runs from the Restoration to the mid-Victorian period. Whitmore wrote it as a survey of the women who built the English novel.

The contents proceed by author. Margaret Cavendish, Aphra Behn, and Mary Manley open the story. Sarah Fielding, Eliza Haywood, and Charlotte Lennox follow, and Frances Burney receives a chapter alone. Hannah More, Charlotte Smith, the Gothic writers, Maria Edgeworth, and Jane Porter fill the middle chapters. The introduction notes how few women's names appear in the records of the past. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
34668-the-young-yagers-a-narrative-of-hu:
The Young Yagers is a hunting adventure narrative by Captain Mayne Reid. Ticknor and Fields published it at Boston; this edition is dated 1857. Its subtitle places the adventures in Southern Africa. Chapter one shows the camp of the young yagers. The camp stands near where the Yellow and Orange rivers meet. Babylonian willows fringe both shores as far as the eye can reach.

Reid pauses over the weeping willow before the tale starts. In England it emblems sorrow and drapes the tomb, he writes. In dry Southern Africa it signals water, and so means joy. Laughter rings across the river from the camp under its shade. The young hunters sit around a camp fire at night. Reid promises their portraits by its light in turn. Reid's African tales taught geography through the rifle and the camp.
34889-reminiscences-incidents-battles-ma:
Barrett, late a lieutenant of Company B, wrote these reminiscences of the Old 4th Michigan Infantry in the War of the Rebellion, from 1861 to 1864. Ostler published the book at Detroit in 1888, and Barrett dedicated it to the survivors of the regiment: hope for the living, tears for the dead. The regiment was organized at Adrian and mustered in on June 20, 1861, for three years, under Colonel Woodbury, with 1025 officers and men.

The ladies of Adrian gave the regiment its flag, and Cleveland's papers praised the splendidly equipped Michigan men on their way to Washington. Barrett remembers the first hardtack, round and tough as a prohibitionist's conscience, and boys sailing the crackers from the car platforms. Such regimental books kept the war of the ranks alive when the generals' versions were done.
34909-ancient-chinese-account-of-the-gra:
Alexander M'Allan wrote a curious tract, copyrighted at Brooklyn in 1913, arguing that ancient Chinese records describe America. He begins with the old Chinese tale of a place of ten suns, where ten suns rose and shone together. Scoffers, he says, call those writers liars.

Yet Arctic explorers of his own day report five suns at once, an effect the dictionaries call a parhelion. M'Allan then turns to maps: Chinese sages place a mulberry land ten thousand miles east, over three thousand miles wide, which he reads as North America. The Mexicans, he notes, pictured that continent as a tree. Grand Canyon and Colorado course are tied into his scheme.
34994-morning-and-evening-prayers-for-al:
John Habermann wrote Morning and Evening Prayers for All Days of the Week, a German prayer book long treasured in its homeland. Emil Rausch, editor of the Lutheran Herald, put it into English for the Wartburg Publishing House in Chicago, in printings from 1918 to 1920. Habermann, who died in 1590, served as superintendent at Zeitz and knew Hebrew deeply.

The translator's preface praises the prayers as the fruit of a rich inner life, steeped in the language of the Bible and above all the Psalms. The book gives prayers for each morning and evening of the week, plus prayers for confession, communion, and other occasions, with hymns for the same hours. Because the great war was raging, Rausch added a set of prayers for times of war. Readers get a full manual of daily devotion, carried from German Lutheran homes into English ones.
35397-christmas-stories-containing-john-:
Christmas Stories holds three moral tales, John Wildgoose the Poacher, The Smuggler, and Good Nature, or Parish Matters. W Baxter at Oxford printed the book in eighteen twenty three for J Parker and for F C and J Rivington in London. The first tale is called The History of John Wildgoose. A short note dated January twenty seventh, eighteen twenty one, states the aim of that tale.

The note says the author long wished to warn folk of the evil and risk of poaching. Poaching, he holds, leads on to base habits and grave crimes. Tale and talk, he thought, would teach more than a plain lecture. Thomas Wildgoose, an honest, hard working man, waits to wed Susan Jenkins till he has a house and means. The book stands in the line of Trimmer tales and Cheap Repository Tracts for the poor.
35594-the-radio-boys-at-ocean-point-or-t:
The Radio Boys at Ocean Point, or The Message That Saved the Ship, is a boys' tale by Allen Chapman. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty two. It stands in a set of tales of boys and the new wave craft. A first word by a famed wave man leads the book in. The front plate shows the hard, hot work of the raise of the air wire.

The set list at the front gives the kin tales of the book. The first wave tale tells of a prize won by the boys. Tales of a hill pass, of a send room, and of a voice trailed on the waves stand past it. The same hand's rail tales are list as well.
35612-three-philosophical-poets-lucretiu:
George Santayana, professor of philosophy at Harvard, wrote Three Philosophical Poets, published at Cambridge in 1910 as the first volume of Harvard Studies in Comparative Literature. The book studies three poets who each built a whole view of the world into verse: Lucretius, Dante, and Goethe.

On Lucretius, Santayana traces Greek cosmology through Democritus and the moral turn Epicurus gave it. He weighs the melancholy of materialism and calls Lucretius a true poet of nature. On Dante, he treats Platonism, Beatrice, and the scheme of virtues and vices in the Divine Comedy. The last study takes up Goethe's Faust, the romantic spirit, and the Renaissance ideals behind the legend. Santayana writes as a philosopher who loved poetry, ranking these three as its supreme world-builders.
35663-two-addresses-one-to-the-gentlemen:
A Catholic priest of Ugthorpe wrote these two addresses in 1851. Horne and Richardson printed the pamphlet at Whitby for one shilling. One address goes to Whitby gentlemen who called a queen meeting. The meeting answered the late so called aggression of the Pope.

The second address speaks to the Protestant clergy of the land. A dedication thanks Yorkshire Catholic gentlemen for their York stand. They faced sneers and threats for their faith, he writes warmly. Loyalty to the sovereign stood beside their faith, he adds. Two verse mottos on blazing light and naked truth front the pamphlet title page.
35750-history-of-roman-literature-from-i:
John Dunlop surveys old letters in a History of Roman Literature, from its earliest period to the Augustan Age, in two volumes. Littell of Philadelphia and Carvill of New York print this first volume in 1827, from the last London edition. Dunlop had writ the History of Fiction.

His preface grants Rome its due. Few subjects have drawn more laborious volumes than the history and antiquities of Rome, he writes. Its foreign policy, its civil constitution, and even the domestic manners of its citizens have been profoundly investigated. The mysterious origin of Rome, veiled in fable, and its stupendous increase of power, hold all enlightened nations. But less attention has been paid to the history of its literature, he holds, than to that of any other country. That gap is his field.
35751-history-of-roman-literature-from-i:
A History of Roman Literature, from its earliest period to the Augustan age, is a scholarly work by John Dunlop. Dunlop also wrote a history of fiction. This second of two volumes follows the last London edition and was issued in America in 1827. Its contents list the fields of Roman writing one by one.

Agriculture comes first, with Cato and Varro, then history, with a line of named writers. An appendix and tables place poets and playwrights in their order, from the earliest names to Catullus. The text opens with a general claim about all nations. Poetic making, Dunlop holds, is used and improved before prose in almost every state. Imagination spreads sooner than reason, he argues, and early speech best suits the aims of verse.
35998-manual-of-the-enumeration-a-text-b:
Manual of the Enumeration is a textbook on the sciences of the Enumeration, by C J Coffman of Los Angeles. Coffman is styled Dean of the Enumeration on the title page. The book was copyrighted in nineteen twenty seven and printed in the United States. It is meant for personal study or classroom use by teacher and pupil alike.

Two Bible verses stand on the title page as mottoes. The general contents list tables of the system, explained first. Definitions from numerology follow, then astrological influences. Later items treat the meaning, value, and colour of each planet and name. Soul path, personality, destiny, and public appearance are all covered in the scheme. Charts and numbered sections carry the system through the book.
36613-the-kentuckian-in-new-york-or-the-:
A Virginian wrote The Kentuckian in New-York, or The Adventures of Three Southerns, issued in New York in 1834. This copy holds Volume I of two. The title page quotes Burns, that the tale may turn out a song or a sermon. The tale opens late in summer at Harper's Ferry, on a cool southern morning.

Two travellers leave the main hotel with a stately southern slave in attendance. An old ferryman in his flat-bottomed boat spots them as men from the far South. Victor Chevillere leads a fine southern horse into the boat and stands facing the ferryman. He is about twenty-three, well formed, and fashionably dressed. Early experience has already left a grave calm on his bold face.
36741-astronomy-with-an-opera-glass-a-po:
Astronomy with an Opera-Glass, by Garrett Serviss, is a popular guide to the starry heavens for readers with no telescope. Published by Appleton in New York in a third edition, the book assumes only an opera-glass or field-glass and eyes of average quality. Serviss promises that everything he describes was seen by him with such an instrument from the latitude of New York.

Maps and directions help the reader find the constellations and the principal stars visible to the naked eye. Serviss mixes practical guidance with the facts and lore of each object, keeping the detail light enough not to scare off beginners. The guide became a classic of amateur astronomy, proof that serious sky watching could start with the humblest of instruments.
36860-the-ple-biscite-or-a-miller-s-stor:
The Plebiscite, or A Miller's Story of the War, is a novel by Erckmann-Chatrian, translated from the French. Scribner's Sons published this edition in New York in 1911. It belongs to a series called Historical Romances of France. The byline credits one of the seven and a half million who voted yes. An introductory note ties the tale to the plebiscite of 1870. That vote gave an air of popular approval to the Imperial regime in France. War with Prussia followed that vote with great speed.

The note describes the web of chicane and corruption behind the result. Illustrations show grapeshot mowing men down in the war. One frontispiece line reads, he robbed you, that's all. A miller tells the story of the war from his own place in it. The novel joins peasant life to national collapse. It is the French pair's tale of the Franco-Prussian War.
36971-the-captured-scout-of-the-army-of-:
H Clay Trumbull wrote The Captured Scout of the Army of the James. Nichols and Noyes issued the sketch at Boston in eighteen sixty nine. Sergeant Henry H Manning of the Twenty Fourth Massachusetts is its man. Trumbull had served three years as a chaplain near that regiment.

A Massachusetts boyhood and a noble bent open Manning’s short life tale. James Island and the Charleston siege works mark his soldier years. He chose scout duty in the Virginia campaign of the late war. Capture, a dungeon, and the gallows threat fill his darkest span. Escape, recapture, and bloodhounds tear at his prison road home. Andersonville’s horrors stand in that grim march of prisons. Loyal still in rebel ranks, then free with friends, he rose in rank. Home, Andover study, failing health, and rest at last close the tale.
37000-the-proper-limits-of-the-governmen:
The Proper Limits of the Governments Interference with the Affairs of the East-India Company is a tract by John, Earl of Stair. It came out at London in seventeen eighty-four, in a time of strain for the realm. A long stage quote on the fair form of a just cause heads the work. The tract seeks to set the bounds of state meddling in that great trade house.

The Earl opens with the cost of peace for the state, which he puts past sixteen and a half million pounds a year at the least. Gains of the crown, he says, scarce past twelve million in the best years. From that gap he draws the need of a fund past wars and great needs, and of a peace tax past eighteen million a year.
37082-a-short-view-of-the-laws-now-subsi:
A Short View of the Laws Now Subsisting with Respect to the Powers of the East India Company is a legal tract printed at London in 1767. Its subject is narrow and hotly argued: how far the Company may borrow money under its seal and run up debts in trade. The writer says false views on the point have been spread with care, and he writes to set the misled right.

He works through the governing statute, passed under William the Third, clause by clause. The law, he shows, lets the Company borrow for its trade under seal, but bars it from letting its debts outrun its funds. Dividends paid beyond that line, he notes, fall on those who took them.
3731-disturbances-of-the-heart-discussio:
Oliver Osborne wrote this medical book for doctors facing the most common grave illness of his day, disease of the heart. It works through the organ chamber by chamber, valve by valve, and explains how narrowed openings, stiffened cusps, and scarred tissue change the way blood moves. Each fault gets its signs at the bedside, its course over time, and the treatment then in use, with diet, rest, and drugs weighed in turn.

Long passages deal with endocarditis, the inflammation of the heart lining that often follows acute illness and may heal without a trace or may leave a valve unable to open or close. Osborne writes in a plain clinical style, with cases rather than theory in the foreground. The book now serves as a record of cardiology before modern surgery, useful to students of medical history and to curious lay readers with patience for detail.
37340-the-clan-fraser-in-canada-souvenir:
Alexander Fraser's The Clan Fraser in Canada, a souvenir of the gathering at Toronto on May 5th, 1894, was printed by the Mail Job Printing Company at Toronto in 1895. Fraser's prefatory note says the volume aims to furnish, in concise and inexpensive form, information about the Clan Fraser not readily accessible to clansmen in Canada.

The book is essentially an account of the first annual gathering held by the clan in the province of Ontario, published under the auspices of the Clan Fraser in Canada. Its contents move from Fraser's Highlanders and the formation of the clan in Canada to the first annual clan dinner and its toasts. The toasts treat the origin of the clan and of the name Fraser, and the succession of the chiefs. The volume closes with the constitution and by-laws of the clan.
37615-ocean-to-ocean-on-horseback-being-:
Ocean to Ocean on Horseback is a travel narrative by Captain Willard Glazier. It tells the story of a tour in the saddle from Atlantic to Pacific. Glazier was a cavalry veteran whose earlier books sold by subscription. Three Years in the Federal Cavalry heads the list of his popular works.

The subtitle promises more than a diary of the road. Early history and development of cities along the route are included. Towns beyond the Mississippi receive the same attention in his plan. Incidents, anecdotes, and adventures of the journey fill out the matter. Glazier had meant to publish soon after returning from California in 1876. A variety of circumstances, he explains, compelled him to postpone the task. His journal waited while other pressing duties claimed his years.
37942-a-tale-of-the-kloster-a-romance-of:
Brother Jabez wrote a romance of the German mystics of the Cocalico. The book came out in Philadelphia in 1904. Frank McKernan drew the pictures. A verse by Johann Conrad Beissel heads the book in English dress. Beissel led the lone band of brothers and sisters at the Kloster.

The tale is given to the author's mother in warm words. Its folk seek God in a quiet, lone life apart. Faith, love, and hope are their staff, the verse says. A queen of roses holds court in one drawn scene. Past and faith fans get a rare tale of Ephrata life. The tone stays soft and grave.
38005-psyche:
Louis Couperus wrote Psyche, a fairy tale of a small winged princess. B S Berrington turned the Dutch book into English prose. Alston Rivers issued it in London in nineteen hundred eight. Twelve plates by Dion Clayton Calthrop grace the dream tale.

Three hundred towers crown the king’s castle on its basalt rock. The pile spreads for miles like a town lost in the high clouds. A torrent foams below it in a gulf that turns the head to view. Psyche, with her tiny wings, roams the high walls from tower to tower. She sits in a nook with knees drawn up, like a still moth at rest. Past each bright rim of sky a new rim waits, on and on for aye. Green vales with sheep, ships on canals, and corn fields lie below. In the world there is nothing more than a story, its motto runs.
38017-schools-school-books-and-schoolmas:
Schools, School Books and Schoolmasters is prefaced, in the head, by a select list of works by William Carew Hazlitt, chronologically arranged from 1860 to 1888. His history of the Venetian republic heads the list: four volumes, with maps and illustrations, from 1860.

Old English jest books, edited with introductions and notes, follow. Remains of the early popular poetry of England, in four volumes with woodcuts, comes next. A handbook to the early popular, poetical, and dramatic literature of Great Britain is listed at over seven hundred pages. Bibliographical collections and notes comprise a full description of about six thousand early English books, from the books themselves. Hazlitt was the great Victorian bibliographer of old English literature. The work behind this front matter applies his learning to education history. Readers get his contribution to the history of English schooling, school books, and masters.
38146-mr-punch-on-the-warpath-humours-of:
Mr Punch on the Warpath picks the best war jokes from Punch for the Punch Library of Humour. Hammerton edits the set, which mines the comic paper from its start in 1841. The theme here is the army, the navy, and the reserve forces.

One hundred and thirty six drawings fill the book. The artists named include Reginald Cleaver, Caton Woodville, and Tom Browne, with George du Maurier, Phil May, and Charles Keene among the rest. A front joke has a general ask the use of cavalry in modern war. The reply: to give tone to a mere brawl. Soldiers and sailors bear the wit with good grace.
38404-a-journey-from-prince-of-wales-s-f:
Samuel Hearne tells his journey from Hudson Bay to the Northern Ocean. The Champlain Society printed this new form in Toronto in 1911. Tyrrell adds a front essay, notes, and plates to the journal. Just five hundred copies went to members and subscribing libraries.

Hearne sought a vast copper store told of by native peoples there. Twice he failed, but the third try reached the Coppermine River mouth. The trip ran through the years 1769 to 1772 in hard country. His is the first kept account of such a trek from the bay.
38431-the-corner-house-girls-snowbound-h:
The Corner House Girls Snowbound, by Grace Brooks Hill, was copyrighted in 1919 by Barse and Hopkins of New York, with illustrations by Thelma Gooch. It is one of a series about the Kenway sisters of the old Corner House in Milton. Chapter one is called A Ghost and a Goat, and opens with feet tramping up and down the back stairs.

Dot Kenway objects to calling the big heated room a nursery, since the girls never had a nurse: Ruth helped bring the younger ones up after their mother died. Her sister Tess agrees it should be the playroom. Twenty five chapters promise a straw ride, twins and trouble, and a village on the ice. A run into the wilderness, a timber cruiser, and a cave with primitive housekeeping follow. A boy named Rafe, who is cross, has a chapter of his own.
38823-clayton-s-quaker-cook-book-being-a:
H J Clayton wrote Clayton's Quaker Cook Book, printed at San Francisco in 1883 by the Women's Co-operative Printing Office. The full title calls it a working treatise on the cook's art for all classes. Clayton says the book holds the fruit of a life of work feeding fine tastes. Plain, clear steps are the pledge.

The front note owns that many cook books exist. Clayton holds that room stays for one more of a plain, daily kind. The aim is food that is sound, tasty, and full of strength. Both plain and rich dishes are in scope. The book speaks to home cooks who want clear help, not show. Its Quaker name points to plain worth over fuss.
39009-the-history-of-the-great-and-might:
The History of the Great and Mighty Kingdom of China is the Hakluyt Society edition of Mendoza's history of China. The society first issued it in 1854, and it was reprinted in New York in 1970. Mendoza, a Spanish friar, wrote the first great European book on China. He drew on the reports of travellers and missionaries of the fifteen hundreds.

The head of this text is given to the Hakluyt Society itself: its president, Sir Roderick Murchison, its vice-presidents, and its council. Admirals, geographers, and scholars fill the lists. The society existed to print rare accounts of voyages and travels. Mendoza's China was the wonder of its age: an empire of cities, canals, printing, and exams, described for readers who would never see it. The reprint keeps that first window on China in circulation.
39055-the-trial-of-henry-hetherington-on:
Henry Hetherington printed a full report of his own trial for a foul libel on faith, held in London in 1840. The trial sat on Tuesday, December 8, 1840, with Lord Denman and a picked jury. Hetherington sold books at a shop in the Strand. The charge grew from his sale of a work called Letters to the Clergy by Haslam.

The book gives the charge in full, with its three counts set out. A man named Bult opened the case for the Crown. The plea in his own cause then fills most of the book, with all its cited laws at full length. A piece from The Sun sheet and a verse to Lord Denman close the work. Hetherington gave the book to James Watson, a book man and friend of free speech. The price was sixpence.
39083-the-iron-boys-in-the-mines-or-star:
James Mears wrote a boys' novel of mine work, issued at Philadelphia in 1912, in his Iron Boys series. Stephen Rush, a slight lad of sixteen, asks to see Carrhart, the head of a mining firm, and is blocked by a rude office boy. He wants a job, and he means to get one.

Steve and his mate Bob start at the bottom of the shaft, two thousand feet down. Chapters bring a missed hole, a wrecked drift, a flood, and a search for a lost boy. The boys expose a plot and earn their first step up. Young readers get mine work shown as hard, risky, and worth doing well.
39090-travelers-five-along-life-s-highwa:
Travelers Five Along Life's Highway is a story book by Annie Fellows Johnston. The front pages list her works, led by the famed Little Colonel set. Those tales of a small Kentucky girl ran to eleven cloth volumes in all. Johnston's books sold at set prices, boxed as gifts for young readers. The title page names the five who travel life's road in this tale.

Jimmy, Gideon, and Wiggan stand among the named folk of the title. Johnston wrote for girls and boys in a warm, plain home style. Her Cosy Corner set held short tales at fifty cents each in cloth. Names like Ole Mammy's Torment and Cicely fill that cheaper line of hers. The Little Colonel's Good Times Book and Doll Book round out the list. This volume sits in that same shelf of tales for the young.
39285-william-shakespere-of-stratford-on:
Scott Surtees's William Shakespere of Stratford-on-Avon, printed by Henry Gray in London in 1888 at 2s in cloth, argues that the Stratford man did not write the plays. Its subtitle promises his epitaph unearthed and the author of the plays run to ground. Surtees opens on the gravestone doggerel: a man, he says, cannot be believed the author of the plays who left such verses to be fathered on his memory.

The chapters handle the epitaphs and the chairs at Stratford, the strange marriage licence, and the later home at New Place. A central chapter asks who wrote Shakespeare's plays, and guesses at the truth. A supplement takes up Donnelly and the cryptogram, the cipher case for another author. Surtees, a clergyman of Dinsdale-on-Tees, builds his brief from the records of the life: the early marriage, the poaching warrant, and the retirement to New Place.
39356-the-political-doctrines-of-sun-yat:
The Political Doctrines of Sun Yat-sen is a scholarly exposition by Paul Myron Anthony Linebarger, of the Department of Government at Harvard University. The Johns Hopkins Press first published it in 1937, and Greenwood Press reprinted it in 1973. Linebarger sets out to explain the San Min Chu I, Sun's Three Principles of the People.

The chapters first lay the background: nation and state in Chinese antiquity, the Confucian world-society, and the impact of the West. Then come the three principles in turn. Nationalism is traced from the rise of the Chinese race-nation. Democracy is unpacked through five justifications, the three natural classes of men, and the split between power and ability. The last principle, Min Shêng or livelihood, gets its own theory and programs. The book remains a standard guide to Sun's thought in English.
39385-the-jester-s-sword-how-aldebaran-t:
Annie Johnston wrote this tale of Aldebaran, a king son, and a sheathed sword. The book came out in Boston in 1908 with the Page Company. It stands in her small Johnston Jewel set of tales. A quote from Stevenson on renouncing heads the tale.

Aldebaran was named for his birth in Mars month, ruled by war. The sword of conquest stays sheathed as the tale unfolds its point. The theme is strength held back by will and grace. Johnston writes for old and young in a clear fairy tone. The tale belongs to the Johnston Jewel Series of small cloth books.
39747-a-manual-of-ancient-history-partic:
A Manual of Ancient History is a handbook of the ancient world by Heeren, professor of history at the University of Goettingen. It treats the governments, trade, and colonies of the states of old times. The text here is the second edition in English, corrected and improved, printed at Oxford in 1833 and translated from the German.

The translator's preface praises German historians for first making history manuals and matching time tables. It singles out Heeren's wide range of inquiry and care for detail. Heeren spent much of his life lecturing on these subjects and went to the first sources for his facts, which gives the manual its weight as a study aid.
40698-address-to-the-people-of-the-unite:
Printed in St. Louis in 1855, this address sets out the case of a pro-slavery convention held at Lexington, Missouri, in July of that year. The writers speak for citizens in the Missouri counties that border Kansas. They say that part of the state held fifty thousand slaves, valued at about twenty-five millions of dollars, half the state's slave population.

The address praises the soil, climate and hemp trade of those counties, and warns how Kansas affects their wealth and safety. Read today, it is a stark record of how slavery's defenders argued their cause in public, in plain economic terms, on the eve of wider conflict.
40966-the-trial-of-jesus-from-a-lawyer-s:
The Trial of Jesus from a Lawyer's Standpoint, volume one, by Walter Chandler of the New York bar, came out in 1908. This volume treats the Hebrew trial. Plates show works by Rembrandt, Durer, and da Vinci, among others. Part one asks if the Gospel accounts can stand as a record of fact. It tests the writers by legal rules for proof.

Part two sets out Hebrew criminal law in five chapters. Topics run from the Mosaic code and the Talmud to courts, judges, and witnesses. Part three, called the brief, takes up set questions one by one. It asks if the Great Sanhedrin could try a capital case under Roman rule. Chandler writes as a lawyer weighing an old case.
40967-the-trial-of-jesus-from-a-lawyer-s:
Walter M Chandler of the New York bar wrote this legal study of the trial of Jesus, printed by the Empire Publishing Company of New York in 1908. The part held here is volume two, The Roman Trial. Munkacsy's Christ Before Pilate fronts the book, with plates of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate, and the Crucifixion after Munkacsy and Doré.

Chapters weigh the twofold jurisdiction, the number of regular trials, and the powers and duties of Pilate. Roman forms of trial in capital cases and Roman punishments follow, then the Roman law that bore on the case. Chandler opens by granting the Hebrew trial done and the Roman begun, under the two mightiest jurisdictions of the earth.
41169-sharps-and-flats-a-complete-revela:
John Nevil Maskelyne, the stage conjurer, wrote a complete revelation of the secrets of cheating at games of chance and skill, published at London in 1894. Its frontispiece shows the detection of Kepplinger, the great master-cheat, seized and searched, with the most ingenious holdout ever devised found upon him.

Chapters expose common sharpers and their tricks, marked cards and how they are used, reflectors, holdouts, and sleight manipulation. Collusion, the game of faro, prepared cards, and dice each take their turn. High ball poker, roulette, and the sporting-houses close the survey. Maskelyne addresses the book, with Carlyle's blessing, to the majority that includes all gamblers.
41410-dick-hamilton-s-football-team-or-a:
Howard R Garis wrote Dick Hamilton's Football Team, dated nineteen twelve, a tale of a young millionaire on the gridiron. Garis had written Dick Hamilton's Fortune and other books in the series. The tale opens with cadets in an uproar over a letter.

A fat, good-natured cadet holds the letter while friends call it a direct insult. They joke of challenging the writers to a sham battle instead. Chapters bring Dick's plan, practice, coaches, and a try-out. An accusation and a midnight alarm stir the school. Games with Dunkirk and Blue Hill test the team. Treachery, a desperate race, and a winning touchdown close the listed heads. Uncle Ezra arrives to complicate matters.
41443-the-audiencia-in-the-spanish-colon:
Charles Henry Cunningham wrote this study of the high court of the Spanish lands past the sea, printed at Berkeley in 1919. He taught the tale of the past at the University of Texas. The case put to proof is the court of Manila, from 1583 to 1800. The list of parts maps the work. A first part treats of the courts of the Spanish lands in the main. A next part tells of the set-up of the court of Manila in its first years.

The heart of the book is the work of that court. Parts treat of its work as a court of law, and of the set probe of a judge at the end of his term. More parts treat of its near-court work and its work of rule.
41920-the-moths-of-the-british-isles-sec:
Richard South describes the moths of the British Isles in a second series issued in London and New York in 1909. South edited The Entomologist and had already written on British butterflies. This volume covers the families from Noctuidae to Hepialidae.

Across both series more than seven hundred and fifty species are pictured and described, with eggs, caterpillars, chrysalids, and food plants drawn as well. South notes in his preface that the mass of small micro moths is left for a later work. He thanks fellow workers for rare specimens lent for the plates and for fine colored drawings. Names and order follow the newer practice of his day, kept close to the old. Readers get a full field guide to Britain's larger moths in a popular form.
42360-the-hart-and-the-water-brooks-a-pr:
John Macduff wrote this practical exposition of the forty-second Psalm, published in London in 1860. Macduff was author of 'Morning and Night Watches' and 'Memories of Gennesaret' among other devotional books. The title takes its image from the psalm's opening, of a hart panting after the water-brooks.

Two quotes at the front call the psalm precious and soul-comforting in strong terms. One comes from a life of Harrington Evans, the other from a life of Captain Hammond. Macduff opens the psalm verse by verse for troubled readers, drawing comfort for sorrow, distance from God and longing for worship restored.
42551-the-history-of-the-great-and-might:
The History of the Great and Mighty Kingdom of China, in its second volume, is an early European account of China. The Padre Juan Gonzalez de Mendoza compiled the original work. The text follows the early English translation made by Parke. George Staunton edited this edition, with an introduction by Major.

The Hakluyt Society first issued the edition in the eighteen-fifties. Burt Franklin of New York later reprinted it in a reference series. Mendoza gathered his history from the reports of Spanish friars and soldiers. Friar Martin de Herrada, an Augustinian leader in the Philippines, heads those witnesses. His companion, another friar, and the soldiers who went with them add their testimony. What they saw and learned in that kingdom fills the first part. The volume is a foundation document of European knowledge about China.
42680-sixty-years-in-southern-california:
Sixty Years in Southern California, by Harris Newmark, was published in 1916. The Knickerbocker Press issued it at New York, with 150 illustrations. Two sons edited their father's reminiscences: Maurice Newmark and Marco Newmark. A memorial page opens the book. Harris Newmark died on April 4, 1916, aged eighty one and more. The contents run year by year from 1853. Childhood and youth, 1834 to 1853, come first.

The road west ran through New York and Nicaragua to the Golden Gate. First adventures in Los Angeles fill 1853: lawyers, merchants, and the old plaza. The rush for gold and a great horse race mark 1855. Rancho domains, orchards, bandidos, and marriage follow. Newmark writes the merchant's memory of a city growing up.
43151-cartouche:
Cartouche, by Frances Peard, stands in a Leipzig edition of 1879. Tauchnitz published the novel there. Chapter one is called Love Me, Love My Dog. A young Englishman walks through Florence from the station. He stops before a small house near the Cascine, in view of the Arno. Green shutters and striped awnings brighten its white walls. He calls a name: Cartouche. No answer comes, and he calls again. A dull thud answers from the right. A great black poodle has jumped from an upper window. The dog recovers at once and breaks into wild welcome.

Leaping, barking, and rushing about, it nearly upsets its friend. Jack Ibbetson warns it not to try the jump too often. The house, he finds, was built to an English fancy under Italian skies.
43283-the-correspondence-of-madame-princ:
The Correspondence of Madame, Princess Palatine is a volume of letters from the court of Louis the Fourteenth, printed at Boston in 1899 in a limited Versailles edition. The letters are those of Madame, mother of the Regent, of Marie-Adelaide of Savoy, and of Madame de Maintenon, in relation to Saint-Cyr. Sainte-Beuve wrote the introductions, and Katharine Prescott Wormeley selected and translated the letters.

The contents run by years. Madame's letters are grouped from 1695 to 1722, the year of her death. The letters of Marie-Adelaide, duchess of Burgundy, follow. Madame's letters are among the great documents of the French court: shrewd, funny, and unsparing, written home to Germany across fifty years. Maintenon's letters on Saint-Cyr, her school for poor girls of good family, close the design. Three women's hands describe one court.
43416-rambles-in-rome-an-arch-ological-a:
Rambles in Rome is a guide book by Russell Forbes on Roman antiquities. Forbes lectured on Roman antiquities as his calling in the city. This fifth edition guides visitors to museums, galleries, and villas there. Churches and antiquities of Rome and the Campagna complete its scope. Spurgeon praised it as a high class companion and guide for travellers.

Try it, that quote urges, and see the difference from trade books. Mere guide books produced to sell lack its chatty, masterly touch. Forbes walks the visitor street by street through the eternal city. Forums, baths, and country roads outside the walls fill its rambles. Transcriber notes record small fixes to names in the old text.
43646-female-warriors-vol-1-of-2-memoria:
Ellen Clayton, who wrote Queens of Song, gathered these lives of women who fought. Tinsley Brothers printed the first volume of Female Warriors in London in 1879. Her title calls them memorials of female valour and heroism, from mythic ages to her own era.

Warlike goddesses and the Amazons open the roll. Sarmatians and other tribes of fighting women follow. Semiramis of Assyria, Harpalyce, Atalanta, and Camilla take the next chapter. Tomyris, who beat Cyrus, the poetess Telesilla, and two queens of Caria share its pages. Cleopatra and Candace head the third list. Clayton gave the book to Madame Ronniger, in love and esteem.
43756-tales-of-my-time-vol-1-of-3-who-is:
An unnamed author wrote tales of the time in three volumes, here the first. Henry Colburn and Richard Bentley issued Who Is She at London in 1829. The writer of Blue-Stocking Hall stands behind the set, unnamed. A front note says the tale rests on facts the author knew.

Francis Hartland lives in a neat square house near a market town in England. His lawn, elms, and gravel walks show a man of precise, kept habits. No one knows whence he came or how he chose the place. Readers gain a slow, sly tale of mystery in quiet country life.
43766-with-porter-in-the-essex-a-story-o:
With Porter in the Essex is a story of the War of eighteen twelve by James Otis. It tells of Captain Porter's famous cruise in southern waters. The Boston and Chicago edition was copyrighted in nineteen oh one. Pictures by William F Stecher go with the text. A list of the author's other tales stands at the front, among them stories of Perry and Preble.

Contents run to fifteen chapters, from Introducing Myself to On Parole. The coast of Chile, whalers, and an island port fill the early list. A chapter is set among the Typees, and one at Valparaiso. The battle and the Britishers close the tale. A note says the story's manuscript was written by a cousin of a man captured in the Essex action. That action, against two British ships, ended the cruise the book celebrates.
43857-catalogue-of-books-on-philately-in:
Catalogue of Books on Philately in the Public Library of the City of Boston was printed in January 1903. Philately is the study and love of postage stamps. The list marks with a special type the items given by the Boston Philatelic Society.

Entries give each book or paper on stamps held by the library, with its shelf mark. The range runs from stamp lists and price guides to public papers on revenue and telegraph stamps. One entry cites a full list of the revenue stamps of the United States, with private and state issues. Marks in the margins sort the stock in ways the book does not spell out. Stamp fans and library staff of the day could find each item fast from this plain list.
44599-beyond-the-marne-quincy-huiry-vois:
Beyond the Marne is a war diary by Henriette Cuvru-Magot. Katharine Babbitt translated it into English. Small, Maynard published it in Boston in 1918. Photographs illustrate the villages named in the subtitle. They are Quincy, Huiry, and Voisins, before and during the battle.

The diary opens on August 2, 1914. War is declared, and the writer cannot believe it. She takes her brother to the station at Esbly. He goes to Paris for his mobilisation orders. She wishes she were a man and could go with him. The tocsin rings like a funeral knell over the villages. A dedication thanks an American friend for comfort given to the family. The entries follow the first battle of the Marne from home ground.
44682-speeches-of-benjamin-harrison-twen:
Charles Hedges gathered the speeches of Benjamin Harrison, twenty-third president, in this full collection. The United States Book Company printed it at New York in 1892. Harrison's portrait heads the book, and its span is exact: February 1888 to February 1892.

Campaign speeches, the letter of acceptance, and the inaugural address stand in their time order. The many speeches of his tours fill the bulk, a president then spoke from train platforms across the land. Extracts from his messages to Congress close the sweep. Hedges owns his aim in the preface: not a few polished gems, but the man's full public voice. A polished piece, worked for days, gives a poor mirror of the man, he holds.
44716-baseball-joe-captain-of-the-team-o:
Baseball Joe, Captain of the Team is a boys' sports novel by Lester Chadwick. Cupples and Leon published the book at New York in 1924, with pictures. The subtitle promises bitter struggles on the diamond. A list at the front names ten earlier volumes of the Baseball Joe series.

The hero is Joe Matson, a pitcher with the Giants. The first chapter opens at the Chicago ball park, where the team walks to its dugout in low spirits. A fellow pitcher tells Joe the club seems to be on the toboggan. Chapter titles promise a hidden ball trick, a new captain, and a package of mystery. Later parts bring revenge, a warning buzz, and a final battle. The series mixed game action with a light mystery for its young readers.
44785-the-beaked-whales-of-the-family-zi:
Frederick True wrote a full count of the beaked whales in the state store. The book is Bulletin 73 of the United States National Museum. It came out in Washington on September 28, 1910. True was head keeper of the life arm of that museum. Finds in more American stores are told as well.

Beaked whales are rare, deep sea kinds with few finds to hand. Each find is set out by place, date, bone, and tooth. True weighs old names and sorts kinds with close care. The state store's set grounds most of the book's claims. Sea beast men get a firm base for more work. Plates of skulls aid the eye in the full book.
44882-the-boy-scouts-through-the-big-tim:
The Boy Scouts Through the Big Timber, or The Search for the Lost Tenderfoot, is a boys' adventure novel by Herbert Carter, published in 1913. Here the Silver Fox Patrol of the Cranford Troop is out in the big timber country. A roll call opens the story, a mere form, since the whole patrol is present.

Bob White gravely reads the names from his little book and each boy answers. The chapters that follow bring trouble in sequence. Something frightens the pack mules, the foxes take to the trees, and then the newest boy, the tenderfoot, goes missing. A mean trick, a bob-cat, a storm, and a snake bite fill the march to find him.
45165-peter-parley-s-own-story-from-the-:
Peter Parley's Own Story is the autobiography of Samuel Goodrich, the children's writer. Sheldon and Company published it in New York in 1864. It is drawn from Goodrich's own personal narrative, printed after his death. Under the name Peter Parley he had written shelf upon shelf for the young.

The early chapters return to his boyhood home at Ridgefield, in Connecticut. The old house, the meeting-house, and Keeler's Tavern set the scene of that world. A cannon-ball relic and an aunt's school enter the family memories. Ridgefield society fills a long chapter of trades, courtships, and customs. The habits, dress, and amusements of the people receive a chapter of their own. Schooling under Master Stebbins and the boy's first Latin follow.
45205-novanglus-and-massachusettensis-or:
Political essays from 1774 and 1775, on the chief points of dispute between Great Britain and her colonies, were reprinted in Boston in 1819. John Adams, late president of the United States, wrote the Novanglus letters. Jonathan Sewall, then king's attorney general of Massachusetts Bay, wrote Massachusettensis on the other side.

Letters lately written by President Adams to William Tudor are added, some never before published. The copy used came from a presentation set in the John Adams Library at Boston. Readers see the Revolution argued in real time, pen against pen. Adams defends colonial rights and Sewall defends the crown, in the full heat of the years just before war.
45332-illuminated-manuscripts-in-classic:
J. Henry Middleton wrote this book on the rich books of old times, printed at Cambridge in 1892. He was Slade Professor of Fine Art and head of the Fitzwilliam Museum. The title page states the scope of the work: the art of those books and the craft by which they were made. The list of the book's parts shows how the tale is built up. It starts with the books of the old world, made with a stilus.

The first part deals with the ways of those days that lived on in the mid ages. It treats of books on plates of metal, rolls of lead and of tin, and charms of gold. The Petelia tablet is named, as are waxed boards and pairs of boards bound as one. From such plain stuffs the book moves to the painted page.
45366-history-of-the-anglo-saxons-from-t:
Thomas Miller wrote this history of the Anglo-Saxons, from the first dim age to the Norman Conquest, in a second edition printed by David Bogue in London in 1850. Miller was known for tales and country sketches such as Royston Gower and Pictures of Country Life. The book opens with the dawn of history, when the first people of Britain are lost in mist and their tongue is unknown.

Chapters move through stone monuments, the Welsh Triads, and the Druids, with their groves, rites, and dread of sacrifice. The conversion of Ethelbert fronts the book as a plate. Miller writes for general readers, mixing story with fact to make the Saxon past vivid and clear.
45435-history-of-the-cathedral-church-of:
Three lectures on Wells Cathedral by Edward A Freeman. Macmillan published them at London in 1870. A local society at Wells heard them in December 1869 and January 1870. A local paper printed them at the time. Freeman, formerly a fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, adds notes here. His subtitle makes the larger claim plain.

Wells illustrates the cathedral churches of the old foundation. Freeman joins local history to national history deliberately. Local historians, he complains, rarely connect their church to the kingdom's story. General historians return the neglect in kind. He also attacks the state of the cathedral institutions. Reform thirty years earlier, he says, was made in ignorance. It crippled rather than reformed the chapters. Friends must reform them, or enemies will destroy them.
45786-their-majesties-as-i-knew-them-per:
Xavier Paoli wrote Their Majesties As I Knew Them, personal reminiscences of the kings and queens of Europe, translated by A Teixeira de Mattos and published at New York in 1911. A frontispiece shows Queen Amelie of Portugal. Paoli had served royalty as a kind of chamberlain and bodyguard.

Chapters treat the Emperor and Empress of Austria, King Alfonso the Thirteenth of Spain, and the Shah of Persia. The Tsar and Tsaritsa, the King and Queen of Italy, and George the First of the Hellenes follow. Queen Wilhelmina, the late King of the Belgians, and the English royal family close the main set. Readers get an insider's portraits of Europe's courts on the eve of their fall.
45878-the-ayesha-being-the-adventures-of:
The Ayesha is a tale of the great war at sea by Hellmuth von Mucke, a chief of the fleet of his land. Its full name calls it the deeds of the land band of the Emden. Helene White made its English form. It was put out at Boston in nineteen seventeen. Two forms of the book were print in its first two months.

She has had such joy in the make of this small book, that word says, that she must speak of it. She hopes it may find ma ny who will track its writ of bold deeds with as great joy. That men in day risk of their lives can keep their jest and a kind heart past men and past fate is a glad proof, she holds.
45910-legends-of-saints-sinners-collecte:
Legends of Saints and Sinners gathers Irish folk tales of holy men and sinners, collected and Englished from the Irish by Douglas Hyde. A picture of Saint Patrick facing Crom Dubh fronts the volume. The contents open with that same meeting of saint and pagan god. Mary's Well, and how greed came into the church, follow among the early tales.

A stone of truth, the adventures of a creature called Leithin, and a tale comparing ages fill the middle list. The death of Bearachan, a story of Solomon, Christmas alms, and the burial of Jesus stand in one run. Saint Peter and Saint Declan close the visible heads. Hyde, scholar and later first president of Ireland, saved these tales from the lips of Irish speakers.
46001-a-parody-on-iolanthe:
Dalziel, editor of the Chicago News, wrote this parody on Iolanthe. Halch printed the book in New York in 1883 with McVickar plates. The play is given to conductors of the Chicago and Alton Railroad. Its scene is a fairy glade on that line at Holy Cross.

Rocky Mountain fairies dance over wheat stocks as the chorus opens. Leila sings of Pullman Palace cars free from dust and jars. Three cities stand linked, Chicago, Kansas City, and Alton, in song. The queen banished Iolanthe, and fairy life lost its shine since.
46025-charities-and-the-commons-the-pitt:
Charities and the Commons, volume twenty-one, number nineteen, dated 6 February 1909, is a journal issue given to the Pittsburgh Survey. The Charity Organization Society of New York published the journal, which calls itself a journal of constructive philanthropy. This number is part two of the survey: The Place and Its Social Forces.

The issue sold for twenty-five cents, two dollars a year. Among its news is an account of a hearing before a House committee on expenditures in the Interior Department. The hearing followed the White House Conference on Dependent Children, held in Washington on 27 January. Advertisements in the front matter include the Sheltering Arms of New York, opened in 1864 to receive children between six and ten for whom no other institution provides. The Pittsburgh Survey was the great social investigation of its age.
46131-the-adventures-of-captain-john-pat:
Captain John Patterson tells the story of his years with the 50th, or Queen's Own Regiment, from 1807 to 1821. His memoir came out in London in 1837. He dedicates the book to the Queen, who had given the regiment its colours and its proud name.

Early chapters cover his start as a soldier and the first hard marches. The tale moves through Spain and Portugal, with the battles of Rolica and Vimeiro told in detail. Patterson also gives short notices of the officers who served beside him. The result is a plain, first hand record of war in the field. His eye for officers and men gives the campaigns a human face throughout.
4629-home-scenes-and-home-influence-a-se:
T. S. Arthur published Home Scenes, and Home Influence in 1854, as the fifth volume in Arthur's Library for the Household. His preface says many scenes show a mother's influence with her children, a few include the marriage relation, and a few give other domestic pictures. In all, readers should find motives for self-denial and right action in the various conditions of social life, since home is the centre of good as well as bad influence.

Contents include Taking Comfort, Children, Losing One's Temper, and Trouble with Servants. They go on to Old Maids' Children, The Mother and Boy, The Christmas Party, Is She a Lady?, A Mother's Influence, and The Power of Patience. Arthur argues that those trusted with the home-circle hold its true power over the heart. Readers get a set of short domestic tales, warm and instructive, for family reading.
46591-the-strange-voyage-and-adventures-:
The hosted copy is the second edition, printed at London by John Lever in 1768 and sold for one shilling. The long title page gives the whole plot. Gonsales lives some years on the island of St Helena, where he plans his wonderful voyage.

Hunted there by savages, he gives the signal and the birds rise with him toward the moon. On the way he meets devils who tempt him and feed him with choice food. He leaves that hellish crew and lands safe on the moon. The book tells the manners, customs and tongue of the moon's emperors, kings and people. The Lunars load him with jewels at his parting, and his birds set him down in China. The tale ends with his report to the King of Spain, and a description of the Pike of Tenerife is added.
46796-the-pioneer-boys-of-the-mississipp:
The Pioneer Boys of the Mississippi is a boys' frontier novel by Harrison Adams, published by Page in Boston in 1913 in the Young Pioneer Series. Companion volumes follow the same boys on the Ohio and the Great Lakes. The contents promise floods, renegades and a mystery: a treasure box forgotten and a wampum belt missing.

The chapter headings name the frontier's cast. Simon Girty the renegade, Daniel Boone the pilot of the settlers, Blue Jacket giving warning, and Kenton the reckless borderer all appear. The boys run a gauntlet of period perils: a cabin that braved the flood, a target for arrows and bullets, a buffalo bagged, and figures against the sky. The frontispiece shows Sandy crying out over the precious wampum belt. Adams writes the Stratemeyer-era formula at full stretch: real border heroes borrowed to season a boys' adventure of settlement on the Mississippi.
46799-the-pioneer-boys-of-the-columbia-o:
The Pioneer Boys of the Columbia, or in the wilderness of the great northwest, by Harrison Adams, was published by the Page Company of Boston in 1916. Walter S Rogers drew the pictures. It closes the Young Pioneer series, whose volumes sold at a dollar and a quarter each. The Armstrong boys, followed down the Ohio, along the Mississippi, and up the Missouri to the Yellowstone, here end their westward story.

A letter to the reader bids the pioneer friends goodbye. The Armstrongs stand, the author says, for the class of pioneers who peopled the continent. Restless spirits, they yearned always for richer lands where game was more plentiful. That desire led them on and on into the country of the setting sun. The volume carries them through the wilds of the Columbia country to their journey's end.
46989-a-soldier-s-experience-or-a-voice-:
A Soldier's Experience is a personal narrative by Gowing, a late sergeant-major of the Royal Fusiliers. Its subtitle calls it a voice from the ranks. The book shows the cost of war in blood and treasure. It was printed for the author at Nottingham in 1896. The preface notes that 22,500 copies of early editions sold. This enlarged edition goes deeper into the subject.

The narrative covers the Crimean campaign from the ranks. It then treats the Indian Mutiny and its horrors. The Afghan campaigns of 1863 come later in the book. Sketches of Havelock and Hedley Vicars close the plan. Gowing says he kept strictly to facts. He drew on Napier, Alison, and Wellington's despatches. Rank-and-file memoirs were rare in his day. Officers wrote most war books then. His voice from below gives the volume its worth.
47248-the-heroic-record-of-the-british-n:
Archibald Hurd and Bashford wrote The Heroic Record of the British Navy, a short history of the naval war of nineteen fourteen to eighteen, printed in nineteen nineteen. The authors thank many who took part in the events, among them Admirals Jellicoe and Sims. The tale begins with a test call-up of the fleet in July, nineteen fourteen. Guests on the gunboat Niger watched the king review the ships at Spithead.

Twelve parts carry the war from the first of August to the harvest of sea power. They treat the Bight, Coronel, the Falkland Islands, and the seamen at Gallipoli. Jutland, the Dover Patrol, and the sealing of Zeebrugge and Ostend follow. The last part tells of the coming of the Americans and what sea power won.
47460-practical-skunk-raising-a-book-of-:
Practical Skunk Raising is a manual by William Edwin Pratt on raising skunks for profit, published by the author in 1915. Its twenty-two chapters run the whole business, from choosing the ground to shipping the animals. Fences, pens, dens, cage litter, and food and water troughs each get a chapter.

Pratt opens with the state of the fur trade. The supply of wild fur, he says, has fallen behind demand, and the time is in sight when wild fur will be a small part of the fur in use. Fur from a trapped animal is the poorer for its suffering, he argues, and nearly all fur will one day be grown on fur ranches. Later chapters treat feeding, diseases, rats, disinfectants, a hospital pen, breeding, barren females, the young, escapes, and how to disarm a skunk.
47588-friedrich-nietzsche:
Friedrich Nietzsche is a critical study by George Brandes of Denmark. Heinemann of London issued the English edition in nineteen fourteen. The core essay, On Aristocratic Radicalism, dates from eighteen eighty nine here. A sculpted portrait of Nietzsche by Davidson fronts the volume in photo.

Brandes calls Nietzsche the most interesting writer in German letters of the day. Little known even at home, he deserves study, dispute, and mastery, Brandes holds. In eighteen years Nietzsche wrote a long series of books and pamphlets. Most are aphorisms, and the best of them concern moral prejudices, Brandes finds. Nietzsche was born in eighteen forty four and taught philology at Basle.
47745-a-sub-and-a-submarine-the-story-of:
A Sub and a Submarine is a boys' sea novel by Percy F. Westerman, a lieutenant in the Royal Air Force. Its full title tells the story of His Majesty's Submarine R19 in the Great War. The front matter lists many Westerman sea tales, among them The Submarine Hunters and With Beatty off Jutland.

The book belongs to the war-story shelf Westerman built for young readers in those years. A praise line from the Outlook promises that no boy alive will read its pages without a quickening of his pulses. The tale follows a young submariner, a sub, and his boat through patrol work in wartime seas.
47789-the-doctor-s-red-lamp-a-book-of-sh:
Charles Wells Moulton edited this set of short stories on doctors and their work. The Doctor's Red Lamp belongs to the Doctor's Recreation series, and Saalfield issued it in 1904. A doctor's red lamp, hung out at night, is the sign of help at hand.

Tales of practice fill the book: night calls, hard cases, and the quirks of patients. Men of medicine wrote many such pieces for the magazines of the day. Moulton gathered them as rest reading for the trade, and for the lay reader who loves a surgery door tale. The series framed each volume the same way, with its editor's name and logo at the front in a ruled box.
47908-greater-greece-and-greater-britain:
Greater Greece and Greater Britain is a pair of talks by Freeman, the chair of the new past at Oxford with a row of high marks. A set of adds stands at its end. It came out at London in the mid eighteen eighties, printed at Oxford, with all rights kept.

Its two talks make its case in their names. First, the Greek world of old grew past its seas by plant towns, and the British world does the same. Next, its great son of America is shown as the man who spread Britain most, by the free land he won. His word at the front tells that the talks were spoke to hearers in his own school town.
48136-the-complete-works-in-philosophy-p:
Volume one of the complete works of Benjamin Franklin in philosophy, politics, and morals, printed at London in 1806. It is the first collection to bring his writings together in one uniform publication, with memoirs of his early life written by himself.

The editor's advertisement traces the earlier partial collections: the 1751 pamphlet of letters on electricity, grown by additions into a quarto, and the political and philosophical volumes that followed. This edition gathers them all, plus papers from pamphlets, foreign collections, philosophical transactions, newspapers, and magazines. A series of essays called The Busy-Body is flagged as likely new to English readers. A portrait engraving fronts the volume. Readers get Franklin entire, as his own century first assembled him.
48137-the-complete-works-in-philosophy-p:
The Works of Benjamin Franklin, volume two, gathers his letters and papers on philosophical subjects. The three volume set of his complete works in philosophy, politics, and morals was printed at London in 1806. The set was the first to collect and arrange his writings, with memoirs of his early life written by himself.

This volume opens with physical and meteorological observations, conjectures, and suppositions. Long pieces treat water spouts and whirlwinds, comparing the two and describing a spout seen at Antigua. Shooting stars get a short paper. A gentleman in Connecticut answers Franklin's meteorological paper, and Franklin replies. The volume also prints his scheme for a reformed alphabet with six new letters.
48138-the-complete-works-in-philosophy-p:
The Complete Works of Benjamin Franklin, volume three, gathers his papers on philosophy, politics, and morals. London publishers issued the set in 1806. Johnson and Longman shared the printing. The set claims to be the first collected arrangement of his works. Memoirs of his early life, written by himself, accompany them.

This volume treats American subjects before the Revolution. The Albany papers lead the contents. They give Franklin's plan of union for the colonies from 1754. Reasons against partial unions follow. Letters to Governor Shirley treat taxes imposed without consent. One letter proposes colonial members in Parliament. A plan for settling two western colonies dates to the same year. A history of Pennsylvania's government rounds out the volume.
48815-mistress-spitfire-a-plain-account-:
Mistress Spitfire, by Fletcher, is a plain account of episodes in the Revolution of 1642 to 1644. Dent printed it in London in 1897, with McClurg in Chicago, and this is the second edition. Fletcher says he revised and edited it from an original manuscript.

The heroes are Richard Coope and his cousin, Mistress Alison French. A map drawn for the book by Lewis Kaberry tracks the ground. The frontispiece, by Walter West, catches Alison in full cry: good day to you, Master Poltroon. The first chapter fixes time and place. Events at East Hardwick Manor House on August 27 and 28 of 1642 open the tale. Fletcher had written When Charles the First Was King in the same vein. The frame lets a home voice tell great events from inside one household.
49264-my-escape-from-donington-hall-prec:
Gunther Plüschow of the German Air Service tells a war adventure in My Escape from Donington Hall, translated by Pauline de Chary and published at London in 1922. The book first covers the siege of Kiao-Chow, where Plüschow flew his Taube against the Japanese, then his capture and imprisonment behind walls and barbed wire. A photograph shows him in the dock-labourer disguise in which he escaped.

The opening chapter recalls August 1913, when leave in England and a visit to Schwerin ended with the news he longed for: appointment to the Naval Flying Corps. Chapters end with black nights on the Thames, a stowaway passage and the way to freedom.
49266-the-wars-of-religion-in-france-155:
James Thompson, a Chicago history teacher, wrote this account of French religious wars. The University of Chicago Press issued the book in 1909. It covers the years 1559 to 1576 in full detail. Huguenots, Catherine de Medici, and Philip the Second frame the tale.

Chapter one treats the Huguenot revolt and the Amboise plot of 1560. Catherine stands between Guise and Conde in the next chapter. The States General of Orleans and a unity plot follow closely. The Colloquy of Poissy and the Edict of January 1562 come next in line. A view of Paris from a Callot sketch fronts the book.
49316-the-philosophy-of-friedrich-nietzs:
Mencken wrote the first full English book on Nietzsche's thought. A third form came out in Boston in 1913. A Schopenhauer line heads it on truth told with no soft words. Part one tells the man: youth, first paths, and the superman's seer. The man and the thinker meet in its last first part.

Part two takes the thought head by head in plain terms. Dionysus gainst Apollo, morals' roots, and past good and ill lead it. The superman, the world's wheel, and faith get their own parts. Truth, towns, women, rule, and crime fill the late list. Wagner stands at the end as foe and old friend. Clear, tart prose rules it.
49550-a-select-collection-of-old-english:
A Select Collection of Old English Plays reprints Robert Dodsley's set of 1744. Carew Hazlitt revised and enlarged this fourth edition of the old plays. Benjamin Blom of New York issued this later printing of the work. The plays now stand in time order for the first time here. Notes of all the commentators plus new notes fill the margins.

A notice up front lists fresh plays added to the old Dodsley stock. Life and Death of Jack Straw of 1593 dramatizes Wat Tyler's rising. Mucedorus of 1598 and Look About You of 1600 join the set. The Contention between Liberality and Prodigality of 1602 stands there too. Two plays of 1659, London Chanticleers and Lady Alimony, close the list. All are of the greatest rarity, the editor insists in his notice. Randolph's and Suckling's plays were dropped, new editions being announced then.
49654-battle-honours-of-the-british-army:
Battle Honours of the British Army, published by John Murray in 1911, is Norman's record of the honours borne on regimental colors. Norman had served in the 90th Light Infantry and the Indian Staff Corps. The book runs from Tangier in 1662 to the start of the reign of King Edward the Seventh. It is dedicated to the officers and men who fell for their country.

An alphabetical list gives every honour with its page: Abu Klea, Alma, Blenheim, Corunna and hundreds more. A portrait of the Duke of Marlborough fronts the volume. Each honour then gets its account of the fight that won it. Maps and illustrations support the text, which serves soldiers and students of the army alike.
49708-the-garden-of-eden-stories-from-th:
George Hodges retold these stories from the first nine Bible books. Houghton Mifflin printed The Garden of Eden in 1909 with plates. Everett drew the scenes, Lot choosing the pleasant land among them. Hodges gives the book to John Hodges, who likes these stories.

Contents run Eden, Noah ark, and the adventures of Lot first. Isaac and Rebekah, the mess of pottage, and Jacob visit follow. The coat of many colours and seven years famine come next. Burning bush, ten plagues, Red Sea, and golden calf fill on. Walls of Jericho, a wedge of gold, and the relief of Gibeon follow in the tales.
50132-the-river-motor-boat-boys-on-the-c:
The River Motor Boat Boys on the Colorado is a boys' adventure novel by Harry Gordon, issued in New York in 1913. It belongs to a series that sent the same crew down the Mississippi, the Saint Lawrence, the Amazon, the Columbia, and the Ohio. The subtitle promises a clue in the rocks.

The chapter list maps the fun. It opens with mysterious disappearances and a ten thousand dollar reward, then runs through a phantom boarder, a haunted stern deck, river pirates, and a headless ghost. Names in the cast include Alex, Clay, Don, Captain Joe, and Deputy King, with a teddy bear that makes a hit. The front plate shows two boys crawling down a canyon wall like flies. The book is fast, cliff-hung serial fare for young readers of its day.
50166-the-boy-allies-with-marshal-foch-o:
The Boy Allies with Marshal Foch is a boys' war novel by Clair Hayes, published in New York by Burt in 1919. Its subtitle calls it the closing days of the great world war. The front pages list a shelf of Boy Allies books, at Liège, on the Somme, at Verdun, and with Pershing in France.

The two lads of the series slip through the German lines in the first chapters. One of them, Chester, is indiscreet, and an enemy plot is bared. The tale then joins the great advance toward Sedan. The battle and the capture of the town follow. German envoys arrive to treat for peace. The Kaiser gives up his throne. A message from the enemy and the closing of the net bring the long war, and the book, to their end.
50212-dionysius-of-halicarnassus-on-lite:
Dionysius of Halicarnassus On Literary Composition presents the Greek text of the De Compositione Verborum. The edition supplies an introduction, an English translation, notes, a glossary, and appendices. Dionysius wrote the treatise in the first century BC. It studies how words are joined into prose that pleases the ear. Rhythm, metre, and the music of sentences fill its chapters.

The editor keeps the original page numbers throughout. Greek examples carry their metrical marks above the line. A full errata list corrects small faults in the Greek. The critical apparatus records variant readings at the foot of the page. This is a scholar's working edition of a classic of ancient criticism. Students of Greek prose style used it to learn how Dionysius judged the great authors. His tests rest on sound: clauses balanced, syllables weighed, and style praised when composition hides its art.
50581-remarks-on-the-production-of-the-p:
Remarks on the Production of the Precious Metals is an economics tract by Léon Faucher, translated by Thomson Hankey. Smith, Elder of London printed the second edition, revised, in 1853. Hankey's prefatory letter tells how he first read the remarks in the Revue des Deux Mondes for August. They later appeared, amplified, in the reports of a French academy.

Since Faucher wrote, the letter notes, Australian gold had outrun his figures. Reports put the gold shipped or ready for shipment from Australia at not less than eight million pounds sterling for 1852. A gentleman just arrived from Victoria had told Hankey more of the diggings. The tract itself weighs the demonetization of gold in several European countries, and the alarm that new gold might sink its value. It is a banker's-eye view of the great gold rushes.
50710-cassell-s-history-of-england-vol-2:
Cassell's illustrated history of England continues in a second volume, the King's edition of 1909. It runs from the Wars of the Roses to the Great Rebellion, with coloured and Rembrandt plates among its many illustrations. Its first chapter is the wars themselves, laid out in a dense summary of campaigns and claims.

Cade's rebellion, York's coming from Ireland, his protectorates, and the first battle of St Albans open the account. Wakefield kills York; Towton crowns his son. The reign of Edward the Fourth follows, with Warwick the kingmaker's rise, rupture, and fall at Barnet, and Tewkesbury ruining the Lancastrian cause. A popular national history, sold on its pictures as much as its narrative, is the volume.
50776-a-natural-history-for-young-people:
A Natural History for Young People: Our Animal Friends in Their Native Homes, by Mrs Phebe Westcott Humphreys, bears a copyright of 1900 and holds more than one hundred and fifty plates. Its preface tells why it was made. As a girl she loved the study of beasts, but found no book that sorted mammals, birds, and fishes in their right groups in words a child could read. Works of science were too hard, and tales for the young were too loose.

So she built the book she had missed: kinds set in their ranks, hard terms kept plain, and the best old and new names checked with care. Goldsmith, Figuier, and Brehm are among her guides.
