Young readers get a sound first tour of the animal world, from bears to small fish, with plates on page after page.
50860-the-ottoman-turks-and-the-routes-o:
Albert H Lybyer, a teacher at the University of Illinois, wrote on the Ottoman Turks and the routes of Eastern trade. His piece was reprinted from the English Historical Review of October 1915. In a span of just over 200 years, Turkish power spread across the Levant, from the Russian steppes to the desert.

Two views clash on what that spread did to trade. One holds that the Turks blocked the old roads and forced the hunt for new ones. The other holds that the new sea road round Africa won by its own worth. Lybyer says the proof leans hard to the second view. He then tracks trade from the Crusades to the 1700s. Scholars get a calm test of a famed claim.
51259-the-pantropheon-or-history-of-food:
Soyer wrote this history of food and its making from earliest ages. Ticknor, Reed, and Fields printed it in Boston in 1853. Forty two steel plates show great marvels of ancient feasting. Soyer was known for The Gastronomic Regenerator and Modern Housewife.

Contents start with agriculture, cereals, and the grinding of corn. Flour work, grains, vegetables, and the kitchen garden follow in order. Cabbage, beet, spinach, asparagus, and cucumber get their own notes. Seasoning plants, fruits, stone fruit, and pip fruit fill later parts. Olive, palm, cherry, apricot, peach, and plum trees each earn a place in the survey.
52230-catalogue-of-the-manuscripts-in-th:
Pascual de Gayangos compiled this catalogue of the Spanish-language manuscripts in the British Museum, printed by order of the Trustees in London in 1893. This fourth volume continues the classified lists, with entries describing each manuscript by shelfmark, material, and contents.

The volume finishes the history of Spain with ecclesiastical history and relations with Rome. Then it turns to works on Asia, Africa, and America: geography, voyages, the East Indies, China, and Japan, and the Spanish settlements in America. An appendix ranges wider, through theology, poetry, the histories of England and Italy, state papers, law, and finance. A sample entry lists papers on church controversies with the Roman court from 1508 to 1736, including letters to an archbishop of Saragossa who was Grand Inquisitor of Spain.
52296-the-deaf-shoemaker-to-which-are-ad:
Philip Barrett wrote tales for the young, issued at New York in 1859 by Dodd of Broadway. He gave the small book to Erskine Rodman, rector of Christ's Church at Norfolk in Virginia. A short preface, signed from Rural Retirement in Virginia, speaks straight to his young friends.

Barrett says he drew his stray sketches as one set to lead children to the Saviour. Scores of short pieces fill the book: John McDonough, an orphan, a rose, a lantern, and the deaf shoemaker himself. Tales of a rail road, a poor sick girl, prayer, and a death room mix faith with daily life in plain, warm terms.
52321-twelve-months-with-the-eighth-mass:
Harry E Webber's Twelve Months with the Eighth Massachusetts Infantry was printed by Newcomb and Gauss at Salem, Massachusetts, in 1908, with an introduction by Major General J P Sanger. Webber dedicates the volume to the officers and men of the Eighth Massachusetts Infantry, United States Volunteers.

The contents run from call to arms and muster in through Chickamauga and sickness at Chickamauga to Lexington, Americus, and Matanzas, then muster out and welcome home. Rosters follow for each company, from Company A of Newburyport to Company M of Somerville, with a roll of honor and statistics. The preface prides old Essex County on sons ever ready to take up arms at the country's call.
52767-the-time-of-the-end-or-the-world-t:
The Time of the End is a set of lectures on prophecy by Edward Hoare. Hoare was curate of Richmond. Hatchard published the book in London in 1846. Its full title names three subjects. They are the world, the visible church, and the people of God at the Lord's coming.

A letter to the parishioners of Richmond opens the volume. The lectures grew from three Advent sermons of the year before. Hoare now leaves the parish for another sphere of labour. He gives the book as a parting memorial. He argues that the times are of peculiar peril. Seduction and apostasy, he warns, will grow within the church. His charge to the parish is to pray the more.
52937-russian-prisons-st-peter-and-st-pa:
Major Arthur Griffiths wrote on Russian prisons for a set on crime. The Grolier Society issued the work in London in a run of one thousand sets. The copy shown is Number 307 of the National form. A front plate shows a young girl revolutionist bound for the scaffold.

St Peter and St Paul, the Schlusselburg, and the ostrog at Omsk lead the survey. Vera Phillipova, held for life at Schlusselburg, stands among the named sufferers. Chapters treat exile roads, Tiunen and Tomsk, and the isle of Saghalien. Readers gain a grim tour of the tsar's prisons and exile system.
53168-in-the-royal-naval-air-service-bei:
In the Royal Naval Air Service is the war letters of Harold Rosher to his family, published in London in 1916. An opening essay is by Arnold Bennett. Rosher was a flight lieutenant, and the title calls him late, for he did not survive the war. Two impressions came out in September 1916 alone.

Contents move in sections: training, home service, and raids on the Belgian coast. He serves with the British force in France, takes a new machine to France, and returns to home service again and again. Pictures show him in uniform, seaplanes at anchor off Spithead, and a fighting biplane photographed from another. One shows a pilot being brought ashore after a flight. Readers get a young airman letters home, from first training to the front, in the first years of war flying.
53424-the-life-of-robert-lord-clive-vol-:
The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, volume one of three, is a biography by Sir John Malcolm. John Murray of London published it in 1836, with a portrait and a map.

The work rests on family papers communicated by the Earl of Powis, Clive's son. The papers lay among the family records at Walcot. They held nearly the whole of Clive's correspondence from his first post in India. Originals of letters received stand beside copies of important answers. Memoirs of his enterprises and minutes of council complete it. Parliamentary committee reports and other materials aided the author. Charlotte Malcolm's dedication letter calls the book Malcolm's last and favourite work.
53620-the-life-of-friedrich-nietzsche:
Daniel Halevy wrote a life of Friedrich Nietzsche, here in English by Mone, printed in London in 1911. Kettle wrote the introduction. The tale starts with the father, Karl Ludwig Nietzsche, a young Lutheran clergyman from a long line of clergy. King Frederick William the Fourth of Prussia took him under his wing.

Headaches and nerves forced the father to a quiet country parish at Rocken. There his first child was born on October 15, 1844, the king's own birthday. Later chapters tell of youth, of friendship with Richard Wagner at Triebschen and Bayreuth, of crisis and illness, and of the labour of Zarathustra. A final chapter faces the last solitude.
53902-a-soldier-of-the-legion-an-english:
A Soldier of the Legion, by George Manington, is a memoir of French service. John Murray issued it at London in 1907 with map and plates. Manington, an Englishman, served in the Foreign Legion in Algeria and Tonquin. Two friends saw his manuscript through the press while he chased work east.

The editors note his past: student, near doctor, soldier, merchant, interpreter, journalist. Malaria caught in Tonquin dogged him as he wrote in rest spells. Most pages treat the Tonquin fighting in forest fastnesses against rebels there. His friendship with a native sergeant, Doy-Tho, warms the tale throughout. The book is dedicated to comrades who fell in those forests.
54148-love-s-old-sweet-song-a-sheaf-of-l:
George H Ellwanger gathered a sheaf of latter day love poems from many sources, published at New York in 1903 and dedicated to the memory of Gleeson White. An envoy in verse opens the book. It asks strains attuned by master fingers to resound, breathing love's consuming fire. Some poems are sweet as a lingering chord, others grave and plaintive.

A publishers' note explains the volume's making. Most of its poems appeared before in two volumes called Love's Demesne, now out of print. The compiler revised the selection for this handier form. The note claims a distinct field: most pieces are otherwise found only in scattered volumes. Ellwanger also wrote garden and table books.
54329-symmes-s-theory-of-concentric-sphe: Symmes's Theory of Concentric Spheres sets out the hollow earth doctrine of Captain John Cleves Symmes, written by a citizen of the United States in his support. Its title carries the whole claim: demonstrating that the earth is hollow, habitable within, and widely open about the poles. The book opens with Shakespeare's words, that there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in philosophy. A second epigraph, from Milton, begs a gentle hearing for an erroneous but persevering man.
54380-a-battle-of-the-books-recorded-by-:
A Battle of the Books, recorded by an unknown writer, was edited and published by Gail Hamilton at Cambridge in 1870. A transcriber note names Gail Hamilton as the alias of Mary Abigail Dodge. The title page dedicates the work to authors and publishers alike, for doctrine, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness.

The editor's introduction claims the papers were found in a state-room after a violent storm at sea, stained with salt water. Contents chapters march from the Rise and Progress of Suspicion through a Declaration of War and Skirmishing to the Battle of Gog and Magog. Publishing's royalty wars are the field.
54493-the-dungeons-of-old-paris-being-th:
The Dungeons of Old Paris is a story and romance of the famous prisons of France by Tighe Hopkins, printed at New York and London in 1897. Hopkins also wrote Kilmainham Memories and other tales. A French proverb at the start calls a thing sad as the gates of a prison, and the book shows how thick those gates once stood in Paris.

Chapters treat the prisons one by one: the Conciergerie, Vincennes, the Chatelet, the Temple, and the Bastille. Pictures show the cell of Marie Antoinette and a plan of the Bastille. Hopkins mixes record with romance, telling who was held, who escaped, and who died, from the old monarchy to the Revolution.
54558-the-life-of-henry-bradley-plant-fo:
Smyth wrote this life of Henry Bradley Plant, printed in New York and London in 1898. Plant was founder and president of the Plant System of railroads and steamships, and also of the Southern Express Company. The preface argues at length for the worth of biography itself before it turns to its subject.

No two lives, Smyth holds, are alike in every point, and each has its own lessons for others. He urges that trade and industry deserve honour like war or science. Plant's share in the growth of the Cotton States, he says, was so large that the best history of that region in his time could not be written without him.
54633-the-life-of-robert-lord-clive-vol-:
Major General Sir John Malcolm wrote The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, collected from the family papers communicated by the Earl of Powis. John Murray issued it in London in MDCCCXXXVI, in three volumes with a portrait and map. Chapter nine opens with success in the Northern Circars. Colonel Forde expedition of seventeen fifty eight leads it.

Transactions at Madras and the siege of that place by Lally fill the same chapter. Chapter ten destroys the Dutch armament against Bengal in seventeen fifty nine. Clive letter to Pitt and his return to England in seventeen sixty follow. Chapter twelve takes up his politics and his quarrel with Mr Sulivan. Chapter thirteen covers India in his absence. Chapter fourteen has him resume the government of Bengal in seventeen sixty five. Historians get the central volume of the standard Clive life.
54693-a-book-for-a-rainy-day-or-recollec:
John Thomas Smith, keeper of prints and drawings at the British Museum, collected these recollections of the years 1766 to 1833, edited by Wilfred Whitten in an edition of 1905. Smith calls the book a salmagundi in his own preface.

The success of his Nollekens and His Times, he says, led him to gather scattered biographical papers and arrange them by the years of his life. He quotes Johnson that all knowledge is of some value, and Lord Orrery that anecdotes are debts due to the public. The illustrations draw the world he knew: Nancy Dawson, Vauxhall, Mrs Siddons, and London beggars from his own etchings. Readers get a print-room man's London, remembered name by name.
54843-a-short-discourse-concerning-pesti:
A Short Discourse Concerning Pestilential Contagion is a medical pamphlet by Richard Mead. It was printed in London in 1720. Mead was a fellow of the physicians' college and the Royal Society. He wrote at the command of the government of the day. Sickness then raged in France, and England feared its spread. The piece is addressed to Secretary Craggs.

Mead sets down heads of caution rather than full rules. The first part treats the quarantine of ships and goods. His rules there follow practice in other countries. New regulations are added to that practice. The second part treats the stopping of infection at home. Its methods differ from those of former times, he says. The plague at Marseilles had set all Europe on guard. Mead's plan shaped English policy for a century.
54848-the-life-of-robert-lord-clive-vol-:
Malcolm, a major-general, wrote this life, The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, drawn from the family papers given by the Earl of Powis. It was printed at London in 1836, with a portrait and map. The hosted text is the third of three volumes. Contents of this last volume carry the story from mutiny to death and judgment.

Chapter fifteen treats combinations among the officers of the army, put down by Clive, and his conduct toward the army in 1766. The salt trade, gold coinage, and the general measures of his government follow, ending with his resignation in January 1767. Later chapters take up honours in England, disorder in the Company's affairs, charges against Clive, and his answer in the Commons in 1772, closing with debates, votes, and his death. The chapter opens on the harder task that waited in Bengal: cutting officers' allowances by the directors' orders.
54944-the-last-days-of-mary-stuart-and-t:
Samuel Cowan wrote the Last Days of Mary Stuart, in 1907. Nash at London put out the history that year. The journal of her physician stands in its second title. Cowan had written on the casket letters before this book. The last act of the drama opens the contents here.

Two ministers are engaged against the queen. A spymaster fills the first chapter's heads. Plots against her life stand in it. Babington conspirators crowd that chapter. Mary's pathetic appeal to an ambassador follows in the list. Texts of her first and second letters stand in the contents. Memoranda about kidnapping the queen fill the middle heads. Her money and cabinets were seized by force in chapter two. Her secretaries' letters stand examined in that chapter too. Cowan gives a captive queen her last keepers' paperwork.
54958-among-the-an-ko-me-nums-or-flathea:
Thomas Crosby's Among the An-ko-me-nums, or Flathead Tribes of Indians of the Pacific Coast, was published by William Briggs at Toronto in 1907. Crosby, missionary to the Indians of British Columbia, is pictured in a photograph of 1874 at the front. An introduction says his name has been a household word in Methodist circles for a generation.

The accounts of his labours so far, the introduction says, had been fragmentary, striking incidents without a connected story, and Crosby alone could supply the whole. Such foundation work, it argues, is done underground and out of sight, by men content to take the work nearest them and leave results with God. Yet these are the true empire-builders, on whose foundations alone an enduring civilization rests. The volume begins the connected story of the man and his mission work on the coast, with the hope expressed that other volumes will follow.
55425-war-and-the-arme-blanche:
Erskine Childers wrote a study of war and the arme blanche, with a foreword by Field Marshal Earl Roberts. Roberts says he read the book with the greatest interest. He agrees with its main thesis and claims he foresaw its arguments in Cavalry Training of 1904. He views the 1907 rules with some concern.

The question is the worth of steel weapons against firearms for cavalry. Lancer regiments, Roberts notes, once depended wholly on lance and sword, since smooth bore carbines were short ranged and inaccurate. Chapters treat mounted charges in South Africa and the Russo Japanese War. A long final chapter argues for reform in armament, mounted infantry, and yeomanry.
55519-the-afghan-war-of-1879-80-being-a-:
Howard Hensman wrote The Afghan War of 1879-80, a war narrative. Allen at London put out this second edition with maps. Hensman was special correspondent of two newspapers in the field. The Pioneer of Allahabad and the Daily News of London sent him. Kabul's capture heads the long title.

Sherpur's siege and Ahmed Khel follow there. A march to Kandahar and Ayub Khan's defeat follow. Helmand operations and a settlement close it. Abdur Rahman Khan is the amir of that settlement at its end. The book is dedicated to two Highland regiments by the author. Their hospitality in Afghanistan earned it, he writes. Roberts congratulated him on the march account in a printed letter. Nothing could be more accurate or graphic, the general wrote. Hensman gives the war from a correspondent's saddle.
55650-stray-leaves-from-strange-literatu:
Lafcadio Hearn retold tales from the old books of many lands in Stray Leaves from Strange Literature. Houghton Mifflin published the set in 1922, bound with his early short pieces called Fantastics. The stray leaves begin with a tale drawn from an Egyptian papyrus. A legend of the South Pacific and an Esquimau tale stand beside it.

Later leaves retell tales from India and from Buddhist books. Hearn also gives runes from the Finnish Kalewala and stories of Moslem lands. Tales retold from the Talmud close the first part. The Fantastics are short prose pieces first printed in New Orleans papers between 1879 and 1884. Names among them include The Ghostly Kiss, The Black Cupid, and When I Was a Flower.
55838-signers-of-the-declaration-histori:
Signers of the Declaration is volume 18 of the National Survey of Historic Sites and Buildings. The National Park Service printed it at Washington in 1973, with Robert Ferris as series editor. Its theme is the places that mark the signing of the Declaration of Independence.

The work rests on a broad survey by Charles Snell and the late John Littleton and co-authors. Front plates show Independence Hall in 1776 and the famed Trumbull painting of the signing scene. Site by site, the book ties houses and halls to the men who signed. History fans get a guide to ground where the new nation was proclaimed.
56094-allegheny-episodes-folk-lore-and-l:
Allegheny Episodes is a set of folk tales and legends by Henry Shoemaker. It gathers lore from northern and western Pennsylvania. The book is volume eleven of a Pennsylvania folk lore series. A photo of the Allegheny outposts fronts it. The index lists some twenty-five pieces. Tulliallan and The Prostrate Juniper stand early. Indian tales and ghost tales are mixed through the list.

Hugh Gibson's Captivity tells a frontier ordeal. Girty's Notch and Poplar George keep border names alive. Black Alice Dunbar and a bad Indian named Antoine follow. A haunted house and a fountain of youth close the range. The front matter tells of the Alligewi, a mighty old nation. The Lenape still name the river for them, it says. Shoemaker spent his life saving such mountain lore. His books fixed a vanishing oral world in print.
56245-india-and-indian-engineering-three:
Julius George Medley delivered these three lectures at the Royal Engineer Institute, Chatham, in July 1872. Spon of London published them in 1873. Medley was a lieutenant-colonel of Royal Engineers. He also headed the Thomason Civil Engineering College at Roorkee.

The syllabus sweeps across India whole. Land, climate, peoples, castes, and faiths come first. English life in the station and in tents follows. Then come the Public Works Department and the Roorkee workshops. Building materials fill one long list, from stone and bricks to limes and timber. Foundations in Indian rivers use well-cylinders, the syllabus notes. Barracks, bridges, roads, and railways each get their turn. Irrigation closes the course, with the Ganges Canal as its great example.
56781-midnight-sunbeams-or-bits-of-trave:
Edwin Coolidge Kimball wrote Midnight Sunbeams, bits of travel through the land of the Norseman, issued at Boston by Cupples and Hurd. He gave the book to Walter Camp, in memory of years of friendship. The sketches tell of a journey in Norway, Sweden, and Denmark. Kimball hopes they will give facts about the peoples and sights of lands that Americans visit more and more each year, and sport for those who travel only through books.

The chapters open with Copenhagen and its environs: the road from Lübeck, the Thorvaldsen museum, an evening at the Tivoli, and the Frederiksborg palace. Then comes the crossing of Sweden by the Gotha Canal, past the Trollhätta falls, to Lake Mälar and Stockholm. Kimball writes with warmth for the people and the grand sights of the North, and his memories shape the whole book.
56966-motion-pictures-1894-1912-identifi:
Howard Lamarr Walls made this list of the first films of America, printed at Washington in 1953. It is a book of the Copyright Office of the Library of Congress. Its full head states its source: the films are known from the files of that office. The price of the book was two coins. A list of the claim men stands at page 71, as a key to the main list.

The main list runs from page 1. The bits of each line are given in a set order, the book states at its head. In the main, a line gives just the name of the film. It gives the name of the man who claims the right as well. It gives the date the term of the right starts, and the count of its place in the files.
57020-the-regulating-silver-coin-made-pr:
An anonymous lover of his country offered this plan for regulating the silver coin to both Houses of Parliament, printed in London in 1696. The contents list the crisis in order: the present badness of the coin, the scarcity of silver coin in England, and importation.

Later chapters treat altering the coin, its export, the melting of current coin by goldsmiths, and hoarding, then set out the author's method and its advantages. The writer confesses his weakness for so great an undertaking and asks that his theorem, the main of the work, not suffer for his plain style. He credits Lowndes with clearing the way. Readers get a working pamphlet from England's great recoinage debate.
57026-the-last-of-the-bushrangers-an-acc:
Francis Augustus Hare, late superintendent of Victorian police, wrote The Last of the Bushrangers, an account of the capture of the Kelly Gang. Hurst and Blackett at London issued the fourth edition in 1895. A portrait of Ned Kelly faces the title page. Richard Clay printed the volume.

Hare opens with his own early days at the diggings, fever, and store-keeping, then his police service on gold-escort duty. Power the bushranger gets a chapter, with £500 blood-money and a peacock as sentinel in his tale. The Kelly gang chapter names Ned and Dan Kelly, Steve Hart, and Joe Byrne. The murder of Kennedy, the Euroa bank robbery, and the sticking up of Younghusband's station follow from the police side.
57554-the-comedy-tragedy-of-the-second-e:
The Comedy and Tragedy of the Second Empire is a society history by Edward Legge, printed by Harper in 1911. Its subtitle promises Paris society in the sixties. Letters of Napoleon the Third, of Pietri, and of Comte de la Chapelle stand inside. Legge also wrote a life of the Empress Eugénie. He dedicates the volume to a veteran statesman and historian of the Empire.

The frontispiece is a scoop. It shows Napoleon the Third in a bust by Bruce-Joy, cast by the sculptor, with the Empress's permission, from the death mask taken just after the Emperor died on January 9, 1873. The bust had never been exhibited, and was photographed for this book in June 1911. Legge writes the Empire as comedy on the surface and tragedy underneath, from court ball to Sedan's shadow.
57555-the-early-life-of-abraham-lincoln-:
Ida Tarbell, with help from Davis, wrote this life of Lincoln's early years for McClure in 1896. One hundred sixty plates fill it, with twenty portraits of Lincoln. A front plate shows the earliest portrait of him, hitherto unpublished.

That plate is a daguerreotype held by Robert Lincoln, his son. It shows Lincoln as a young man, not over thirty-five, the note says. It beats all other portraits by six or seven years at least. Tarbell gathered fresh papers and the memories of Lincoln's early friends, as her title boasts. Her work in McClure's magazine set a new mark for life writing in America, close to the soil.
57724-a-cyclopaedia-of-canadian-biograph:
George Maclean Rose edited A Cyclopaedia of Canadian Biography, a book of men of the time. The Rose Publishing Company issued it in Toronto in eighteen hundred eighty eight. The set forms part two of Rose’s National Biographical Series. Its lives span trade, law, church, school, and state craft.

Old custom kept such books for men of state alone, Rose says. Any life that built the land earns a page in his plan. Men who hewed homes from the wild bush head his honour list. Their toil laid the base for towns and ripe farm land. Skill in engines and shop craft gets its fair due here. Great clergy, judges, doctors, and school men stand by statesmen. Each small town life forms part of the whole land’s tale. Rose grabs the record now, ere stream and time bear it off.
57840-the-prophecies-of-the-brahan-seer-:
Mackenzie gathered these sayings of the Brahan Seer, in a fourth edition, much enlarged, printed at Inverness in 1888. He edited the Celtic Magazine and wrote clan histories. A piece on the old beliefs of the Highlanders, by Macgregor, comes at the back of the book.

Mackenzie gives the book to Macgregor, his old friend. Macgregor, he says, kept Celtic writing alive for half a century in Gaelic papers. The preface notes that the second edition had long been out of print. Stray copies sold at more than twice the first price. This larger edition was made to meet the call for it.
57877-a-history-of-postal-agitation-from:
A History of Postal Agitation is a reform tale of the post, from fifty years back to the day of its print. A list of new novels at six shillings stands at its front, the house ads of its age. Its full title tells that it takes in the fight for cheap stamps and fair mail.

The cause it serves is plain from its name. Post rates were once high and paid by the mile, a tax on kin who lived far apart. The fight it tells won the penny post and kept on for more: cheap books by post, fair pay for sorters, and a post for all. It stands as a case book for how a long, loud public push can move the state.
57979-mother-nurse-and-infant-a-manual-e:
Mother, Nurse and Infant is a drill book for dames and for the month nurse, by Sackett, a man of the heal craft. It was put out at New York in eighteen eighty nine. Its full bill tells its whole aim. It gives full words on the months past birth, on the gear up for the birth day, and on the care of dame and child.

The first words set out the aim of the hand in more plain words. That aim is to give to nurses the drill they need for their work. It is spoke most to those dames who would make the month nurse trade their call in life.
58010-a-feast-for-serpents-being-the-sub:
A Feast for Serpents is the substance of a sermon Church preached at the Obelisk Chapel on Sunday evening, March 21, 1813, and printed at London that year. His texts are sharp ones: the Saviour's words, ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, and Hosea's charge that they eat up the sin of my people. The sermon is aimed at the corrupt-minded men who, Church says, had long tried to prejudice his flock against him.

The long preface is a defense of his ministry, addressed to the church that had stood with him in the furnace of affliction. He writes, he says, not for the worldling, the proud Pharisee, or the hypocrite, but for those who know the plague of their own hearts. It is fierce, personal preaching from the London dissenting world.
58020-the-trial-and-conviction-of-john-c:
Trial and Conviction of John Church is a court report from eighteen seventeen. Church was preacher of the Surrey Tabernacle in the Borough Road, London. He was tried at the Surrey Assizes at Croydon on August sixteen of that year. The charge was an assault with intent to commit an unnatural crime. The report was taken in shorthand by a barrister, the title page says.

The edition sold for two shillings, printed at London the same year. Its profits were to go to the prosecutor, toward the costs of the case. A note to the public disowns any wish to echo party triumph. The publishers say they hold the man up to view so that innocent youths may not fall victim. Sorrow, not joy, is the proper mood for the tale, they add.
58025-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Friedrich Nietzsche is a finding list compiled by David Widger. It gathers the tables of contents of Nietzsche's books available in English through Project Gutenberg, so a reader can locate a chapter or discourse without opening each volume.

Works listed include Thus Spake Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, Thoughts Out of Season, The Antichrist, The Dawn of Day, and The Birth of Tragedy. Ecce Homo, The Twilight of the Idols, The Genealogy of Morals, and both halves of The Will to Power also appear. Under Zarathustra the index names each discourse, from The Three Metamorphoses to The Bestowing Virtue. Widger compiled many such indexes, and they served readers as maps to a whole author's shelf.
58108-facts-and-assertions-or-a-brief-an:
Facts and Assertions is a theological tract by George Stanley Faber. Rivington printed it in London in the year 1831 for church readers. Faber was rector of Long Newton and prebendary of Salisbury then. His subtitle promises a brief, plain exhibition of doctrinal incongruity. Peculiar doctrines of the Church of Rome stand measured against two tests.

Those tests are the sacred scriptures and the early church writers. A quote from Athanasius fronts the tract as its governing motto. It is for triflers, that quote says, to speak things not written. An advertisement says friends suggested such a brief work might prove useful. Protestant readers of 1831 got a compact case against Rome in print.
58151-an-essay-on-the-encroachments-of-t:
Hewitt, a surgeon, wrote an essay on the encroachments of the German Ocean along the Norfolk coast, printed at Norwich in 1844. The book is given to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty. Eccles church in the present state of the beach at Happisburgh is pictured at the front. A talk with the Admiralty in 1843 led him to think an essay on the subject would be received with attention, he says.

Its worth would be weighed by its merits and by the importance of the object. Many persons may think it remarkable that a man whose profession eats his leisure should write on coasts, he owns. Villages lost to the sea, cliffs eaten year by year, and churches standing in the surf fill his record. He adds a design to arrest the sea's further raids. Norfolk's drowning coast gets an early, careful witness.
58332-autobiography-of-miss-cornelia-kni:
Cornelia Knight left journals and a life story that fill two volumes, here in a third form from 1861. W H Allen and Company issued the set in London that year. Knight served as lady companion to Princess Charlotte of Wales. Her papers passed to kin at her death and then to an editor.

Journals span more than half a century, joined by notes and tales of court life. A portrait of Princess Charlotte by Sir Thomas Lawrence fronts the work. Readers meet royals, hosts, and guests through a sharp, near eye. The book gives rare close views of court manners and of a woman who watched them for years.
58557-autobiography-of-miss-cornelia-kni:
Autobiography of Miss Cornelia Knight, volume two, tells of the companion to Princess Charlotte. Allen published it at London in 1861 from her journals and anecdote books. Knight was lady companion to the Princess Charlotte of Wales in her youth. Contents of this volume open with the rupture of the Orange marriage.

Events attending that rupture and the dismissal of the household fill chapter one. A letter to the Regent and the pension of Miss Knight close that summary. The Princess birthday and suspected intrigues fill the second chapter heads. A letter to the Queen and the year 1815 continue the journal in the contents. Court secrets of the Regency come from a woman who stood in the room.
58710-the-land-of-darkness-along-with-so:
The Land of Darkness, along with some further chapters in the experiences of the Little Pilgrim, is a visionary tale published by Macmillan at London in 1888. It continues the journeys of the Little Pilgrim, whose earlier wanderings in the unseen had won many readers. The contents join the title tale with The Little Pilgrim and On the Dark Mountains.

The narrator finds himself standing on his feet, tingling, as if he had come down fast from a height. The whirling, sickening sense of falling through air recalls Dante's descent, he thinks. All his aching of wonder, doubt, and fear is gone, yet no distance meets his eye. A lurid light hangs over the place. Above him lowers a dark canopy of cloud with a faint reddish tint. The tale walks a soul through a shadow land of trial.
58771-the-lost-tribes-of-the-irish-in-th:
Irvin Cobb, the Kentucky humorist, delivered this address at the annual dinner of the American Irish Historical Society at the Waldorf-Astoria on January 6, 1917. The Society printed it at New York the same year. Cobb opens with a confession: he is one who is Irish and did not know it. Now that he knows it, he is prouder of it than of anything on earth except being an American citizen.

His theme is the lost tribes of his title, the Irish who helped build the early Southern states and were forgotten in the telling. He ranges over the temperaments of north and south in many lands to make his case. The speech is Cobb at his best: pathos, infectious humor, and keen observation in the service of the Society's motto, to make better known the Irish chapter in American history.
58972-life-of-johann-wolfgang-goethe:
Life of Johann Wolfgang Goethe, by James Sime, came out in London in 1888 in the Great Writers series. The book tracks Goethe from his birth at Frankfort on August 28, 1749, through a full and restless youth. Early parts treat his home, his sister Cornelia, and his first love.

At Leipzig and then Strasburg he read, wrote, and fell ill, and men like Herder shaped his mind. Back home he wrote the drama of Goetz von Berlichingen, which won wide fame in 1773. His love for Charlotte Buff at Wetzlar stands behind the sorrows of Werther. The chapter heads go on through Weimar, Italy, and old age, giving dates and works at each step of the long life.
59542-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of the Project Gutenberg works of George Barr McCutcheon, the popular novelist. The index lists more than thirty books, from Brewster's Millions and Graustark onward. The Prince of Graustark, Beverly of Graustark, and Truxton King continue the famed Graustark romances. Castle Craneycrow, Green Fancy, and The Hollow of Her Hand stand in the list as well.

For each book the index gives its full table of contents, chapter by chapter. Brewster's Millions opens with a birthday dinner, shades of Aladdin, and a second will. Readers and librarians can trace McCutcheon's whole shelf at a glance and find any chapter fast. The index serves as a map to a best selling author's work in free editions.
59890-our-union-and-its-defenders-an-ora:
J Howard Pugh, a physician, delivered Our Union and Its Defenders before the citizens of Burlington, New Jersey, at their celebration of the eighty-sixth anniversary of Independence Day, July 4, 1862. The oration was printed at Philadelphia that year. A letter from Burlington citizens, dated July 8, asks leave to put it on record.

The writers say the address expressed their own sentiments so ably that they want it spread among reading and thinking members of the community. The occasion matters: a Fourth of July speech in the second summer of the Civil War was no empty ceremony. Readers get Union patriotism argued from a small-town platform.
59955-blue-beard-a-contribution-to-histo:
Thomas Wilson wrote a study of Blue Beard as history and folk lore, printed at New York in 1899. Wilson kept the early remains at the national museum and had served as consul at Ghent, Nantes and Nice. The book names Gilles de Retz of Brittany as the first Blue Beard of the Mother Goose tales.

Gilles was tried at Nantes and put to death in 1440. Early chapters cover his name, kin, marriage and schooling. Then comes his soldier's life from 1420 to 1429. He fought for Brittany, joined the French host, served with Joan of Arc, and was made marshal of France at the king's crowning that same year.
59995-an-historical-sketch-of-the-concep:
An Historical Sketch of the Conceptions of Memory among the Ancients was a thesis by William Burnham. He submitted it for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy at Johns Hopkins University in 1888. Six parts divide the sketch in the table of contents. Views of memory before Aristotle fill the first part of the work.

Aristotle conceptions of memory take the largest share, from page twelve to forty. Stoics and Epicureans, with Cicero and Quintilian, follow in the third part. Plotinus and Augustine form the fourth stage of the historical survey. Diseases of memory noted by ancient writers get a short fifth part. Ancient systems of mnemonics close the thesis in its sixth part. Hesiod made Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses, the text notes at its start.
60028-mary-the-queen-of-the-house-of-dav:
A Stewart Walsh wrote Mary: The Queen of the House of David and Mother of Jesus for A S Gray and Company at Pittsburgh in 1889. T De Witt Talmage wrote the opening essay. Walsh dedicated the story of Mary's life to womankind throughout the world. A plate by Frederick Goodall shows Mary with the infant Saviour.

Talmage praises the author's graceful pen and his use of tradition beside fact. Gabriel's greeting, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, faces the title page. Mary's own words, All generations shall call me blessed, supply the motto. Walsh traces her life as queen of David's house and mother of Jesus, in a warm and popular style.
60209-the-bear-family-at-home-and-how-th:
The Bear Family at Home was written by Curtis Wilbur. Bobbs-Merrill published it at Indianapolis in 1908. Lohse drew the illustrations. Copyrights of 1908 and 1923 stand on the title page. Wilbur gives the book to the memory of Ralph Gordon Wilbur. Some twenty two stories fill the contents. How the little cub bear got back into the woods opens the set. A monkey goes to school in the second tale. One hero returns in story after story: the little cub bear who would not mind his papa. He takes a bath, nearly drowns among logs, and meets dynamite. A club-foot bear earns his own series of scrapes.

A lion and a parrot tell of narrow escapes. The animals plan their defence against the circus men. How the circus crossed the ocean is told near the end.
60211-the-outdoor-girls-around-the-campf:
Laura Lee Hope's The Outdoor Girls Around the Campfire, or The Old Maid of the Mountains, was copyrighted in 1923 by Grosset and Dunlap at New York. The frontispiece shows Mollie crying out for the camp life she loves. Twenty-five chapters open with the girls speeding their motor boat across a glassy lake, daring any rival to race. Plans for a mountain camping trip follow, with an almost-collision and the twins entering the story.

A will, a little old lady client, and her death give the camping plot its mystery. The girls start their adventure, meet tramps, find a toy pistol, and make camp through a prowler, a shadowy bulk, and a storm. A hold-up, a clew, and a lean-to lead to the old maid of the mountains herself, and romance closes the book. Hope also wrote the Bobbsey Twins series.
60375-the-colored-people-of-chicago-an-i:
The Colored People of Chicago is a social investigation made for the Juvenile Protective Association and published in 1913, with the text by Louise de Koven Bowen. Four investigators gathered the material. The study began in the county jail, where the Association was startled by the numbers of Black boys and girls confined there.

The figures frame the inquiry. Black Chicagoans were about one fortieth of the population, yet supplied an eighth of the jailed boys and nearly a third of the jailed girls. Investigators also found employment agencies openly sending Black maids to houses of prostitution. So the study widened into the whole industrial and social status of Black Chicago, from the first settler's cabin of 1779 onward. Bowen argues that shut doors of opportunity, not character, explain the delinquency. It is an early work of urban race sociology, written in the language of its time.
60441-class-book-for-the-school-of-muske:
Colonel Wilford, assistant-commandant and chief instructor, prepared this class book for the School of Musketry at Hythe, printed there in 1861 for the use of officers. An introduction says the school was founded in 1853 by the late Viscount Hardinge, then commander-in-chief. It was set up as a normal school of instruction in musketry. Its special object is the forming of officers and sergeants as instructors for the battalions of the Army.

Regulations quoted in the book order each battalion's officers to be gathered twice a year for theory. The whole history of small arms, from the first invention of gunpowder to the present rifle-musket, is to be traced in those meetings. Wilford calls his lectures mere aids to teaching, to be expanded by the instructor in spoken lessons.
60453-the-border-bandits-an-authentic-an:
J W Buel compiled a history of the border bandits Jesse and Frank James, calling it authentic and thrilling and drawn from reliable sources only. Buel had written a life of Wild Bill the scout. Portraits of Frank and Jesse James, engraved from late photographs, open the book. A notice warns that the portraits were copyrighted for this book at some expense and danger.

The James brothers' bands of highwaymen are the subject throughout. Such instant histories sold the outlaw legend while the men still rode. Buel promises the latest facts about the desperate freebooters. The book belongs to the flood of James literature that turned train robbers into folk heroes.
60546-thirteen-years-at-the-russian-cour:
Pierre Gilliard wrote Thirteen Years at the Russian Court. Hutchinson and Company issued it at London. F Appleby Holt translated the French text. Fifty-nine pictures aid the memoir. Gilliard had tutored the Czarevitch at court. A third edition shows the book's reach.

A front plate shows captivity at Tsarskoe-Selo. The Czar clears a snow path there in March 1917. My First Lessons at the Court opens the tale. That was autumn 1905 by his dating. Alexis and the Crimea trips fill chapter two. Spala's illness autumn darkens that chapter's end. His duties as tutor begin in the third. The Czarina and Rasputin take whole chapters. Winter life at Tsarskoe-Selo fills the sixth. Rasputin's influence and Madame Wyroubova crowd the seventh. A Swiss tutor's record of the last Romanovs stands close, kind, and terrible in its hindsight.
60617-the-rise-and-fall-of-prohibition-t:
Charles Hanson Towne wrote an account of Prohibition in America, published at New York in 1923. Its subtitle calls it the human side of what the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act had done to the United States. A frontispiece scolds the soda-fiend, who tears off an ice-cream soda at nine in the morning.

Chapters treat the phenomenon of Prohibition, the nation's great unhappiness, and its endless chain of laws. One is headed Too Much Verboten, another calls the Volstead Act infamous. Towne drew on poems, sermons, and magazine pieces, and on files of a literary digest. The book argues the dry experiment against the grain of its years.
60867-history-of-the-late-polish-revolut:
A History of the Late Polish Revolution is Joseph Hordynski's eyewitness account of Poland's rising and the campaign that followed it. Hordynski was a major of the late Tenth Regiment of Lithuanian Lancers. This fourth edition was printed at Boston for subscribers in 1833, and its frontispiece shows Kosciuszko.

In his address to the United States, Hordynski says he was freed from prison by American citizens and welcomed on these shores. In return he gives a faithful account of the revolution's true causes: fourteen years in which Poland's natural rights and its solemnly guaranteed constitution were trampled under foot. His sources are his own recollections as an eye-witness, the reports of friends and comrades present, and the official reports of the army. He promises to show how small forces beat a colossal power, and what doomed the cause at last.
61196-the-dawn-of-modern-medicine-an-acc:
Albert Buck wrote The Dawn of Modern Medicine, printed by Yale University Press in 1920 on the Williams Memorial Publication Fund. Buck had taught diseases of the ear at Columbia University in New York. The subtitle calls the book an account of the revival of the science and art of medicine in western Europe. That revival ran from the latter half of the eighteenth century into the first part of the nineteenth.

The book carries on the account given in The Growth of Medicine, up to about 1860. A portrait of Antoine Laurent Lavoisier fronts the volume. The caption credits him with the largest share in our knowledge of oxygen. Three generations of the Williams family at Yale Medical School stand behind the fund that paid for the book.
61228-the-big-headache:
The Big Headache by Jim Harmon ran in Worlds of If in September 1962. Two lab men, Ferris and Mitchell, have a cure for the worst of pains and no cash to test it. Their trustees left them short, and Ferris rubs his brow, ripe with the sire of all aches. Mitchell hints he should try the cure on his own head. Ferris cries foul: to test his own find on his own flesh breaks the code of his trade.

So they eye Elliot Macklin, the famed mind the world links with Einstein. Macklin builds a drive to outrun light for the Army, but a past stroke dogs his health. If he fails, the stars wait. Fans of lab tales get a neat knot of pride, ethics, and pain, tied with a smile.
61238-the-diary-of-delia-being-a-veracio:
The Diary of Delia is a comic novel by Onoto Watanna, published in New York by Doubleday, Page in 1907. May Wilson Preston drew its illustrations. Its sub-title calls it a veracious chronicle of the kitchen, with side-lights on the parlour. Delia is an Irish cook in a fine house, and the diary is hers. Her spelling is writ as she speaks it. She got up at siven, she writes, washed, dressed, and set the kittle on the gas stove.

She rings the breakfast bell in fury, but the family does not stir till nine. Mr John pushes his eggs aside and takes up his paper. Delia speaks up for her cooking, and the war of kitchen and parlour begins. The book is a servant's-eye view of a rich house. Watanna gives Delia wit, pride, and a tongue that rules her page.
61610-ralph-osborn-midshipman-at-annapol:
Ralph Osborn, Midshipman at Annapolis is a boys' novel by Lieutenant Commander Edward L Beach of the United States Navy, published in 1909 with pictures by Frank T Merrill. Ralph Osborn wins a place at the Naval Academy and learns the trade of a naval officer through classes, cruises, and scrapes.

Contents follow a competitive examination, the cheating methods of classmate Thomas G Short, and the start of the summer practice cruise. Later chapters bring a man overboard, a boiler explosion, Ralph kidnapped, and Ralph saving Bollup from dismissal. Beach wrote from inside the service, and the story doubles as a tour of academy life, its rules, ranks, and drills in the years before the First World War.
61647-a-popular-history-of-england-from-:
A Popular History of England, volume one, is by Guizot, printed at New York. Guizot also wrote a popular history of France, told to his grandchildren and known everywhere. Lovell issued the authorized edition, illustrated, with a frontispiece of the murder of Thomas A Becket. Pictures inside show Caractacus before Claudius and Alfred in the herdsman's hut.

Guizot's preface says his French history supplied a want felt by children and parents alike. The English volume aims at the same readers. It runs from the earliest times to the reign of Queen Victoria. The book tells a nation's story in the plain, story-like manner that made its French sister famous.
61732-experimental-mechanics-a-course-of:
Sir Robert Stawell Ball wrote Experimental Mechanics, a course of lectures given at the Royal College of Science for Ireland. Macmillan in London and New York issued a second edition in eighteen eighty eight. The first edition had been printed in eighteen seventy one. Ball was Astronomer Royal of Ireland and had taught applied mathematics and mechanism at the college. A plate shows that the path of a projectile is a parabola.

Ball says in his preface that his class was a large evening class made up chiefly of artisans. He holds that teachers of mechanics at all levels want to show working gear to their pupils. Fine, large apparatus and careful measures in front of the class make lessons stick. Ball gives such shows and measures in print, with plates. Workers and teachers alike get a clear, hands on path into mechanics.
61828-a-popular-history-of-england-from-:
A Popular History of England, volume II, continues M Guizot's history from the earliest times to Queen Victoria. John W Lovell published this authorised edition in New York. The parting of Sir Thomas More and his daughter fronts the volume. Chapter thirteen covers the grandeur and decline of Henry V and Henry VI. The years run from 1418 to 1461.

Chapter fourteen is titled Red Rose and White Rose. Edward IV's reign, 1461 to 1483, carries the Wars of the Roses. The illustrations list reads like a gallery of the age. The French chivalry keep vigil before Agincourt. Joan of Arc recognises the French king. Henry Tudor is crowned on Bosworth field. Warbeck confesses, and Henry VII's chapel and tomb appear. Henry VIII lands at Calais, and Wolsey is served by noblemen. Anne of Cleves and Mary Queen of Scots close the plate list.
61966-abraham-lincoln-s-lost-speech-may-:
Abraham Lincoln's Lost Speech is a keep sake book of a great talk of the year eighteen fifty six. It was made for a feast of a club of the chief's camp in New York. That feast fell in the year eighteen ninety seven. The book was one of five hundred struck from type that year. A press note at the front swears to that run.

The lost talk was spoke at the first state meet of the new camp at a town of the west. Its date was the twenty ninth of the fifth month. The stir it made past the crowd was so great, the tale says, that the men of the sheets lost their notes. For years men held that no roll of the talk had been kept.
62277-a-popular-history-of-england-from-:
Guizot wrote A Popular History of England, and this fourth volume carries the story toward the reign of Queen Victoria. The book is illustrated throughout, with plates of kings, queens, battles, and great scenes. Its chapters move in order from one reign to the next, each with its dates set out in the contents.

The volume opens with William and Mary and the settling of rule by Parliament, dated 1688 to 1702. Queen Anne and the War of the Spanish Succession follow, then George the First and George the Second. Long chapters on George the Third take in the American war, Pitt, and the French wars. Plates show the death of Wolfe, the death of Nelson, and Waterloo.
62598-an-essay-on-the-origin-of-language:
Essay on the Origin of Language is a work by Frederic Farrar, published in London in 1860. John Murray issued the book from Albemarle Street in that year. Farrar was late fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, as the title page states. The essay is based on modern researches, and especially on the works of Renan.

Farrar dedicates the pages to Richard Garnett of the British Museum, in remembrance of many acts of kindness. In his preface he wishes the little book to be in every respect as unpretending as possible. He does not presume to represent himself as an original investigator in the field, he adds. The question of how speech began was then a parlour and pulpit battleground of science. Farrar, a schoolmaster and future dean, sums up the evidence for general readers.
62795-a-journey-made-in-the-summer-of-17:
Ann Radcliffe wrote A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794, in two volumes, here in a second edition. Robinson printed it at London in 1795. The trip runs through Holland and the western frontier of Germany, with a return down the Rhine. Added notes tell of a tour to the lakes of Lancashire, Westmorland, and Cumberland. Radcliffe warns that the book speaks in the plural, as a pair, not as one voice.

Her nearest relative and friend, her husband, shared each sight and note on the road. She would have put both names on the title page, by her own wish. He held his share too small for that honor, and she yields the point. The note shows a rare care for truth in a travel book.
62837-ecclesiastical-history-of-england-:
John Stoughton wrote an Ecclesiastical History of England, Volume One, The Church of the Civil Wars, at London in 1867. The full work runs from the Long Parliament to the death of Oliver Cromwell. Praise for Stoughton's past books heads the volume. One past book told of church and state two hundred years past.

Review lines praise his free search and calm, fair tone. One calls his tale of the Puritan ejection the best yet writ. A short note at the front says English letters hold sound church tales but room stays for more. Stoughton writes for church folk and for all who care for the faith past of England. The tone seeks to be just to all sides.
62856-a-treatise-of-human-nature-being-a:
David Hume wrote this treatise, here in the edition of Green and Grose from Longmans in 1874. Hume's Dialogues on natural religion are bound with the Treatise in this set. Green, the Oxford philosopher, supplies introductions to the books and notes throughout the volumes.

A transcriber's note explains that contents now refer to paragraphs instead of pages here. Notes that stood in the margins appear as captions above the paragraphs in this text. Hume, a young Scot in France, tried to bring the experimental method of reasoning into moral subjects, and the Treatise became the boldest work of the British Enlightenment.
62900-opus-21-descriptive-music-for-the-:
Opus 21 is a comic novel by Philip Wylie, first printed in 1949. Rinehart published it in New York and Toronto that April. Its subtitle calls it descriptive music for the atomic age. It bills itself as a concerto for a one man band. Six arias for soap operas are also promised on the title page. Fugues, anthems, and barrelhouse are named as its modes. A warning page says most characters in the book are unreal.

That is particularly true of the author, the warning jokes. Few of the events ever took place exactly, it adds. Wylie had written Gladiator and Generation of Vipers by then. A list of his books fills the front pages here. Seven printings ran from 1949 to 1959. He dedicated this romance to his wife and his daughter. The book is a satirist's musical caper in prose form.
63117-description-of-the-process-of-manu:
Description of the Process of Manufacturing Coal Gas, by Fredrick Accum, came out at London in 1819 with seven plates. Accum shows the gear used at the London gas works and in the chief country towns, with views, sections, and plans. Tables of cost compare the cheapest ways of getting gas light for streets, houses, and public buildings.

Accum had built gas gear by order of government at the Royal Mint. His preface marvels at the speed of the new light's spread and at the flood of capital behind it. He writes as a working chemist who lectured on the useful arts.
63453-john-law-of-lauriston-financier-an:
John Law of Lauriston is a biography by Wiston-Glynn, printed at Edinburgh. Its subject stands named on the title page as financier and statesman. Law founded the Bank of France and started the Mississippi Scheme. A portrait from the National Portrait Gallery fronts the book.

The first chapter follows Law's birth, schooling, and early love of finance. It tells of his London duel with Beau Wilson and his trial for murder. Escaped to France, he gambled across the Continent and studied banking. Later chapters trace his land bank plan, refused by Scotland's Parliament. Then France takes him up, and his bank and scheme shake a kingdom.
63608-dick-merriwell-s-heroic-players-or:
Dick Merriwells Heroic Players is a boys sport tale in the Merriwell line. The full title says its plot is how the Yale nine won their game. Cheap print ads in the front list a long run of Frank and Dick tales. Each book in the line sold for just fifteen cents a copy.

The ads boast half a million fans for the two clean lived brothers. Fun and thrills in all sports form the stock of the whole line. High moral tone is claimed as a prime good of the books for boys. Ball craft and pluck on the Yale field drive this one tale. The set aims to fire a boy to train hard and think straight.
63763-prospects-of-the-church-of-england:
Vaughan, vicar of Doncaster, preached a sermon on August 30, 1868, on the future of the Church of England. The talk marked the first gift plate in place of a church rate in his parish church. Friends in the flock asked him to print it, and he agreed with frank doubt of its worth.

His text asks why the breaches of the house have not been made good, from the Books of Kings. The tale runs through Elijah, Elisha, and the fall of the house of Ahab in the north. Athaliah, a queen of pride and crime in the south, shows how rot can spread in a house of faith.
63983-a-few-remarks-concerning-makers-of:
A Few Remarks Concerning Makers of Singing Bird Boxes of the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries is a small connoisseur's pamphlet issued by Tiffany and Company of New York. It treats the mechanical singing bird snuff boxes made by Swiss watchmakers.

The invention dates, the pamphlet says, from about the middle of the eighteenth century. The boxes were praised so highly that the principal courts of Europe bought them at once. An antique box can be told, we learn, by a triple movement: the bird, while singing and moving its wings, opens its beak as it turns its head. Modern watchmakers, the author laments, cannot match that skill. The discovery belongs to Pierre Jaquet-Droz, a Swiss watchmaker summoned by the King of Spain in 1758. His automata were so marvellous that the Inquisition once wanted to condemn him as a sorcerer.
64143-soil-and-water-pollution-presented:
Moses Runnels, an Indianapolis physician, read this paper to the American Public Health Association at New Orleans in December eighteen eighty. Duncan Brothers printed it the same year. His subject is the filth under cities: soil and water fouled by privies, cesspools, and drainage, and the fevers that follow.

Runnels opens with the sanitary arithmetic of his day. He holds that nearly half of disease could be abolished by correct modes of living, and that over one hundred thousand Americans die each year from preventable causes. His city supplies the proof: deaths from zymotic diseases in Indianapolis rose sharply in eighteen seventy nine, and nearly a third of the city's deaths came from that class. The paper is a piece of the public health movement, when doctors were teaching towns that clean water and clean soil were a government's first duty.
64218-a-journey-made-in-the-summer-of-17:
A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794 is a travel book by Ann Radcliffe. This is volume two of the second edition, printed in London in 1795. Robinson published it at Paternoster Row. The full title promises Holland and Germany's western frontier. A return down the Rhine completes that tour's plan. Observations during a tour to the Lakes are added to it. Lancashire, Westmorland, and Cumberland are those lake counties. This volume opens its travel text at Friburg.

Friburg is an ancient imperial city and capital of the Brisgau. Its name alludes to the privileges of such free cities, she writes. The traveller descends to it and sees the great church spire first. The stones of that spire are laid with open spaces. Light appears through its tapering sides as she describes it. Radcliffe the novelist writes travel with a painter's eye.
64226-ecclesiastical-history-of-england-:
John Stoughton wrote a church history of England that runs from the start of the Long Parliament to the death of Oliver Cromwell. Volume two is called The Church of the Commonwealth. It was printed in London by Jackson, Walford, and Hodder. The date on the title page is MDCCCLXVII. Eight long chapters fill the volume.

Inside, Stoughton tracks fights over church rule under the Commonwealth and the Protectorate. He covers the battles of Dunbar and Worcester and the trial of Christopher Love. He then treats the Little Parliament, the rise of Cromwell as Protector, and rules for preachers. Chapters also deal with Scotland, Wales, and Ireland, and with groups such as the Presbyterians. The book suits readers of church and state in that age.
64233-the-postage-stamps-envelopes-wrapp:
The Philatelic Society of London compiled this handbook on the early stamps of Britain's North American colonies. It came out in London in 1889, with autotype plates of the rare pieces. Canada and the old colonies, before and after their unions, fill its ground.

Its preface opens the hunt with calm pride. The study of the issues of labels, wrappers, and envelopes tied to those postal systems, it says, held fewer bars than other fields of the craft. Pioneer work still stood open here. Each colony's stamps, stamped envelopes, wrappers, and post cards stand in order, with dates, printings, and marks. The society's men were the founders of stamp science, and this is their field manual for one rich corner.
6426-dick-prescott-s-first-year-at-west-:
H. Irving Hancock, in a 1910 Saalfield book, follows Dick Prescott and Greg Holmes through a first year at West Point in cadet grey. Two tiny specks of nothing opens the tale, as Greg whispers to Dick, asking how he feels, spruce as an hour ago, with a half nervous laugh. The tyranny of the cadet corporal, lucky ones taking up new life, and Greg's blues follow.

Candidate Dodge is critical, yearling hazers take the plebes in hand, and a sudden grind at math, Dick's trouble, and a first fight test the chums. Dodge holds post number three, Prescott gets it, a sentry makes a capture, and Greg overhears a pretty girl's tribute. Hancock writes boy's military school life with drill, hazing, and friendship, where two chums learn to stand their ground together.
6427-the-story-of-rome-from-the-earliest:
Arthur Gilman rehearses Rome's lustrous story from myth and fable's mists to the republic's mischievous end, just before empire's brilliant period opens. Once upon a time, Troy's old king, Paris the wayward youth, Helen carried off, and a ten year war lead to Aeneas, son of Anchises, sailing to Italy. Fact and fiction shade into each other in early stories, as Milton, Virgil, and Livy each retell Aeneas in turn.

Shepherds begin the city, with Romulus and Remus on two hills, vultures deciding, Pales god of shepherds, and an asylum for bachelors wanting wives. A game of wife snatching, Sabines wanting daughters back, and Tarpeia on the hill follow. Later, Icilius holds a loved one's body before the forum people, crying Appius's work, and tumult drives Appius home. Gilman writes Rome for young readers, as story first and history second.
64470-biblical-revision-its-duties-and-c:
Henry Alford, Dean of Canterbury, preached Biblical Revision: Its Duties and Conditions at St Paul's Cathedral on Sunday, March the thirteenth, eighteen seventy. The printed sermon came from Strahan of Ludgate Hill that year. Its text is the verse on the scribe instructed unto the kingdom of heaven, who brings out of his treasure things new and old. Alford opens on the scribes as guardians of the law.

Ezra, he says, was a ready scribe who prepared his heart to seek the law and teach it. The scribes acted for the whole people, to whom the oracles of God were committed. The church in all times, Alford argues, is the witness and keeper of Holy Writ. Against that charge he sets the duties of revising the English Bible in his own day.
64499-darwinism-the-noachian-flood-a-lec:
Darwinism: The Noachian Flood is a lecture by Thomas Stebbing, given before the Torquay Natural History Society on January 31, 1870, and printed in London that year. Stebbing had been a fellow and tutor of Worcester College, Oxford. His theme is set out at the start.

Darwinism, he says, implies almost throughout that no world wide deluge has drowned the globe. That holds, he adds, for the last ten thousand years, and for a far longer span. He asks hearers to speak with due respect of the contrary belief. It seems to rest, he says, on the word of the most precious volume in the world. For ages it was taken for granted in science as in religion. Readers get an early, fair minded clash of geology and Genesis.
64876-the-numbering-of-the-people-a-serm:
The Numbering of the People is a church talk by the Reverend George Allen, printed in eighteen sixty-one. Allen held a church post in Islington and a lore post at a London school. He gave the talk on a Sunday night in April of that year, the week of the great count of the realm. The count of souls is its theme.

The text is drawn from the book of Numbers, where a chief of old is told to take the sum of his folk. The talk was not writ for print, but his flock pressed him to print it. Gains from its sale went to buy a new organ for the church. The print gives the talk just as it was spoke from the stand.
65090-report-to-her-majesty-s-principal-:
The Poor Law Commissioners presented this report on the sanitary condition of the labouring population of Great Britain to both Houses of Parliament in July 1842. It is addressed to Sir James Graham, secretary of state for the home department. A covering letter from Somerset House traces its origins.

In May 1838 the commissioners had reported on disallowed charges, with supplements by Neil Arnott and James Phillips Kay on the physical causes of fever in the metropolis. Those causes, the doctors argued, might be removed by proper sanitary measures. This great inquiry, Edwin Chadwick's work, made the case in full. Readers get the founding document of public health in Britain.
65293-owen-s-moral-physiology-or-a-brief:
Robert Dale Owen wrote the first frank English book on birth control, and Ralph Glover reissued it in this form. Moral Physiology, in this second edition with changes, came from Glover at New York in 1846. A plate heads it with a cry: alas that it ever should have been born.

The population question is its plain theme. Bentham gives its law: the principle of utility is the base of the whole work. Chapters weigh the question in the abstract, in trade and state, and in its social bearings. Its tie to the body gets a chapter of its own, and a word to the married closes the text. A brave, banned, much-burned book of its day.
65334-ecclesiastical-history-of-england-:
John Stoughton wrote this Church of the Restoration history volume here. Hodder and Stoughton printed it in London in the year 1870. An advertisement says past volumes stated facts without party favour sought. Critics and friends of opposed views praised the method used there.

Writing this history was the dream of his life long ago. Twenty five years of reading bent toward the church story then. He studied church affairs from Commonwealth to Revolution for years past. Lords and Commons journals and Thurloe state papers fed the work. Cardwell Synodalia and the Parliamentary History stand named among the printed sources he used.
65477-freedom-equality-justice-these-thr:
Freedom, Equality, Justice is a speech by Victoria Woodhull on the revolt to come. She gave it at a music hall in Boston on the first of February in eighteen seventy-two. She gave it again at a hall in New York past that month but two. Her house put it in print that year. Its name ranks three words and calls the last the most great.

She stands on the peak of her age and looks back past the past of man. Realms rose and fell, races grew and waned, yet one tide ran on past all. In old days worth was weighed by the sword, she says. Now the steam ship, the iron horse, the wire that speaks, and the press are the beat men of the age. Ties past lands grow each year till main lands clasp hands past seas.
65487-lightning-jo-the-terror-of-the-san:
Captain Adams wrote this dime novel of the Santa Fe Trail, published in New York by Beadle and Adams in 1874 as a tale of the present day. The story opens at Fort Adams, where a rider gallops in on a black mustang that drops dead at the gate. He carries a penciled plea for help from a besieged party.

The note says the party has fought the Comanches for two days, half its men are killed or wounded, and women and children are among them, forty miles away. Colonel Greaves reads the appeal and feels both its urgency and the near impossibility of answering it in time. From that desperate errand the tale builds its hero, Lightning Jo, in the fast and rough style of the cheap story papers.
65628-the-natural-history-of-the-tea-tre:
The Natural History of the Tea-Tree, with notes on the medical traits of tea and the effects of tea drinking, is by John Coakley Lettsom. A new edition was printed in London in 1799, with a plate of green tea drawn and cut by Miller in 1771. Lettsom notes that his first work on tea was a Latin thesis of 1769.

A fuller study came in 1772, and the book grew from that base. Lettsom treats the plant's form, kinds, and growth, then asks what tea does to the body, for good or ill. Wide tables and notes on past writers such as Kaempfer support the text. The book serves doctors, merchants, and keen tea drinkers alike.
65673-putnam-s-automobile-handbook-the-c:
Putnam's Automobile Handbook: The Care and Management of the Modern Motor-Car is a practical manual by Clifford Brokaw and Charles Starr. Brokaw was principal, and Starr on the staff, of the Automobile School of the West Side YMCA of New York City. Putnam's Sons published it in 1918, with a sectional view of a four-cylinder car as frontispiece. Its chapters begin with what to do on purchasing a car.

A passage preserved in the copy sets the beginner's path. The buyer gets a certain amount of instruction from the salesman: the pedals, levers, and switches, and how to run the car. But more is needed. Later chapters explain what an automobile is and what makes the engine go. Equipment, lubrication, smoking engines, and the carburetor and its failings follow.
65789-sweaters-he-and-she:
Sweaters He and She is a knitting pattern booklet, Star Book Number 223, sold for thirty-five cents. The American Thread Company printed it in the United States. Its cover pattern is an Aran cardigan for men and women alike. Sizes run from ladies' small to men's large, with changes marked in parentheses and bold type.

The pattern calls for Dawn knitting worsted, eight to eleven four-ounce skeins for the cardigan. A beanie takes four ounces and a beret five. Needles number six and eight set the work, at a gauge of eleven stitches to two inches. The back begins with ninety-eight stitches cast on and five rows of ribbing. The booklet gives home knitters a fisherman sweater in full.
65954-general-crook-and-the-fighting-apa:
Edwin Sabin wrote General Crook and the Fighting Apaches, printed in 1918. The book stands in the American Trail Blazers line. That line, a page at the front says, presents in vivid story form the early, bold phases of American history. Each volume treats one of the great men who made that history, or one great event.

The subtitle tells the frame: also the part borne by Jimmie Dunn in the days 1871 to 1886. In those days Crook, the Gray Fox, worked with soldiers, pack-trains, and Indian scouts. But his stronger weapons were kindness, firmness, and honesty. He worked so white men and red men might better understand one another. A word from Chief Red Cloud heads the book: then General Crook came; he, at least, had never lied to us. Plates by Stephens and a map go with the tale.
65972-the-plague-of-athens-which-hapned-:
The Plague of Athens is an English poem on the great pestilence of the Peloponnesian War, rendered by Sprat. It was printed in London in 1665, with leave given by Roger L'Estrange that March. The title page traces the poem's descent in three tongues.

Thucydides first described the plague in Greek. Lucretius then treated it in Latin verse. Sprat now attempts it in English. His dedication to a learned friend at Oxford is modest to a fault. He calls his copy rude and unpolished beside its patterns. He notes that Thucydides had the edge over the poet. The historian was on the spot and sickened of the disease himself. The horror was thus fresh in his mind when he wrote.
6608-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
On and near the Delaware, Skinner turns to war ghosts and brave deeds from the Revolution. A phantom dragoon rides Iron Hill near Newark, where British tents once stood before Brandywine, and a phantom drummer and a missing soldier of Valley Forge follow. Tales of Germantown, Brandywine, and Printz Hall mix battle with haunting.

A Tory's change of heart, a Bible that saves a life, and a father's dream all show how lore grew from real fear and faith. Skinner keeps each tale short and place-bound, so the Delaware country itself feels like a character. This third volume is a fine mix of history, ghost story, and local pride.
66231-wolf-cap-or-the-night-hawks-of-the:
Howard wrote a frontier tale for Beadle and Adams in New York, entered for copyright in 1871. Wolf Cap tells of night hawks in the Fire Lands, near a fort the tale calls bloody. Howard had already written Elk King, Wolf Queen, and Merciless Matt. Fifteen chapters of war and treason follow.

The first chapter opens in a log room at night. A trapper rests by a great fire, his head on a huge yellow mastiff. The dog stirs, and Johnny Appleseed comes down the river with news. Later chapters bring Silver Hand the Wyandot, a battle at Strong's, and a mutiny. Treason in the camp and a wolf den lead to the last chapter, named retribution.
6632-a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-t:
Thomas D'Arcy McGee tells Ireland's story in volume one, from the earliest period to the point where volume two takes up the tale. His publishers' preface paints Ireland rising from dust, drying her tears, and claiming her place among nations. For five hundred years, they say, her life seemed put out, save for a flash of old spirit now and then.

McGee writes as a champion of Ireland, keen to show a fame that spread wide before England's flag even flew. The history that follows is popular in style, meant for wide reading rather than for scholars alone. Volume one lays the ground for the long struggle toward Catholic emancipation.
6633-a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-t:
Volume two of McGee's Irish history picks up at book eight, chapter four, with Sir Henry Sidney's deputyship and the parliament of 1569. The second Geraldine League, the undertakers in Ulster and Leinster, and the plantation of Munster follow in quick, troubled succession. Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, and Hugh Roe O'Donnell rise as the tale moves toward war.

Glenmalure, the Spanish Armada, and the Ulster confederacy fill the later chapters, with campaigns, talks, and escapes. McGee keeps the narrative vivid and partisan, on Ireland's side throughout. Volume two carries the story through its hardest years, toward the long fight for faith and land.
6634-a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-t:
McGee's complete history runs from Ireland's earliest period through to Catholic emancipation, in twelve books rather than in separate volumes. The same proud preface opens it: Ireland lifting herself from dust and tears to claim her place among nations, after centuries when her life seemed put out. This longer text carries the tale past the break that ends volume one.

Readers get the full arc in one place, from ancient fame through oppression, revolt, and the slow road to emancipation. McGee writes with passion and a popular touch, for readers who want a story, not a dry chronicle. The complete history is the best single-volume path through his Irish epic.
66350-the-remains-of-hesiod-the-ascr-an-:
Charles Abraham Elton made The Remains of Hesiod the Ascrean, in a second edition revised and enlarged. Baldwin, Cradock, and Joy printed it at London in 1815. It holds the Shield of Hercules, in English rhyme and blank verse. A dissertation on the life, era, poems, and mythology of Hesiod stands with the verse. Full notes serve the reader at each step of the text.

Elton says the remains draw more than the antiquary's care. Hesiod shows the rude arts and manners of the early Greeks, he holds. His high views of a justice that pays back wrong give weight to the verse. Chapman had Englished the Works and Days as far back as 1618, in a form now very scarce. Elton gives English readers the whole scant store of a poet ranked with Homer.
66466-the-corsair-a-romantic-legend-of-h:
The Corsair is a long poem by an unknown author, first edited in eighteen eighty-five. Wm B Allen and Company published it in New York. Its subtitle calls it a romantic legend of Hell Gate illustrating the beauty of innocence. The action is dated midsummer sixteen twenty-seven.

The preface explains that the historical matter was moved to an appendix. Readers could therefore begin the story at once and read the facts afterward. The appendix gives the history of the strait from the earliest times. Hell Gate is the turbulent passage whose name suggests wreck and disaster. Readers also learn why the pirate's daughter feared as the vessel approached it. The volume pairs a verse romance of early New York waters with that factual sketch.
66555-psyche-the-cult-of-souls-and-belie:
Erwin Rohde's study of the cult of souls and belief in immortality among the Greeks appeared in English at London in 1925, translated from the eighth edition by W B Hillis. Part one opens with beliefs about the soul in the Homeric poems. Islands of the blest form the second chapter. Cave deities and subterranean powers follow.
