Heroes get a chapter of their own, then the cult of souls itself. Rohde was a German classical scholar and friend of Nietzsche. His Psyche became a standard work on Greek religion. The translation carried his learning to English readers. Rohde traced how hero worship and soul cult shaped Greek ideas of life after death.
66716-the-supernatural-in-early-spanish-:
Frank Callcott wrote The Supernatural in Early Spanish Literature, printed at New York in nineteen twenty-three. Callcott taught Romance tongues at Columbia. His study looks at works from the court of Alfonso the Tenth, called El Sabio, the Wise. The opening argues that the mind clings to what it cannot grasp, and drops a trick once the trick is explained.

That pull, Callcott says, has been used by warriors, priests, and singers through all ages. A man face to face with death turns to powers beyond the seen world. Callcott sets out to trace that bent in the beliefs and acts of old Spain. He cites Dorothy Scarborough's study of the supernatural in modern English tales as a guide for his own path.
67041-treatment-of-cholera-in-the-royal-:
John Wilson, inspector of naval hospitals and fleets, wrote this account of the treatment of cholera at the Royal Hospital, Haslar, during July and August 1849. It was printed in London that same year. Wilson adds remarks on the name and origin of the disease to his report of what the hospital actually did.

On admission, he says, the patient went at once into a hot bath, with strong rubbing of the belly and limbs where the spasms struck. Doses followed in a steady routine: tincture of opium, then calomel every hour or half hour, oil of turpentine in mucilage, and enemas of turpentine and opium. Rubbing with turpentine and olive oil went on all the while.
67042-the-aftermath-or-gleanings-from-a-:
The Aftermath is a book of literary gleanings by Hilaire Belloc. Dutton published it in New York under that title. Its subtitle calls it gleanings from a busy life. The outer cover called it Caliban's Guide to Letters for purposes of sale. A page of press opinions opens the volume in jest. Further and yet more weighty opinions are promised there. One paper found the book very tedious, the quote runs. Belloc answers in brackets that the reviewer was drummed out of a regiment.

Another paper cannot see what Caliban's Guide is driving at. It is driving at you, Belloc answers in the same bracketed way. A third paper asks simply what, again, in despair. The joke front matter sets a combative, laughing tone. Gleanings gather the odds and ends of a writing life. Belloc turns his own reviews into part of the entertainment.
67175-legend-land-vol-3-being-a-further-:
Volume three of Legend Land, the Great Western Railway's sixpenny collection of old tales from the western parts of Britain it served, published at Paddington in 1923 and retold by Lyonesse. A map marks the legend places from Narberth Castle to St Govan's Chapel.

The contents mix Wales and Cornwall: St Melangell and her lambs, where King Arthur sleeps, Bronwen and the starling, and the swan of Glasfryn. Cornish tales follow: the fairy gardens of Treen, the charmer of Pengersick, and the spectre of Rosewarne. The first tale retells Manawyddan at Narberth, whose harvest is eaten by sorcery and who resolves to hang a mouse. A Cornish three-man's song supplements the volume. Railway travelers get folklore by the line.
67176-legend-land-vol-4-being-a-further-:
Legend Land, volume four, collects old tales from the west of Britain served by the Great Western Railway. The volume reprints the fourth series of the Line to Legend Land leaflets, with a supplement printing the oldest English song. Maps guide the reader to each tale's ground.

The first tale is the Whispering Knights, the Rollright Stones on a Cotswold spur. High on a Cotswold spur where Warwickshire meets Oxfordshire stands the Rollright Stones, a miniature Stonehenge. The story says they were a king and his courtiers turned to stone by evil spells. A witch promised the marching king the crown of England if he could see Long Compton from the hill; treachery blocked his view at the last moment. The other tales run from King Arthur's Camelot and the Witch of Wookey to Herne the Hunter and Wayland Smith. It is folklore as railway publicity, and charming at it.
67413-ecclesiastical-history-of-england-:
John Stoughton tells church history in The Church of the Restoration, part of his Ecclesiastical History of England. The pages in hand are volume 2 of the part, printed in London in 1870. Chapter heads map a time of plots, tests, and harsh laws.

The Popish Plot opens the book, with Titus Oates and the act to bar Catholics. Then come the fall of Danby, the Exclusion Bill, and the fall of Shaftesbury. Nonconformists face fresh pain, and the Rye House Plot shakes the court. The death of Charles the Second and the reign of James the Second close the span. Monmouth's revolt and the trial of Baxter stand out.
67425-knightly-legends-of-wales-or-the-b:
Knightly Legends of Wales, or The Boy's Mabinogion, retells the earliest Welsh tales of King Arthur for boys. The tales come from the famous Red Book of Hergest, as the title states. Sidney Lanier edited the book with an introduction, following his boy's editions of Froissart and of King Arthur. Illustrations by Alfred Frederick appear in the hosted edition.

A picture shows Kai and his companions at the castle of a giant, setting the tone of quest and wonder. Lanier aimed to give boys the wild Welsh Arthur, older and stranger than the courtly English version. Giants, magic, and hard riding fill these tales. The edition's copyright pages reach back to eighteen eighty one, with later printings for new readers.
67428-type-and-presses-in-america-a-brie:
Type and Presses in America is a short history of type casting and press building in the United States by Frederick Hamilton. It is part eight, number 55, of the Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices. The United Typothetae published it in 1918. Hamilton was that body's education director.

The first chapter tells of the pioneer type founders. For all the early years, he says, every piece of type used in America was imported. The first type cast in the country was made by Christopher Sauer at Germantown, Pennsylvania, about 1735. Later chapters cover the growth of founding, composing machines, electrotyping, and the development of the printing press.
67447-an-authentic-history-of-the-cato-s:
George Theodore Wilkinson's Authentic History of the Cato-Street Conspiracy was printed for Thomas Kelly of Paternoster Row. Wilkinson edited the New Newgate Calendar Improved. A portrait of Arthur Thistlewood fronts the volume. The full title promises the trials at large of the conspirators for high treason and murder. It also describes their weapons and combustible machines, with every particular of the plot's rise, discovery, and end. Portraits of all the conspirators, taken during their trials, illustrate the book.

The preface paints postwar Britain rescued from anarchy, its artisans back at the shuttle and its sailors at their hearths. Against that peace it sets the pestilential air of atheism and infidelity abroad in the land. The conspirators are framed as men who threw off all duty to God, sovereign, and law. The book is a contemporary account of the 1820 plot against the cabinet.
67727-ecclesiastical-history-of-england-:
Ecclesiastical History of England, volume 5, is subtitled The Church of the Revolution. John Stoughton wrote the history, and Hodder and Stoughton published it in London in 1874. The volume covers the church under William III and his successors. In his advertisement Stoughton explains where he gave extra space, and why.

The attempt at Comprehension in 1689 fills a large part of the volume. Stoughton prints the Lords' bill for it in an appendix, apparently for the first time. He worked from the journals of both Houses and a diary in Dr Williams' Library. The Tanner manuscripts at Oxford and the Gibson papers at Lambeth supplied more. Nonjurors, convocation, and Trinitarian disputes all get fresh treatment. He also traces the first religious societies of the reign. The SPCK and the SPG opened their earliest records to him.
67824-a-statement-of-facts-tending-to-es:
Sir Gilbert Blane, physician in ordinary to the King, wrote this statement of facts on vaccination, printed in London in 1820. The paper first ran in the tenth volume of the Medico-Chirurgical Transactions, read on November 10, 1819, and gains additions here. Blane belonged to the Royal Societies of London, Edinburgh, and Göttingen, and to the Imperial Academy of St Petersburg.

He opens with the count of years: twenty-one since Jenner brought vaccination forward in this country, and fifteen since it spread. His aim is an estimate of its true value and present state, built on facts. One case tells of a mother who took smallpox a second time from her own children, while her vaccinated children held out against it.
68072-masks-with-jim-s-beast-tides-among:
Play pages list new pieces for amateur groups, with casts, scenes, running times, and prices. Mrs Partridge Presents, a comedy in three acts by Mary Kennedy and Ruth Hawthorne, calls for six males and six females. Modern costumes and two interiors serve, and it plays two and a half hours.

The heroine is a woman of tremendous energy who manages a business with great success. At home she presides over a growing son and daughter. Her struggle to give them the opportunities she missed, and their revolt against her management, form the plot. In the Next Room, a melodrama by Eleanor Robson and Harriet Ford, follows. A rare Boule cabinet shipped from Paris drives its mystery.
68547-he:
He is a horror story by H P Lovecraft. A plate shows an old man clawing and spitting through moldy air, barking in his throat as he sways with a yellow curtain in his grip. The narrator tells the tale in the first person.

He came to New York in hope of wonder in the old, twisting streets and the black towers under waning moons. He found only horror and oppression that threatened to master and crush him. He had first seen the city at sunset from a bridge, fair above its waters, with peaks like flowers in violet mist. Then it lit window by window and seemed a dream of stars. The fall from that dream drives the tale. Lovecraft fans get a tale of a city secret best left unwhispered.
68575-the-violin-and-the-art-of-its-cons:
August Riechers, a bow and violin maker, wrote this treatise, The Violin and the Art of its Construction, a treatise on the Stradivarius violin, printed in Germany in 1895 with four plates. Riechers dedicated the work to his revered friend and patron, the violinist Joachim. A preface by the editor tells why the book came out after its author's death.

Riechers died in January 1893, denied the pleasure of publishing the work himself, and it now appears by his last wishes. No book, the editor says, has yet treated the subject in so able and thorough a manner. An index maps the craft in order: the wood, the ribs, the back and belly, the arching, the purfling, the thicknesses. Then come the sound-holes, the bass-bar, the neck, the bridge, the sound-post, the strings, the varnish, and the bow.
68906-nearest-the-pole-a-narrative-of-th:
Nearest the Pole tells how the Peary Arctic Club's expedition in the ship Roosevelt came closer to the North Pole than any party before it. Peary's narrative, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in New York in 1907, carries ninety-five photographs by the author, two maps, and a colour frontispiece by Albert Operti. The frontispiece shows Peary planting the American flag at latitude 87 degrees 6 minutes on April 21, 1906.

The book opens with Peary's speech on receiving the Hubbard Medal of the National Geographic Society from President Roosevelt on December 15, 1906. He argues that men and Eskimo dogs are the only machines fit for Arctic work, and that the American route remains the surest road to the Pole. The narrative itself then takes up the voyage of 1905 and 1906.
69084-engineers-and-their-triumphs-the-s:
F M Holmes wrote Engineers and Their Triumphs, a plain account of great works of the past century. Fleming H Revell sold the book in New York, Chicago, and Toronto. Tower Bridge with its leaves raised faces the title page. Holmes wrote for lay readers, not for trained men.

Four fields carry the tale from start to end. Rail engines come first, then steam ships that cross wide seas. Bridge work and tunnel work close the set. Holmes thanks the Cunard and White Star lines for facts. Henry Bell and his ship Comet get a full early strand. Macgregor Laird wins praise for pushing steam trips to America. Feats that shrank the world fill each short chapter.
69108-new-nick-carter-weekly-no-28-july-:
The New Nick Carter Weekly, number 28, dated July 10, 1897, is a five cent dime novel paper from Street and Smith of New York. The story in the number is Nick Carter at the Track, or How He Became a Dead Game Sport. It is signed only by the author of Nick Carter. The weekly cost two dollars and a half a year by subscription.

The tale opens in Carter's office with a Wall Street broker, James Wheeler. The money, it comes out, belongs to two heirs, both minors. Wheeler has risked it on the Brooklyn Handicap. Carter answers coldly: if he is to handle the case he must have the fullest confidence. The number is a fair specimen of the Carter machine at its weekly pace.
69582-the-life-and-times-of-the-rev-john:
L Tyerman wrote The Life and Times of the Rev John Wesley, Founder of the Methodists, issued at New York in 1872 in three volumes. Volume One is shown here. Tyerman had writ a life of Samuel Wesley, father of John and Charles. A print shows Wesley at forty from a scarce 1743 plate.

Tyerman asks why a new life is needed when six lives exist. He faults Hampson's life as thin and writ in anger. Coke and Moore's life was a hasty bid for the market, he says. Whitehead's life was tinged by party strife. Southey's life has charm but is full of faults and poor dates, he holds. Moore's full life leans too much on Whitehead. The new life seeks to fix those faults.
69670-a-voice-from-waterloo-a-history-of:
A Voice from Waterloo is a history of the battle fought on June 18, 1815, by Sergeant Major Edward Cotton. Briard printed it at Brussels. An ad at the front bills the Hotel du Musee at the foot of the Lion Mount, in the very centre of the field.

The hotel is kept by a niece of the late Sergeant Major Cotton. It is praised for its closeness to the scenes of interest and for good lodging at moderate charges. Wines and spirits of the best quality, Bass pale ale, and London porter are on sale. The history itself runs from Napoleon leaving Elba and landing in France. Louis the Eighteenth quits Paris as Napoleon, joined by the army, arrives. War fans get the battle from a man who fought it and later guided its field.
69896-the-book-of-the-child-an-attempt-t:
Frederick Douglas How wrote a book of the child, printed at Bath and published at New York in 1907, attempting to set down what is in the mind of children. Chapter one treats the child's arrival. Children, How says, have come into greater prominence during the last quarter of a century. Memory and imagination follow as separate chapters.

The child's religion, imitation, and pleasures each get a chapter. The child's pathos closes the main sequence. Wayside children and children's meetings form the final chapters, with an appendix. How wrote from a clergyman's and father's observation. The book belongs to the child study movement then reshaping education and parenting advice.
70262-the-tithe:
Rev E B Stewart, pastor of the Third United Presbyterian Church in Chicago, wrote The Tithe, issued by The Winona Publishing Company in Chicago and at Winona Lake, Indiana. The copyright is nineteen oh three, and the copy is the fourth thousand. A layman wrote the intro. A preface sets out the method and limits of the brief work.

Stewart says he has not tried to record every mention of the tithe in ancient writings. Some stress items from five hundred to eight hundred years before Christ, he notes, but they add little to the argument. He treats claims for a religious tithe before Moses with caution. Scholars such as Mr Johns and Professor Sayce are weighed on a key word in Assyrian deeds. His aim is a broad view of tribute and giving. Church readers get a careful plea on tithing.
70619-a-history-of-criticism-and-literar:
History of Criticism and Literary Taste in Europe is a survey by George Saintsbury, in three volumes. The hosted text is volume one, on classical and medieval criticism. Saintsbury taught rhetoric and English literature at the University of Edinburgh. The second edition was issued at Edinburgh and London in nineteen oh two. A Latin motto warns that the judgments of the ignorant are commonly rash.

In his preface Saintsbury owns the audacity of the attempt. No explanations can tone it down, he says. Those offended at first blush will stay offended. He notes how small the first crop of material seemed, then found few persons better furnished. Johnson once projected a history of criticism, he recalls. Such projects have had many fellows since, he adds. The volume aims to trace taste from the earliest texts toward the present day.
71130-the-life-and-times-of-the-rev-john:
Tyerman wrote the life and times of John Wesley in three books. Volume two came out in New York in 1872. A plate shows Wesley at age sixty-three from a 1765 print. That print had Wesley's own nod as a true face. Tyerman wrote the life of Wesley's father as a mate work.

This book starts in 1748 with close calls and Bristol's chapel. Wild harms in Ireland and the Dublin flock fill the first list. A Carmelite friar and Dublin's first Methodist chapel stand there. Kingswood School and thoughts on wed life mark the mid years. Church past fans get a full, sourced life.
7126-the-treaties-of-canada-with-the-ind:
Alexander Morris, late chief officer of Manitoba, the North West lands, and Keewatin, sets down Canada's treaties with the Indians of Manitoba and the North West lands, with the talks behind them. He gives the book to the Earl of Dufferin, ambassador at St Petersburg, moved by Dufferin's keen care for winning Indian friendship and for tribal welfare in the Canadian North West.

Dufferin also backed opening the lands for new homes, by gaining the tribes' fair gift of title to the rich belt on just terms. Morris writes by kind leave, in honor of that care. The book keeps treaty texts, talks, and related notes, as a record of Crown and peoples making terms on a moving frontier.
71517-refraction-and-muscular-imbalance-:
Daniel Woolf wrote a guide to eye tests for his firm in New York. The Woolf Instrument Corporation held the rights in 1921. The guide shows how to use one tool, the Ski-optometer, to test how the eyes bend light and how the eye muscles work.

The tool holds spherical and cylindrical lenses in one frame, with gear to test and fix eye muscle faults. First the book tells how the tool is built and how its lenses work. Next it shows the tool at work in skioscopy, with a short way to do that test. It also shows tests where the wearer judges the view, and short steps for sphere and cylinder tests. Last come notes on how to set the tool, clean the lenses, and dodge the pain of the old trial frame.
7210-the-motor-girls-on-waters-blue-or-t:
Margaret Penrose's Motor Girls on Waters Blue opens with a car swinging into a gravel drive, brakes whining. A sun-bronzed girl lifts gloved hands from the wheel after a fast, glorious run. She locks the ignition, pauses on the bottom step, and gazes over the valley below the high-set house, tired and happy from the drive.

That motor energy soon turns to water, as the strange cruise of the Tartar promised by the title draws the girls from road to lake or sea. Penrose writes brisk, outdoor adventure for young readers, full of motion, friendship, and pluck. The opening run sets the pace for a tale where girls drive the action themselves.
72451-the-physiology-of-digestion-consid:
The Physiology of Digestion, with relation to dietetics, is a health work by Andrew Combe. Combe was a fellow of the Royal College of Physicians in Edinburgh. He also served the King and Queen of the Belgians as physician. Maclachlan and Stewart of Edinburgh printed this second edition in 1836. Simpkin, Marshall of London shared the selling of the enlarged book.

The first edition of two thousand copies sold out in five months. Twice the book had already been reprinted in the United States. About twenty pages of new matter stand added in this revision. Desire for knowledge of the human frame spreads fast, Combe rejoices. Such knowledge lies within every ordinary capacity, he insists throughout. A critic wished the physiology part more condensed for general readers. Combe kept his fuller course, trusting readers to follow the science.
72622-narrative-of-the-portuguese-embass:
Father Francisco Alvarez tells of the Portuguese Embassy to Abyssinia during the years 1520 to 1527, printed for the Hakluyt Society in 1881. Lord Stanley of Alderley translated it from the Portuguese and added notes and an introduction. The editor calls it the earliest extant work on Abyssinia.

Pedro de Covilham reached the country more than thirty years before Alvarez, sent out by King John the Second in 1487, but left no written memorial of his long stay. Alvarez's own book was first printed in black letter in 1540 and spread through many tongues, often cut down. This version gives it whole.
73128-a-history-of-criticism-and-literar:
History of Criticism and Literary Taste in Europe, volume two, is a work by George Saintsbury of Edinburgh. Blackwood and Sons published the second edition at Edinburgh and London in 1905. Saintsbury was professor of rhetoric and English literature in the University of Edinburgh. This volume runs from the Renaissance to the decline of eighteenth century orthodoxy.

In his preface Saintsbury feels no compunction for the large space given to English critics in the volume. A fashion set by Matthew Arnold, he argues, taught readers to bow to German and still more to French critics. The three volume history, of which this is the middle, was the first full survey of European criticism in English. Saintsbury learning and his combative taste made it a landmark that students of the subject still consult with profit.
73465-expedition-to-discover-the-sources:
Expedition to Discover the Sources of the White Nile is a travel narrative by Ferdinand Werne, covering the years 1840 and 1841. It was translated from the German and published in London by Richard Bentley in 1849, in two volumes, of which this is the first. A map of the White Nile, drawn from Werne's diary, faces the title.

The preface promises lively views of the natural productions and the peoples of regions until then entirely unvisited. It praises the writer's experience, bold energy, and deep devotion to the land of the south. The discoverer of the source of the White Nile, it says, will share the fate of his famed predecessor James Bruce. The book belongs to the great age of African exploration, when the Nile's source was the prize question of geography.
73466-expedition-to-discover-the-sources:
Expedition to Discover the Sources of the White Nile is Ferdinand Werne's account of the Egyptian expedition of 1840 and 1841. This text is volume two, translated from the German by O'Reilly. It was published in London by Richard Bentley in 1849. The contents promise hard travel among the Bari people and visits from the envoys of King Lakono.

Chapter headings tell of sleeping huts, Turkish cruelty, and negroes shot by the Turks. They also describe the religion, arms, and ornaments of the Bari, and a panic made among the people by firearms. Werne went with the force sent by the ruler of Egypt to find where the White Nile begins. His record mixes geography with a harsh picture of the expedition's conduct.
7387-grisly-grisell-or-the-laidly-lady-o:
Charlotte M. Yonge sets this historical tale in the Wars of the Roses, opening with a terrible shriek and an explosion in the great manor house at Amesbury. The heroine is Grisell, the laidly lady of Whitburn, whose story unfolds against the shifting fortunes of York and Lancaster. Yonge takes a Chaucer epigraph on women's steadfastness as her keynote.

Through danger, disgrace, and long patience, Grisell endures what the wars throw at her house and kin. Yonge, famous for family chronicles like The Heir of Redclyffe, writes here with the same moral seriousness, but in a more romantic key. The book offers a Victorian retelling of medieval England: castles and battles on the surface, and underneath, a study of loyalty held firm under pressure.
74136-psyche:
Walter Cramp wrote Psyche, published at Boston in 1905 with illustrations from drawings by W T Benda. He dedicates it to his dear parents. A list of illustrations shows the lovers on a marble bench watching a fountain, and Agrippina and Psyche on a vessel's deck watching the sunset on a smooth sea.

Chapter one opens in the year 23. In Rome there lived a youth named Gannon, a comely lad of seventeen with a bright, happy face and a Greek profile. His head sat gracefully on vigorous young shoulders, his dark eyebrows slightly curved. Readers get a historical romance of imperial Rome retelling the Cupid and Psyche story in novel form.
74234-letters-written-in-france-to-a-fri:
Major Tench of the Marines, late of His Majesty's ship Alexander, wrote these letters in France to a friend in London between November 1794 and May 1795. They were printed in London in 1796. His preface says they were written under very adverse circumstances, in a part of France remote from the beaten track of travellers.

The subject is the great object then concentrating the attention of Europe: revolutionary France. Tench admits much of the collection must be uninteresting to most readers and trusts the subject to compensate. The first letter is dated on board le Marat at Brest. Readers get a British officer-prisoner's France, seen from inside the revolution's own country.
74397-a-history-of-criticism-and-literar:
A History of Criticism and Literary Taste in Europe, volume three, is George Saintsbury's account of modern criticism, published by Blackwood in 1904. Saintsbury, professor of rhetoric and English literature at Edinburgh, had compressed two thousand years of criticism into his first volume and two centuries into his second. This one gives the whole nineteenth century its own book.

In his preface Saintsbury refuses to pad the volume with old prefaces or skirmishes with reviewers. He claims instead to have surveyed the matter with the actual documents in hand, not from abstracts, translations or go-betweens. The work, he notes, was seven years in composition and more than twenty-seven in preparation. The motto, from Polycarp Leyser, warns that the judgments of ignorance are usually rash. The volume is the capstone of the most ambitious history of criticism in English.
7444-psyche:
Molière's Psyche is a tragédie-ballet, a play with music and dance, telling the myth of Psyche and Love. Molière sketched the plan, wrote the prologue, the first act, and the opening scenes of the second and third acts, when the king asked for the play finished before Lent. Pierre Corneille, then sixty, helped and wrote the remaining scenes in a fortnight, while Quinault supplied the songs.

Charles Heron Wall's translation gives the play in English prose, with short introductions and notes. Jupiter, Venus, Love, and Zephyr appear among the persons, and Molière himself once played Zephyr on stage. The result is a rare glimpse of two great French dramatists at work together, turning a classical love story into court spectacle.
7489-through-central-borneo-an-account-o:
Carl Lumholtz, a Norwegian explorer and member of the Society of Sciences of Christiania, spent two years traveling through Central Borneo between 1913 and 1917. He had long wanted to explore the island's interior, large tracts of which were still unknown to the outside world. His project grew to cover other regions of Dutch Borneo as well. The book carries his own photographs and a map.

Lumholtz had camped before with the aborigines of Queensland, and he approached Borneo's peoples, called in the subtitle the land of the head-hunters, with the same patient curiosity. He records their customs, crafts, and daily life, quoting Wallace's judgment that the better specimens of savages surpass the lower examples of civilized peoples. The account is a classic of early ethnographic travel.
7494-the-outdoor-girls-in-army-service-o:
Laura Lee Hope, author of the Bobbsey Twins and the Moving Picture Girls, sent her Outdoor Girls to war work in this 1918 volume. Mollie, Grace, and their friends volunteer, knit sweaters for soldiers, and face grim shadows of war and news from the front. Grace's knitting draws teasing from Mollie, who fishes in vain for a lost stitch and doubts the soldiers would fare well on Grace's sweaters.

The girls' service leads them to a powder mill, a shot in the dark, moonlight and mystery, a robbery, and a spy again and again. Honor flags, a hostess house, and helping Uncle Sam fill the later chapters. The book is a home-front adventure for young readers, full of pluck and patriotism, written while the war it describes was still being fought.
75234-who-he:
Who He is a novel by Alfred Bester, published by Dial Press in New York in 1953. The narrator is a script writer by trade. He specialises in mystery shows for his living. He is married to an actress. Both are second raters in the entertainment business, he says. They are mostly anonymous to the public at large. Between them they make ten to twenty thousand dollars a year. 

He opens with a bleak line about hating to be born each morning. He lives his life within those parentheses, he says. Walking a tightrope over hysteria makes him perceptive, he claims. He sees the dilemmas of others crossing their own chasms. Families think the couple glamorous, which they hate but cannot dispel. He vows to lean over backward to tell the truth. The voice is confessional, cynical, and show business weary.
75247-the-coming-of-peace-a-family-catas:
The Coming of Peace, subtitled A Family Catastrophe, is a play by Gerhart Hauptmann in English. Janet Achurch and Wheeler translated it for a Modern Plays series. Duckworth published the authorised version in London in nineteen hundred. The action falls on Christmas Eve in a lonely country house.

The house stands near Erkner in Brandenburg, in a year left blank in the text. Doctor Fritz Scholz, sixty eight, heads the family gathered for the feast. His wife Minna is forty six, and their three children are grown. The Buchner widow and her daughter Ida join the household party. A hall hung with horns, animal heads, and old pictures forms the scene. A Christmas tree lies on the stone floor waiting for its candles.
75284-an-inquiry-into-the-propagation-of:
Alison, a doctor of Tranent, wrote this medical inquiry, An Inquiry into the Propagation of Contagious Poisons by the Atmosphere, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1839. Its full title adds the rest of its ground. It treats the nature and effects of spoiled air, its forms and sources, and other causes of pestilence. Directions for avoiding contagion and notes on means for promoting public health complete the title.

A motto from Haygarth heads the book: no subject, he held, could better employ a physician's time than tracing how feverish contagion spreads, and by what means it may be prevented. A preface owns the work's defects and explains them. It was written by a country practitioner in short intervals seized after the fatigues of the day. Behind it lies long study of the health and habits of the people around him.
76816-the-great-roxhythe:
Great Roxhythe is a historical novel by Georgette Heyer of the seventeenth century. Small Maynard of Boston issued the book in nineteen twenty three. Heyer also wrote The Black Moth, a romance of the eighteenth century. A Shakespeare line, Under which king, Bezonian, fronts the Stuart tale.

Book one opens on the king and his favourite, then his councillors follow. Christopher Dart enters, then Flushing, Mynheer de Staal, and Roderick Dart come. William of Orange and the king of England close the first book cast. Book two runs January sixteen sixty nine to May sixteen seventy in dates. The ways diverge, her ladyship perplexity, and the first seed of doubt grow.
76882-the-life-and-times-of-the-rev-john:
Tyerman wrote a life and times of John Wesley, founder of the Methodists, in three volumes. This third was published at New York in 1872, with an appendix by Abel Stevens, the historian of Methodism. Wesley at eighty-five, from a painting by Romney, fronts the volume. The general contents proceed year by year through the movement's later decades.

The years 1768 to 1772 alone bring Whitefield's death, the Calvinian controversy, conferences and doctrinal minutes, female preaching, a college at Trevecca, chapel debts, and Wesley's ceaseless publications and journeys. Ireland, America, and Sweden all enter the record. A denominational history built from letters, journals, and conference acts is the substance.
77171-a-diary-of-the-wreck-of-his-majest:
A Diary of the Wreck of His Majesty's Ship Challenger records a loss on the coast of Chili. Longman published it in London in eighteen thirty six, the year after the wreck. The Challenger went down in May eighteen thirty five on South America's western shore. Her officers and crew then camped seven weeks on that wild coast.

The diary opens with the ship sailing from Rio Janeiro on the first of April. She was bound for Valparaiso by way of Concepcion, for wood and water there. Calms and light winds slowed her southing until past thirty one degrees south. Gales, hail, and snow met her off Cape Horn in high southern waters. Plates show the camp at Molquilla, with tents for officers, crew, and Indians. A plan of the camp and a view of the Leubu camp follow.
77212-physical-anthropology-of-the-lenap:
Physical Anthropology of the Lenape or Delawares is a scientific memoir by Hrdlička, issued by the Museum of the American Indian in New York in 1916. It is volume three of the museum's contributions. A note explains the study's base. It rests largely on skeletal remains found in the summer of 1914.

The bones came from a cemetery tied to a historic Munsee settlement near Montague, in the Delaware valley of northwestern New Jersey. The museum's expedition recovered them, and they were given to the United States National Museum. Hrdlička measures and compares them to describe the eastern Indians in general. The memoir is a work of early American physical anthropology.
78826-the-dynasty-of-theodosius-or-eight:
Thomas Hodgkin wrote The Dynasty of Theodosius, or Eighty Years Struggle with the Barbarians, issued at Oxford in 1889. The book began as talks given to the Durham Ladies Educational Association. Hodgkin had writ Italy and Her Invaders. He gives the book to his wife and children.

Hodgkin chose the fall of the Western Empire as his theme. He wrote the talks out in full to keep each to one hour and a quarter. The talks sketch the main events of his large work in brief. One talk on Roman and barbarian life was added for the book. It was not in the first course. The small book suits readers who want the tale without the large volumes.
79056-the-german-arctic-expedition-of-18:
Captain Koldewey commanded the German Arctic Expedition of 1869 and 1870, and this London book of 1874 tells its story with the wreck of the Hansa in the ice. Members of the scientific staff helped Koldewey write the account. Mercier translated and abridged it, and Bates of the Royal Geographical Society edited the English text. Woodcuts, two colored maps, steel portraits, and four colored plates fill the volume.

An introduction gives the object and plan of the voyage, the stocking of the ships, and the instructions drawn up by Petermann. Part One follows the Germania and the Hansa together from June 1869 to their parting on July 20. The Hansa is then beset in the coast-ice of East Greenland. Her crew settle on a floe, drift south through a hard winter, and at last take to boats for Friedrichsthal.
79750-the-beginnings-of-the-egyptian-que:
The Beginnings of the Egyptian Question and the Rise of Mehemet Ali is a study by Shafik Ghorbal, lecturer in history at the Higher Training College in Cairo. It was printed at London in 1928, with a preface by Arnold Toynbee, and it began as a thesis approved for the master's degree at the University of London. Ghorbal gives the book to Toynbee, his teacher, with thanks.

Its full title calls it a study in the diplomacy of the Napoleonic era, built on research in the British and French archives. The chapters run from the genesis of the French expedition to Egypt through the expulsion of the French in 1800 and 1801. Later chapters trace the first British occupation and the rise of Mehemet Ali between 1803 and 1806.
8329-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-29-lame:
Jerusalem has fallen, and these five poems weep over it. Lamentations, linked to Jeremias in the Douay-Rheims tradition, walks the ruined streets in the first poems: a city once full of people now sits alone, its gates broken, its children hungry. The middle poem, the longest, turns personal, as a sufferer speaks of affliction and then of mercies new every morning.

The poems are built with care, the first four in alphabetical acrostics, as if grief itself needed order. The last poem is a communal prayer, asking God to remember and restore. Short enough to read in one sitting, Lamentations gives sorrow a shape and a voice, and Jews still read it on the fast day marking the temple's destruction.
8773-birth-control-a-statement-of-christ:
Halliday G. Sutherland, a Edinburgh physician, argues the Christian case against the neo-Malthusians in this book on birth control. His first chapter attacks the essential fallacies of Malthusian teaching: that population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, that overpopulation causes poverty and disease, and that such teaching rests on false premises. He finds no evidence of overpopulation in the Suez Canal Zone or in closed countries like Japan, and points to a natural law checking fertility.

Later chapters develop a Catholic moral argument against artificial birth control, defending marriage, family, and the natural order as Sutherland understands them. The book is a direct reply to Margaret Sanger and her allies, and it shows the other side of a fierce 1920s debate. Readers should approach it as a historical polemic, valuable for understanding religious opposition to birth control in its own terms.
8815-narrative-of-captivity-in-abyssinia:
Henry Blanc, staff assistant-surgeon of the Bombay Army, lately on special duty in Abyssinia, writes this narrative of captivity under Emperor Theodore. An account of the emperor, his country, and his people. Early chapters trace Theodore's rise and conquests, his army and administration, the causes of his fall, and his personal appearance, character, household, and private life. Europeans in Abyssinia follow: Bell and Plowden, Consul Cameron, French envoys, the Gaffat people, and Mr Stern's mission.

Imprisonment, negotiations, and the British expedition that ended the captivity form the narrative core. Blanc writes as a medical officer and eyewitness, with detail on Ethiopian court life and on the prisoners' suffering. The book remains a key firsthand source on Theodore's Ethiopia and on Victorian Britain's most famous African rescue, readable as adventure and as history at once.
9550-manual-of-gardening-second-edition-:
L. H. Bailey, a noted American plant scientist, issued the second edition of his Manual of Gardening in 1910. The book guides home owners in making grounds and growing flowers, fruits, and vegetables for home use. It starts with the point of view: a garden should form a picture, not a jumble of beds. Plans, walks, lawns, and borders all serve that whole design.

Later chapters take up grading, terraces, trees, flower borders, and seasonal tasks through the year. Bailey stresses form and leaf as much as bloom, and warns against odd beds that spoil the scene. A reader gets a sound, plain handbook for a home garden, still wise on design, soil, and the year's round of work.
9564-among-the-hills-and-other-poems-par:
Part five of Whittier's Narrative and Legendary Poems leads with Among the Hills, a long idyll of New England country life. Whittier first printed the poem as The Wife in the Atlantic Monthly in January 1868, then filled it out for book form that December. He dedicated it to Annie Fields, wife of publisher James T. Fields. The part also holds The Dole of Jarl Thorkell, The Two Rabbins, and Noremega.

Other poems here include Miriam, Maud Muller, Mary Garvin, and The Ranger, each a compact tale in verse. Whittier's voice stays plain and earnest, rooted in farm, faith, and home. A reader gets some of his most loved narrative verse, with country scenes that still feel fresh and clear.
9592-personal-sketches-and-tributes-part:
Part two of volume six of Whittier's works holds his personal sketches and tributes to friends and public men. The Funeral of Torrey opens, honoring Charles T. Torrey, a young minister who died in a Maryland jail in 1846 for aiding runaway slaves. Later sketches salute Edward Everett, Lewis Tappan, Bayard Taylor, and William Ellery Channing. Lydia Maria Child and Oliver Wendell Holmes also appear.

Other pieces mark the death of President Garfield, recall old Newbury, and praise Edwin Percy Whipple. Whittier writes with grief, praise, and moral fire, as one who knew these folk. A reader gets a moving gallery of reformers and writers, seen through the eyes of a friend.
9599-the-works-of-john-greenleaf-whittie:
Volume seven of Whittier's works closes the set with his prose on slavery, politics, the inner life, and criticism. The Conflict with Slavery leads, from justice and expediency to the founding of the Anti-Slavery Society. Reform and Politics follows, with woman suffrage, Indian civilization, and arbitration. The Inner Life and Criticism complete the volume.

Taken whole, the book shows Whittier the essayist at full stretch, from abolition to poetry reviews. His prose stays plain, moral, and warm. A reader gets the capstone of Whittier's works, where a poet's public and private mind meet in one volume.
984-who-was-who-5000-b-c-to-date-biograp:
An anonymous editor, Irwin L. Gordon, compiled this biographical dictionary, Who Was Who, 5000 B.C. to Date, of the famous and of those who wanted to be. Entry requires proof that the person has died; notices from press agents are turned away.

The entries mix real fame with satire, poking fun at vanity, obituary puff, and the hunger for a place in history. The book is a joke with a sharp edge, a mock reference work for readers who enjoy seeing pomposity deflated. It charms as a period piece of American humour, where death alone earns an entry.
9907-the-raid-from-beausejour-and-how-th:
Charles G. D. Roberts joined two stories of Acadia in this book: a raid from Beauséjour and a family's fight to lift a mortgage. The first tale opens with the cry that Beaubassin must go, and follows Pierre to the English lines as French and English forces prepare for a midnight march.

The second story turns from war to home, where the Carter boys work to save their family's farm from debt. Roberts, a Canadian writer, grounds both tales in the woods, forts, and villages of old Acadia. Readers get action and hardship side by side, in a corner of colonial history often left out of schoolbooks.
a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-the-ea:
Thomas D'Arcy McGee tells Ireland's story in two volumes, and this first volume begins with the publishers' preface picturing Ireland lifting herself from the dust to demand her place among the nations. Book one covers the first inhabitants, the first ages, and Christianity preached at Tara, then the constitution and how the kings kept it.

Chapters follow the Irish schools and saints of the first Christian centuries, the Danish invasion, the reigns of Flan of the Shannon and Malachy, and Brian's rise to the battle of Clontarf. McGee writes as scholar and patriot together, from the records and the sagas alike. This volume carries the tale through the age of the Northmen; the second takes it to Catholic Emancipation.
a-portraiture-of-quakerism-volume-1-take: Thomas Clarkson portrays the Society of Friends in this first volume, drawn from how they educate children, order their manners, manage civil and political life, and practise their faith. The opening chapters treat moral education, dividing amusements into useful and hurtful and forbidding games of chance as below the dignity of intellect and Christian character. The volume builds its portrait from rules and reasons, showing how a sect shapes daily life by principle.
a-portraiture-of-quakerism-volume-2-take: Thomas Clarkson continues his portraiture of Quakerism in this second volume, turning from education to peculiar customs. The opening chapters treat marriage, its regulation and celebration after the example of George Fox, and the disownment of those who marry outside the society. The volume weighs objections to that discipline and the terms of restoration, showing a community guarding its boundaries while leaving a road back for the penitent.
a-portraiture-of-quakerism-volume-3-take: Thomas Clarkson completes his portraiture of Quakerism in this third volume, turning to the great tenets of the Society of Friends. The opening chapters argue that governors have no right to interfere in religion. The governed, when conscience is oppressed, should suffer penalties rather than resist by force of arms. Later chapters take up oaths, refused by Christians, and war, held unlawful, as convictions lived out in daily conduct.
amadis-of-gaul-an-opera-as-it-is-perform: Nicola Francesco Haym supplies the text of Amadis of Gaul, an opera as performed at the King's Theatre in the Haymarket. The libretto follows the knight Amadis through acts and scenes of love, magic, and chivalry, in the Italian opera style of early eighteenth-century London. It preserves the words audiences heard in a fashionable house of its day.
among-the-hills-and-other-poems-part-5-f: John Greenleaf Whittier gathers narrative and legendary poems in this part of his works, opening with Among the Hills and its prelude. The poems move through New England scenery, history, and moral reflection, in Whittier's plain, earnest verse. This section shows the Quaker poet at his most characteristic, tender toward nature and firm in conscience.
an-account-of-the-extraordinary-medicina: Matthew Turner writes an account of the extraordinary medicinal fluid called aether, published in Liverpool and London. The short work praises aether's healing powers in the enthusiastic manner of eighteenth-century medical advertising. It now reads as a curiosity of early medicine, when new remedies were sold on hope and bold claims.
an-essay-on-war-in-blank-verse-honington: Nathaniel Bloomfield gathers poems on various subjects, led by an essay on war in blank verse, with Honington Green as a ballad and the Culprit as an elegy. The collection moves from war and village life to moral reflection, in plain, sincere verse. Bloomfield, a Suffolk poet, writes with a countryman's eye and a humane heart.
beaumont-and-fletcher-s-works-vol-01-of-:
The Custom of the Country opens this first volume of Beaumont and Fletcher's works, a Fletcher and Massinger tragicomedy of Lisbon and Italy. The persons list sets the terms: Count Clodio, governor and dishonourable pursuer of Zenocia; Arnoldo, contracted to her; and Hippolyta, a rich lady wantonly in love with Arnoldo. Zenocia's father Charino and the bawd Sulpitia, mistress of the male stewes, complete the machinery.

Hippolyta's frantic love drives the sampled scene. She will bind up her hair and go not like Hippolyta but a bacchanal, before the law can seize her beloved's life. Her servant Zabulon guesses the cause and hurries after. Flight, disguise, and a threatened forced marriage carry the play, whose custom of the country — a lord's claim on brides — Fletcher turns into an indictment of licensed lust.
birth-control-a-statement-of-christian-d:
Halliday G. Sutherland, a doctor of Edinburgh, wrote this statement of Christian doctrine against the neo-Malthusians. His first chapter attacks the essential fallacies of Malthusian teaching: that population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, and that overpopulation causes poverty and disease. Sections find no evidence of overpopulation in the Suez Canal Zone or in closed countries like Japan, and propose a natural law checking fertility instead.

Sutherland concedes the fog around the figures. On the effect of limitation, he quotes, it is plainly impossible to form an accurate judgment. The Registrar-General's reports, he argues, make it highly improbable that contraceptives caused the English birth-rate's decline; occupation and character explain more. Physical and moral catastrophes close his case: a Catholic physician's brief, written when Marie Stopes had just opened the argument in earnest.
britannica-1911-absinthe:
Absinthe receives an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The liqueur takes its character from wormwood species, Artemisia absinthium above all. Angelica root, sweet flag, dittany, star-anise, fennel, and hyssop join the usual making.

A colourless alcoholate comes first off the still. Maceration with green wormwood, hyssop, and mint leaves then lays on the famous green colour. Essence-made inferior kinds skip distillation altogether. French and Swiss kinds divide the market, the Swiss stronger; the best runs very high in alcohol and improves with storage. Dye adulteration with copper or indigo, once popularly feared, is now rare, the entry says. Heavy drinking may harm beyond common alcohol's effects.
britannica-1911-address-the:
The Address is an English parliamentary term. It names Parliament's reply to the sovereign's speech. That speech opens each new session formally. The king's speech falls into three sections. Foreign affairs address Lords and Commons together first. Estimates address the Commons alone as Gentlemen. Proposed legislation addresses both houses together again. The sovereign reads the speech in the Lords. Commons members attend there by summons for it.

Debate on the Address ranges over all policy. Government supporters move and second the reply. They wear levee dress for the honourable task. The opposition introduces amendments to broaden debate. Defeat on such an amendment counts heavily. Governments treat it as a vote of no-confidence. Since 1890 the reply is one single resolution. It thanks the sovereign for his gracious speech.
britannica-1911-aga-khan-i-his-highness-:
Aga Khan the First is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The title was held by Hasan Ali Shah, who lived from 1800 to 1881. He was born in Persia and claimed descent from Ali and from the old royal house of Persia. In early life he settled in Bombay under British protection.

The article tells how he ruled the large province of Kerman with firm and fair rule. Court plots and royal anger at last forced him to flee Persia. He crossed through Afghanistan during the First Afghan War. There he gave valued help to the British army. He gave like help in the Sind campaign that followed. The British commander Napier held him in high regard as a leader and soldier. His lot was cast with the British from then on.
britannica-1911-agassiz-jean-louis-rodol:
Jean Louis Agassiz, the Swiss fish scholar, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1807, he was a pastor's son by Lake Morat. Home lessons, then school at Bienne and Lausanne, shaped the boy. He chose medicine and read at Zurich, Heidelberg, and Munich in turn. Plant lore drew much of his spare time at those schools.

In 1829 Agassiz took a doctor's rank in deep thought at Erlangen. A like rank in medicine at Munich came the next year. Fish study had not yet claimed his life at that point. The tale of how it claimed him turns on a Brazil trip. Spix and Martius brought home the fresh water fish of Brazil. Spix died, and the young Agassiz was picked for that work.
britannica-1911-alhambra-the:
Red walls gave the Alhambra its name. In Arabic the word means the red, most likely from the hue of its sun-dried outer walls, though some tie it to torches lit for night work. The old palace and fort of Granada's Moorish kings crowns a hilly shelf at the city's south-east edge in southern Spain. The shelf runs near 2,430 feet long and 674 feet at its broadest, some thirty-five acres in all, ringed by a strong wall with thirteen towers.

North of the shelf the river Darro rushes through a deep gorge, cutting the grounds off from the Albaicin quarter. A gate leads by a tight passage to the Plaza de los Aljibes, the Place of the Cisterns. That open space parts the Alcazaba fort from the Moorish palace. Charles V's palace in the Renaissance manner stands off to one side, at odds with all around it.
britannica-1911-anquetil-duperron-abraha:
Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil Duperron, who lived from 1731 to 1805, was a French orientalist. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his bold road to India. He was born in Paris and trained for the priesthood. A passion for Eastern tongues soon swallowed that first plan.

Scraps of a Zoroastrian text fired his great project. He meant to find the full works of Zoroaster in India. To get there he enlisted as a common soldier in 1754. Friends won him free passage and a seat at the captain table. At Surat he won over native priests by patience and address. From them he gained Zend and Pahlavi enough to translate rites. War cut his India plans short in the end. He came home in 1762 with one hundred eighty Eastern manuscripts.
britannica-1911-antistrophe:
The antistrophe is the answering half of a Greek ode. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains the dance that gave it shape. The chorus sang the strophe while moving east to west. It sang the antistrophe on the return, west to east. The second part replies to the first and balances its weight. Gray's ode The Progress of Poesy serves as the case in point. Its strophe sings of the beauty and power of verse.

The antistrophe answers in a sadder key. It dwells on labour, want, pain, and death. When the two parts end, the chorus joins for the epode. That close makes the three part form of the old Greek hymn. The form runs from the days of Stesichorus onward. Milton is quoted on the frame: it was a stanza made for the music of the chorus.
britannica-1911-ardeche:
Ardèche is an inland department of south-eastern France, formed in 1790 from the Vivarais district of Languedoc. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 347,140 people in 1906 and 2,145 square miles. The Cévennes mountains cover nearly all of it, with Mont Mézenc, an old volcano, its highest point at 5,755 feet.

Most of its rivers run swift and flood fast, cutting scenes of great beauty such as the Pont d'Arc. The Rhone valley is warm, while the high west has long, cold winters. Rye, wheat, and potatoes are the chief crops, and chestnuts go out in bulk. The department stands second in France for silk-worm rearing, with mulberry trees grown across it for the work. Mines of coal, iron, lead, and zinc are worked, and hot springs at Vals and elsewhere draw many visitors.
britannica-1911-armada-the:
The Armada was the great fleet sent against England by Philip the Second in fifteen eighty eight. Spain called it the Invincible Armada in later fame and song. Its first commander, the marquis of Santa Cruz, died in February of that year. The duke of Medina Sidonia took command in his place. That duke had large estates but no skill or will for the task.

The fleet gathered at Lisbon after many delays and sailed in May. Its strength on paper was one hundred thirty two vessels in all. It carried more than twenty one thousand soldiers and eight thousand sailors. Yet a third to a half of the ships were transports or small craft. The true fighting force was far below the paper strength given. Storms scattered the fleet off Cape Finisterre, delaying its advance north.
britannica-1911-ascension-feast-of-the:
Feast of the Ascension is a great festival of the Christian Church worldwide. Its feast entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It ranks in weight with Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost in the church year. The feast is held forty days after Easter, ten days before Whitsunday.

The day marks Christ rising into heaven forty days after the resurrection. It always falls on a Thursday, called Ascension Day or Holy Thursday. The feast is of great age, though no trace shows before the fourth century. Saint Augustine says it was kept from time beyond memory in church. Writers link its start to the apostles themselves in the first age.
britannica-1911-austrian-succession-war-:
War of the Austrian Succession lasted from 1740 to 1748. Frederick II of Prussia opened it in 1740. He invaded Silesia that year. The peace of Aix-la-Chapelle ended it in 1748. After 1741 nearly all Europe's powers joined. Prussia against Austria over Silesia is its enduring core. South-west Germany, the Low Countries, and Italy were battle-grounds. France and Austria fought on those fields traditionally.

Spain and Bavaria were France and Prussia's constant allies. England and Holland supported Austria almost automatically. They were France's traditional enemies. Sardinia and Saxony aided Austria at intervals. Prussia in 1740 was small and compact. Its army numbered 100,000 men. Few rated that army highly then. Its drill attained unheard-of perfection, though. The huge article follows campaigns year by year. Naval and diplomatic history fill its later sections.
britannica-1911-avalanche:
Avalanche, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, names a mass of snow and ice mixed with earth and stones that rushes down a mountainside. The word came from a French dialect form meaning descent. Snow that is not lost by drying in the air must leave the slopes, slowly as glaciers or suddenly in falls like these.

Loose or packed snow can slide when its base gives way, loosened by spring rain or other causes. A very small trigger may start a poised mass, and thunder or even a loud shout is said to do so. Swiss guides, the entry notes, often kept strict silence at dangerous crossings. The moving snow also drives a strong wind that tears up trees beside its path.
britannica-1911-azais-pierre-hyacinthe:
Azaïs, Pierre Hyacinthe (1766-1845), was a French philosopher born at Sorèze who began as teacher and village organist. The Revolution first pleased, then disgusted him, and a critical pamphlet drew the revolutionists' hatred. Only in 1806 could he settle in Paris.

His great work, On Compensations in Human Destinies, argued that happiness and misery balance out equally on the whole, so men should accept their government rather than risk revolution. Napoleon liked the book enough to make him a professor at St Cyr. The same law of balance, Azaïs held, runs through matter and force in nature. It runs through body and mind as well. In politics, progress and preservation pull against each other. Their pull aims at a harmony thousands of years away.
britannica-1911-bar-the:
Bar, in English law, names both a rail in the court room and the whole body of barristers. The 1911 Britannica article starts from the rail itself. A bar split the old law courts in two, to keep court staff apart from the crowd. Counsel with high rank may sit within the bar. Plain barristers and the public stay without. A person who pleads his own civil case may stand inside. A man on trial for a crime still steps up to the bar.

Parliament keeps a bar of its own, the article notes. In the Commons it is a brass rod drawn from a tube to mark the edge of the House. Those charged with breach of its rights stand before it. New members wait below it to take the oath. The piece also treats the call to the bar, the step that makes a law student a barrister.
britannica-1911-barouche: Barouche is the name of a kind of carriage, and this short 1911 Britannica entry defines it in a single sentence. The word reaches English through German, Spanish, and Italian forms, all traced back to the Latin bi-rotus, meaning double-wheeled. The carriage itself, the entry says, has four wheels and a hood, a folding cover against the weather. Inside, it is arranged for two couples, who sit facing one another as they ride.
britannica-1911-bass-rock-the:
Bass Rock is a small island in the Firth of Forth, Scotland, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies about two miles from Canty Bay in Haddingtonshire, is circular and about a mile around, and rises 350 feet high. Cliffs fall steeply on three sides, shelving only to the south-west, where landing is possible. Geologists read it as a plug of phonolitic trachyte filling an old volcanic vent, in Sir Archibald Geikie's view.

Birds and prisoners share its history. Solan geese, or gannets, haunt the rock in vast numbers, and a lighthouse opened in 1902. St Baldred kept a hermitage there and died in 756. Later the island's castle held Covenanters as prisoners, among them Alexander Peden and John Blackadder. Four young Jacobites seized the rock in 1691 and held it for James until starvation forced surrender in 1694. It was the last place in Britain to submit to William III.
britannica-1911-bertillon-louis-adolphe:
Louis Adolphe Bertillon (1821–1883) was a French statistician, born in Paris on 1 April 1821. He first entered medicine and practised as a doctor for years. After the revolution of 1870 he became inspector-general of benevolent institutions. He helped found the Paris school of anthropology. In 1876 he took a professor's chair there. His main book studied the population of France in figures.

The 1911 Britannica entry praises that book, Démographie figurée de la France (1874). It calls it an able statistical study. Bertillon died at Neuilly in February 1883. The entry then turns to his son Alphonse, born in 1853. Alphonse devised the criminal identification system tied to anthropometry. He also testified on handwriting in the Dreyfus case in 1899.
britannica-1911-black-country-the:
The Black Country is an industrial district in the English Midlands, lying mainly in south Staffordshire and reaching into Worcestershire and Warwickshire. Its name comes from the collieries and furnaces that darkened its buildings, land, and air. Coal, ironstone, and clay are all mined close together there.

Towns named in the entry include Wolverhampton, Walsall, Dudley, West Bromwich, and Bilston, spread over ground running 15 miles north-west from Birmingham. Each centre had its own trade, such as locks at Wolverhampton and Willenhall, glass at Smethwick, and nails and chains at Cradley. Railways and canals cross the district, and at night the glare of furnaces could be seen in every direction from Dudley Castle Hill.
britannica-1911-black-isle-the:
The Black Isle is a peninsula in Ross and Cromarty, Scotland, set between Cromarty Firth to the north and Moray Firth to the east. It is shaped like a diamond, about 20 miles long and 12 miles across, with a coastline of 52 miles. Snow rarely lies there in winter, so it looks black against white country around it.

Readers get the old Gaelic name Ardmeanach, the parishes inside the district, and its links by rail, steamer, and ferry to Inverness, Dingwall, and other towns. Cromarty and Fortrose are given as the chief towns. The entry also notes seats such as Rosehaugh near Avoch and traces local place names to their Gaelic roots.
britannica-1911-blankenberghe:
Blankenberghe is a seaside resort on the Belgian North Sea coast in West Flanders. It lies 12 miles north-east of Ostend and about 9 miles north-west of Bruges, joined to Bruges by rail. Its fixed population in 1904 was 5925, yet the season drew far larger crowds.

From June to September more than 60,000 visitors, many from Germany, came for its bracing air and a parade over a mile long. The town also kept a small fishing port and a fair-sized fishing fleet. Two miles north along the dunes lay Zeebrugge, where the new ship canal from Bruges reached the sea. The entry is short, factual, and wholly about place, season trade, and fishing.
britannica-1911-blanqui-jerome-adolphe:
Jérôme Adolphe Blanqui (1798–1854) was a French economist who wrote the first large history of his subject in Europe. Born at Nice, he began as a schoolmaster in Paris and was drawn to economics by the lectures of J. B. Say, whose pupil and assistant he became.

On Say's word he was made professor at the Conservatoire des Arts et Métiers in 1825, and in 1833 he took Say's own chair of political economy there. His chief work, a history of political economy in Europe from ancient times to his own day, appeared in 1838. He travelled over most of Europe, and to Algeria and the East, gathering facts, and he wrote much on the state of the working classes in France.
britannica-1911-bouilhet-louis-hyacinthe:
Louis Hyacinthe Bouilhet (1822–1869) was a French poet and playwright, the schoolfellow and close friend of Gustave Flaubert. Born at Cany in Seine-Inférieure, he dedicated his first work to Flaubert: Méloenis (1851), a tale in verse in five cantos about Roman manners under Commodus. His Fossiles drew notice for trying to make poetry out of science.

On the stage his first play, Madame de Montarcy (1856), ran seventy-eight nights at the Odéon. Hélène Peyron and L'Oncle Million were also well received, though of his later plays only the Conjuration d'Amboise (1866) had great success. He died at Rouen in 1869. Flaubert published his posthumous poems in 1872 with a notice of his friend, the entry closes by noting.
britannica-1911-brocken-spectre-of-the:
Spectre of the Brocken is the name for a strange mountain sight first observed in 1780 on the Brocken peak in Germany. It is the hugely magnified shadow of an observer thrown onto a bank of cloud when the sun hangs low in high mountain country. Mist turns the shadow into a giant, ghostly copy of the person watching.

Every motion of the observer is reproduced in that vast misty image, so the figure seems to move on the cloud as its maker moves. The whole entry is only a few lines, yet it fixes the name, the date and place of first record, the low sun and high ground the effect needs. The cloud bank that serves as its screen.
britannica-1911-bronx-the:
Bronx, The, is the northernmost of the five boroughs of New York City, holding that standing since 1898. Before the merger it was a district made up of several towns in Westchester county, New York. The whole hosted notice is only a few lines, giving the borough's rank in the city, its older county place and its first settlement.

Settlements in the Bronx were made by the English and the Dutch between 1640 and 1650, the twin roots of its early population. Readers wanting the full account are pointed onward to the New York City entry, marked with a cross-reference. This record serves as a short pointer: name, merger date of 1898, Westchester past and 17th-century settlement are all it states.
britannica-1911-caran-d-ache:
Caran d'Ache was the pen name of Emmanuel Poiré (1858–1909). He was a French artist and illustrator. The name means “lead-pencil” in Russian. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born and educated at Moscow. His grandfather was one of Napoleon's officers, settled in Russia. Poiré set his heart on being a military painter. He came to Paris and found a guide in Detaille.

He served five years in the French army. His chief army work was drawing uniforms for the war ministry. He illustrated a short-lived journal, La Vie militaire. His caricatures of the German army showed sharp military knowledge. His special gift lay in pictorial anecdote. He told a story in stages of drawings, with plain force. His work ran in Le Figaro illustré and Le Chat noir. He also issued albums of sketches. One album mocked the Panama scandals of the day.
britannica-1911-cartouche:
Cartouche is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word adapted from the Italian cartoccio, a roll of paper. It first named a roll of paper or parchment holding the powder and shot for a firearm, the thing English calls a cartridge, itself a corruption of cartouche. In architecture the term passed to scroll-shaped ornament, such as the volute of an Ionic capital.

The word settled on the sculptured tablet shaped like a partly unrolled scroll, made to carry an inscription or device. Such tablets serve as titles on engraved maps and plans. Popes and high-born churchmen bore their arms on an oval cartouche. In Egyptian archaeology the term names the oblong ring, properly a knotted rope oval, that encloses royal names on monuments. A matching amulet, the symbol of the name, was worn as a guard against the name being blotted out after death.
britannica-1911-cid-the:
Cid, The, is the favourite hero of Spain and the most prominent figure in her literature, though myth and fable obscure his name. Some writers classed him with the Amadises and Orlandos of romance, and the Jesuit Masdeu denied that he had any real existence at all. Cervantes, through the Canon in Don Quixote, held that there was such a man. Research by Professor Dozy of Leiden confirmed that view, the entry says.

The historical Cid is Rodrigo Diaz de Bivar, born probably between 1030 and 1040, called El Seid, the lord, by the Arabs. His second name, El Campeador, the champion, came from slaying the enemy champion in single combat. Backing Sancho of Castile against his brother Alphonso brought him the new king's hatred after Sancho's death in 1072. Marriage, embassies to Seville and high commissions fill his recorded life beyond the legends.
britannica-1911-cochery-louis-adolphe:
Cochery, Louis Adolphe (1819–1900) was a French statesman, born at Paris, who studied law and soon entered politics in his early career. He was on the staff of the ministry of justice after the revolution of February 1848. From the coup d'état of 1851 to May 1869 he devoted himself to journalism instead of office. Then, elected deputy by the department of the Loiret, he joined the group of the Left Centre in the chamber.

He supported the revolution of 4 September 1870, and his talent in finance won him a distinguished place in the chamber's work. From 1879 till 1885 he was minister of posts and telegraphs, a long tenure in that office. In January 1888 he was elected to the senate, where he sat for his remaining years. He died in 1900, and his son Georges followed him into finance office and the chamber.
britannica-1911-cordeliers-club-of-the:
The Club of the Cordeliers was a famed people's group of the French revolt years, also styled the Society of the Friends of the Rights of Man. It formed when a Paris district was wiped out by the ruling body and its members regrouped as a club. They met first in the church of a friary, from which the name came.

The 1911 Britannica entry says the club set itself to watch the state, and stamped an open eye on its papers as its sign. It pushed hard steps against the crown and the old order, and spread the famed watchwords of liberty and equal rights for all. It took a lead part in two great drives on the crown. Later, its more mild chiefs drifted away from its meets.
britannica-1911-creche:
A crèche is a day-nursery where infants are fed and cared for while their mothers work away from home. Children are usually taken in when over a month old and kept until they can look after themselves. Trained nurses give the care, and the nurseries usually sit under medical supervision. Fees are small, averaging three to four pence a day in London and about twopence on the continent.

Such nurseries began in France in 1844 and spread to most large towns on the continent. In French and German industrial centres they helped to check infant deaths. Public grants aid most of them, but private societies give the main support and run them. In Britain provision was left to private effort and lags behind, Paris holding near twice London's share of places. A National Society of Day Nurseries was founded in 1901 to spread good practice.
britannica-1911-cumbraes-the:
Cumbraes, The, is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes two islands in the Firth of Clyde in Scotland. The larger isle lies a short sail from a mainland resort town. Low hills crown it, and fields and shore homes ring its coast.

The entry gives the size of the big isle and its top height. Fish work and small farms give some work to island folk. Summer guests who crowd its chief town form the true mainstay. That town holds a church seat, a school, and a sea life study base. Its bay and mild air draw crowds in the warm months each year.
britannica-1911-deluge-the:
The text hosted here begins partway through its argument, weighing how one shared flood story might first have been told. In its shortest form a creator, finding earth and its people flawed, looses the subdued serpent of the cosmic ocean to drown the world, then remakes it better. The warned survivor and his family then father a new human race, and variants let the serpent act alone or die so that his blood makes the flood.

The article tests those variants against the myths of many peoples, from the Babylonian Xisuthrus warned in a dream to Manu warned by the sacred fish. Details such as the chest, the three birds sent out, and the landing on a mountain are weighed one by one. A long bibliography of flood scholarship closes the piece.
britannica-1911-ephesians-epistle-to-the:
Ephesians, Epistle to the, is a book of the New Testament, the most general and least occasional of all the Pauline epistles. The entry calls it a solemn oration meant to stir the feelings of absent hearers, a true letter in the grand style.

The entry dwells on the puzzle of the title and address. “To the Ephesians” stands in the Muratorian canon, the early fathers, and all the oldest copies, yet Marcion used copies titled “To the Laodiceans.” The words “in Ephesus” in the first verse were likely absent at first. Origen's text lacked them, Basil says ancient copies omitted them, and the Vatican and Sinaitic codices omit them still. The entry argues the letter was a circular one, written to a group of churches in Asia Minor. That would explain its general tone and its lack of personal greetings.
britannica-1911-feuillants-club-of-the:
The Club of the Feuillants was a French party group that played a large part in the revolt years. The 1911 Britannica entry dates its birth to a split in the Jacobin Club. Some members would not sign a plea to cast down the king, and broke off to form their own body.

The entry takes the club name from the friary rooms in Paris where the group met. Its members kept a title that meant friends of the new frame of rule. Their line was to back that frame as writ and fight all change to it. They scorned both those who had fled the land and the Jacobins, and called their own group a mere guard of the state, not a place for debate.
britannica-1911-fronde-the:
The Fronde was a civil war in France lasting from 1648 to 1652, with a sequel war against Spain to 1659. The name means a sling, taken from the Paris mob stoning the windows of Cardinal Mazarin followers. It began as a bid to redress grievances and slid into a faction fight among nobles out to undo Richelieu work and bring down his successor Mazarin.

In May 1648 the parlement of Paris refused a tax on judicial officers and demanded constitutional reforms. That August, after Condé victory at Lens, Mazarin arrested the parlement leaders, Paris barricaded its streets, and the court fled. Condé army, freed by the peace of Westphalia, besieged Paris, and the peace of Rueil followed in March 1649. The Princes Fronde opened with the arrest of Condé, Conti, and Longueville in January 1650 and Turenne in revolt with Spanish aid. The entry centres on the campaigns of this costly, needless war.
britannica-1911-gouache: Gouache is a way of painting with water-based colour that does not let light through, and this short 1911 Britannica entry defines the term and the method. The paints are mixed with gum or honey. In plain water-colour the bright spots are left as bare paper. In gouache they are laid on with white or pale paint. The entry adds that the method is often used in miniature painting, and that the French word comes from an Italian one tied to washing.
britannica-1911-graces-the:
Graces, called Charites in Greek myth, are the subject of a god lore entry in the 1911 Britannica. They stand for grace and charm in the world and in good deeds. Homer shows a shift from one Charis to a group in his verse. As a rule there are three, named Brightness, Joy, and Bloom. Their parents are told in more than one way in old tales. In Sparta and Athens folk knew just two by local names.

They live with the Muses on Mount Olympus and walk with Aphrodite. Rites for them were old at Orchomenus, where stones said to have fallen from the sky stood in their shrine. Night dances and song meets marked their feast there. In art they stand hand in hand, first clad and later bare, with rose and myrtle as their signs.
britannica-1911-hardt-the:
Hardt is a hill district of Germany in the Bavarian Palatinate, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica maps it in brief. It forms the north end of the Vosges range. In the main it is a high plain of sand stone with a rolling face. Its mean height is one thousand three hundred feet, and its top peak past two thousand feet.

The east slope drops soft toward the Rhine. Deep vales with thick woods cut that slope, and cone hills crown it. Ruins of old lord castles and of houses of monks crown more than one hill. One famed fort on that slope long held a king of England as a jailed guest. Three fifths of the whole tract is in woods of oak, beech, and fir. The low east slope is tilled with care and yields fine wine.
britannica-1911-hebrides-the:
The Hebrides, or Western Isles, are a group of islands off Scotland's west coast. They lie between 55 and 58 degrees north. The Minch and Little Minch divide them in two. Outer Hebrides lie beyond those channels; Inner Hebrides lie inside. Geologists call the groups Gneiss Islands and Trap Islands. Lewis-with-Harris heads the Outer list. North Uist, Benbecula, South Uist and Barra follow.

More than 500 islands make up the whole group. Only about one-fifth of them are inhabited. Skye, Mull, Islay and Jura lead the Inner Hebrides. Iona, Staffa and the Slate Islands enrich that list. The Outer chain runs 130 miles from Barra Head to the Butt of Lewis. Long sections treat the islands' geology and climate. Their Norse and later history closes the survey. Mackenzie's history of the Outer Hebrides is a cited source.
britannica-1911-heidelberg-catechism-the:
The Heidelberg Catechism is a church teaching book of the Reformed faith. Frederick III, ruler of the Palatinate, had it made. It came out on 19 January 1563.
