The land's faith had grown up under Melanchthon's lead. Its teachers then split in a sharp fight. The clash was over Christ's true presence in the Supper. Heshusius held hard Lutheran views. He cast out his fellow teacher Klebitz.

Frederick sent both chief fighters away in 1560. That year he declared for Calvin and Zwingli by decree. A clear new teaching book was his chosen cure. Two young men got the task. Zacharias Ursinus had won praise at Wittenberg. He taught with skill and calm at Heidelberg. Caspar Olevianus of Treves was his mate in the work. The book's three parts are set out in full. Sin, man's rescue and thanks frame its questions. The sacraments sit in part two, prayer in part three.
britannica-1911-holy-alliance-the:
The Holy Alliance was a treaty, or declaration, signed on the 26th of September 1815 by Alexander I of Russia, Francis I of Austria and Frederick William III of Prussia. Alexander proclaimed it the same day at a great review of the allied troops near Paris. Its text, printed in full, opens in the name of the Most Holy and Indivisible Trinity.

In it the three sovereigns declare their fixed resolve to take the precepts of their holy religion as their sole guide, in ruling their own states and in dealings with other governments. Those precepts are justice, Christian charity and peace. The long discussion weighs what the Alliance became in practice. Its use against popular liberties, the account argues, was an accident of how men read it. It also inspired Nicholas II's rescript of 1898, which issued in the first peace conference at the Hague in 1899.
britannica-1911-homburg-vor-der-hohe:
Homburg-vor-der-Höhe is a town and watering-place of Germany, in the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau, at the south-east foot of the Taunus Mountains, 12 m. N. of Frankfort-on-Main. Its population was 13,740 in 1905. An old town stands beside a new one, regular and well built. Palatial buildings serve the mineral water cure, and churches of several communions stand in the town.

On a hill nearby stands the palace of the former landgraves, built in 1680, with grounds laid out like an English park; its White Tower is said to date from Roman times. The town's draw is its eight mineral springs, saline and iron-bearing waters used for diseases of stomach, intestines and skin, and for rheumatism. The Kurhaus of 1841–1843, with a theatre, anchors the cure buildings round a park. Iron founding, leather and hats are minor trades; visitors are the town's real wealth.
britannica-1911-indian-mutiny-the:
Indian Mutiny is the name for the great revolt of the Bengal native army in eighteen fifty seven, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The revolt led to Indian government passing from the East India Company to the Crown in eighteen fifty eight. Its deeper cause was the great gap in numbers between British and native troops.

For a century the Company had relied mainly on native troops, stiffened by British soldiers. Hindu and Muslim fighting races gave fine material when led by British officers. At the close of one governor's term, native troops outnumbered British by about five to one. When the revolt broke out the gap was wider still. Some who knew India best had already seen the danger in that balance, the entry says.
britannica-1911-jacobins-the:
Jacobins, The is a history article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the most famous political club of the French Revolution. It began as the Club Breton, set up at Versailles soon after the States General opened in 1789. At first it held only deputies from Brittany. Others from across France soon joined, among them Mirabeau, Sieyes, Robespierre, and the Lameth brothers.

Its early meetings were secret, and little is known of what passed at them. After the rising of the fifth and sixth of October 1789, the club followed the National Assembly to Paris. There it rented the dining hall of the Jacobin friary in the Rue Saint Honore, near the Assembly. The name Jacobins had first been a French label for Dominican friars. Foes of the club used it in scorn, and the name stuck.
britannica-1911-junot-andoche:
Andoche Junot, duke of Abrantes (1771–1813), was a French general born at Bussy le Grand on the 23rd of October 1771. He was at law study in Paris when the Revolution broke out, and he joined a volunteer battalion. His valour in the first wars brought him under the notice of Napoleon Bonaparte at the siege of Toulon, where he served as his secretary.

A tale is told of that service. A shell burst near him as he wrote, covering the paper with sand, and he joked that they now had sand to dry the ink. He stayed loyal through his chief's fall from favour and went to Italy as his aide. At Millesimo he fought so well that he was chosen to carry the captured colours to Paris. He was badly wounded in the head at Lonato. In Egypt he became a general of brigade.
britannica-1911-khalifa-the:
The Khalifa, Abdullah et Taaisha, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in eighteen forty six in south west Darfur, he was a member of the Taaisha section of the Baggara Arabs. His father had hoped to move the family to Mecca. The unsettled state of the land long blocked that plan.

The entry tells how Abdullah fought against the Egyptian conquest of Darfur. After his father's death he set out for the Nile valley. On the way he heard of Mahommed Ahmed, who had not yet claimed a sacred role. Abdullah later became that leader's successor, known as the Mahdi. The entry follows his rise from that meeting.
britannica-1911-la-fleche:
La Flèche is a town of western France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Sarthe. It stands on the Loire, 31 miles S.S.W. of Le Mans by rail. In 1906 the town held 7800 people and the commune 10,663. Its chief interest is the Prytanée, a famed school for the sons of officers. The school began as a college founded for the Jesuits in 1607 by Henry IV. Its buildings rose between 1620 and 1653 and stand in a park.

 La Flèche is the seat of a sub-prefect and of a court of first instance. Its trades are tanning, flour-milling, and the making of paper, starch, wooden shoes and gloves, and it is a market for farm goods. Its lords became counts of Maine about 1100. The lordship passed in the 16th century to the Bourbons, and so to Henry IV.
britannica-1911-la-roche:
La Roche is a small town in the Belgian Ardennes, noted for its age and its comely setting. It held 2065 people in 1904. Its name comes from its place on a rock above the river Ourthe, which winds round the town. On the rock stand the ruins of the old castle of the 11th century. The counts of La Roche held it in fief from the Carolingian kings. In the 12th century they sold it to the counts of Luxemburg.

French and Imperial troops often fought near La Roche in the 16th and 17th centuries. At Tenneville nearby is shown the tomb of an English officer, Barnewall, killed in one such fight in 1692. The town is a famed centre for tourists for its fine wooded scenery. A steam tramway links La Roche with Melreux, on the main line from Marloie to Liége.
britannica-1911-landsberg-an-der-warthe:
Landsberg-an-der-Warthe is a town in the Prussian province of Brandenburg, where the Warthe and Kladow rivers meet. The 1911 Britannica article puts it eighty miles north-east of Berlin by rail. Its count in 1905 was 36,934 people. Engine works, boiler shops, and iron foundries lead its trades. Other works make tobacco, cloth, carriages, woollen goods, and leather.

A brisk trade moves in wood, cattle, and the crops of the land around the town. Landsberg gained the rights of a city in 1257. In later years it stood sieges by the Poles and then by the Hussites. The short entry points readers to a German history of the town printed in 1890 for the full tale.
britannica-1911-le-sueur-eustache:
French painter Eustache Le Sueur, born at Paris in sixteen seventeen, is one of the founders of the French Academy of painting. A 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry separates fact from fable in his life. Tales said he was hounded by a jealous rival, grew close to Poussin, and died of grief in a monastery.

All that is pure fiction, the entry states. In fact he was son of a turner and wood sculptor who placed him with the painter Vouet. In that studio the boy stood out fast. He joined the master painters' gild young, then left to help set up the academy of painting and sculpture. He was one of its first twelve professors. Works that were copied in tapestry brought him notice, and a set of decorations in a great Paris house raised his name further.
britannica-1911-marches-the:
The Marches is a land division of Italy that takes in four provinces in a row from north to south. Its area and its folk count at the turn of the age are given in the 1911 Britannica entry. It is bounded by a region north, the sea east, a wild land south, and two regions west.

Each of the four provinces holds a share of coast line. The chief rivers all run east and north east to the sea. One of them forms the south bound of the division for a long reach. Past the river vales and the thin coast strip, the land stands high above the sea. The low hills are of loose clay earth that slips with ease. The great range at its back is built of pale stone.
britannica-1911-middle-ages-the:
Middle Ages is the name commonly given to the period of European history between ancient and modern times, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. It has in general been taken to run from about the middle of the 400s to about the middle of the 1400s. Old textbooks used the dates 476 and 1453, from the setting aside of the last emperor in the West to the fall of Constantinople.

In truth, the article argues, no exact dates can be fixed for the opening and close of such a period. Recent study even leads some to doubt whether a set medieval period can be said to exist at all. The growth of modern European society has been unbroken, it holds, though not even in pace. New peoples brought setbacks, but there is no century from the 900s on without some clear gain toward the attainments of modern life.
britannica-1911-muses-the:
Muses are goddesses of song in Greek myth, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. They were at first nymphs of springs in the old tales. Later they became goddesses of the kinds of poetry, and then of the arts and sciences in general. In Homer they have no fixed names or number and are simply goddesses of song. 

Hesiod first gives the accepted names and number of the Muses. He makes them daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, the figure of memory itself. Others made them children of Uranus and Gaea in older tales. Three older Muses were at times set apart, with worship said to start on Mount Helicon. The text holds that three was the first number, raised to nine by their grouping in threes in the sacred choruses.
britannica-1911-niche: Niche comes through French from an Italian word for a shell. In building, it names a hollow sunk in a wall, most often to hold a statue. The hollow is at times capped by a plain label. More often it is capped by a canopy, with a bracket or corbel for the figure. In that form it is often called a tabernacle. The brief article gives the root of the word and that one use in the art of building, and no more.
britannica-1911-nile-battle-of-the:
Nile, Battle of the, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a sea fight of 1798. British and French fleets met on the 1st of August that year. The fight took place in the roadstead of Aboukir in Egypt. The peace of Campo Formio had left France free on land.

War with Britain went on, and France masked a bold plan. Talk of a raid on Ireland hid work for a strike at India by way of Egypt. At Toulon the French fleet was got ready with slow, flawed care. Some thirty-six thousand troops were to sail from French and Italian ports. Word of the move reached the British fleet chief in good time. Nelson was sent out to hunt the French force.
britannica-1911-panache: Panache is a French word for a plume of feathers on a helmet or hat, as a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The word comes through Italian from the Latin word for feather. A panache is a large bunch of feathers fixed on top of a helmet and falling over it. A plume, by contrast, is one feather at the side or the front. In French the word is also used in a loose sense for a showy piece of ornament, or a purple patch in writing.
britannica-1911-papier-mache:
Papier mache is a French term for mashed paper, used for a host of wares in which paper pulp is pressed and shaped in moulds. The forms made are all save flat sheets. The craft has long been worked in the East, the 1911 Britannica entry says, with famed goods from Persia and Kashmir.

In Kashmir the trade goes by a name that means pen tray work, for its small painted boxes, trays, and cases. In Japan wares are made by glue of damp sheets of paper on moulds, layer on layer. China too makes fine goods of the kind. In the mid past age the craft rose in Europe in trays, boxes, and small home wares. They were glossed and trimmed in the style of the East, or of fine dark wood.
britannica-1911-pearl-the:
Pearl is a Middle English poem preserved in a single manuscript, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. That manuscript, Cotton Nero A Ten, is held at the British Museum in London. It also holds the poems Cleanness, Patience, and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. All four are in the same handwriting and are now held to be by the same author.

Pearl is a lament by a poet for the loss of a girl child who lived not two years on earth. In grief he visits her small grave and falls into a vision there. He sees his Pearl across a stream, beneath a crystal rock, now a queen of heaven. She has grown in wisdom as in stature in that state. From the far bank she instructs him, while he longs in vain to cross over to her side.
britannica-1911-person-offences-against-:
Offences against the person is a class name in English law in this 1911 Britannica law entry. It groups crimes of force that harm the life, free state, or safety of a man. Some wrongs of morals sit in the class though no force is used in them. Most of its rules rest in the great act of eighteen sixty one. Acts of eighteen eighty, eighteen eighty five, and nineteen oh four hold the rest.

The class in those acts is not built on a clean plan, the text notes. Bigamy sits in the act of eighteen sixty one by its terms. Robbery and like force wrongs sit in acts of their own kind. The acts name each wrong in full under its own head in law. In the Indian code such wrongs fall under harms to the human body.
britannica-1911-peter-of-aigueblanche:
Peter of Aigueblanche (died 1268) was bishop of Hereford, and his career at the court of Henry III is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from a noble family of Savoy and reached England in 1236 in the train of Queen Eleanor of Provence. By 1240 he had been chosen bishop of Hereford.

The entry stresses his role in 1255 as the king's chief agent in taking the crown of Sicily for Henry's son Edmund. His harsh, crooked ways of raising money for that scheme deepened the king's unpopularity. In the civil war he stayed loyal, was captured at Hereford in 1263, freed, and died in Savoy in 1268.
britannica-1911-praguerie-the:
Praguerie, a revolt of the French nobility against King Charles the Seventh in 1440, is explained in a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The rising took its name from a like revolt in Prague. It was sparked by reforms the king made at the close of the Hundred Years War. Those reforms sought to curb disorder in France.

New rules cut down bands of hired soldiers who lived by plunder. Laws from 1439 gave the king a grant of funds and a say in army posts. Nobles saw a threat to their power and rose in protest. The duke of Bourbon led the plot and won over the young dauphin Louis. Royal troops moved fast, and cannon broke the strongholds of the rebels. In two months the revolt was crushed in the main. Looting still dragged on in two provinces.
britannica-1911-primitive-methodist-chur:
Primitive Methodist Church, The is a church article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a body of Nonconformists born of revival fire. As Methodism settled down after its first age to the work of self government, some ardent spirits held to the old lines, and their watchword was revivalism.

One founder was Hugh Bourne, a millwright of Stoke-upon-Trent. Moved by the ignorance of the colliery villages, he began open air preaching with prayer and song, the seed of the famed camp meeting. A chapel rose at Harrisehead, and in January 1805 William Clowes, a potter of Burslem and once a dancer of national fame, was converted. After the American revivalist Lorenzo Dow told of camp meetings in his land, Bourne's party held the first true English camp meeting on Mow Cop in May 1807.
britannica-1911-primrose-league-the:
The Primrose League is the subject of an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a group formed to spread Conservative principles among the British public. The primrose flower was linked with the name of Lord Beaconsfield. He was said to prefer it to all other flowers.

The entry tells how Queen Victoria sent primroses to be placed on his coffin. A card in her own hand called them his favourite flowers. On the day his statue was unveiled, Conservative members in the Commons wore the flower. A small group had long talked of a league in his honour. The text traces how that idea became a national group.
britannica-1911-revolutionary-tribunal-t:
Revolutionary Tribunal was a court set up in Paris by the Convention in the French Revolution. The 1911 Britannica article calls it one of the most strong tools of the Terror. It was made to try men charged with crimes against the state. Word of French losses in Belgium sparked riots in Paris in March 1793. On the tenth of March, at the call of Danton, the Convention set up the court. A decree that October gave it its famed name.

No appeal lay from its verdicts. With Hermann as president and Fouquier-Tinville as prosecutor, it struck fear in royalists and priests. Robespierre bent it to strike down his own foes as well. A law of June 1794 barred counsel and witnesses and made death the sole sentence. In the forty-nine days that followed, 1,376 souls were condemned.
britannica-1911-rigaud-hyacinthe:
Hyacinthe Rigaud (1659–1743) was a French painter born at Perpignan on the 20th of July 1659, from a line of artists. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his training at Montpellier and Lyons and his move to Paris in 1681. There his portraits won such praise that Le Brun urged him to drop the Rome trip and give himself to portrait work.

Rigaud took the advice and for sixty-two years painted thirty to forty portraits a year, each finished with great care by his own hand. His grand portraits of Bossuet and Louis the Fourteenth hang in the Louvre, as do tender ones of his mother, Marie Serre. He pressed the Academy to take him as a history painter and won that rank in January 1700. He died on the 27th of December 1743, a year after losing his wife.
britannica-1911-romans-epistle-to-the:
The Epistle to the Romans, a book of the New Testament by the apostle Paul, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. Paul opens by saying he has long been kept from a hoped for visit to the church at Rome. He then sets out the gospel he preaches. Its leading theme is the righteousness of God, reached by faith.

Both Gentile and Jew have missed that righteousness so far, the piece sums up. In Jesus Christ it is brought within reach of all, by faith and not by birth. Abraham is shown as a man of faith before the law came. Grace has won over sin and life over death. Yet grace does not loosen the moral bond, since faith means death to sin.
britannica-1911-round-table-the:
Round Table, the table of King Arthur and his knights, is explained in a legend entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Knights sat round it so that no man held a higher place than the rest. The name is also used for the knights as a famed order. No one knows where the tale first came from.

Geoffrey of Monmouth does not name the table at all. Wace gives the first record, of a Yuletide fight over who should sit first. To stop such strife, a craftsman from Cornwall made a vast round table. In that tale it could seat more than sixteen hundred knights. Romance tales tell a unlike tale. There Merlin made the table for Uther, or it came to Arthur as a gift at his wedding. In romance only the best knights earn a seat.
britannica-1911-seven-sleepers-of-ephesu:
The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, an old tale from Syria, are treated in a 1911 Britannica article. Seven Christian youths hid in a cave in the year 250, fleeing a time of harsh rule. Their cave was found and its mouth was blocked. The youths fell asleep in each other's arms.

Near two hundred years later a herdsman found the cave and let in the light. One youth went to buy food and was stunned to see the cross over the city gates. His old coin raised doubts, so he led men to the cave. His six friends were found young and bright faced. The emperor heard their tale, then they slept once more.
britannica-1911-seven-wise-masters-the:
The Seven Wise Masters is a story article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a famous cycle of tales that began in the East. A Roman emperor sends his son away from court to be taught by seven wise masters. The boy learns the seven liberal arts under their care.

On his return, his stepmother tries to lead him astray and then accuses him. Bound by the stars to a week of silence, the prince cannot defend himself. The empress tells the emperor seven tales urging the boy's death. Each time, one of the sages answers with a tale of women's craft. At last the prince speaks, the truth comes out, and the empress is executed. The entry traces how the cycle travelled west through many tongues as the book of Sindibad.
britannica-1911-seven-wise-men-of-greece:
The Seven Wise Men of Greece is a joint name for some sages who flourished from about 620 to 550 BC. The list most men accept runs Bias, Chilon, Cleobulus, Periander, Pittacus, Solon, and Thales. Old sources differ as to the names and the count. These men won great sway in their own cities as lawgivers and counsellors. Their fame spread through the whole Greek world.

The rules of life of the Seven were set down in poems and in short sayings in common use. The article points the reader to the life of each sage in his own entry. It also lists works in German and Latin that treat the group, their verses, and their sayings. Short lives of the men are given in one of those works, Mullach's Fragments of the Greek Philosophers.
britannica-1911-sierra-morena-the:
Sierra Morena is a range of mountains in southern Spain, treated in this 1911 Britannica article. It forms the largest section of the mountain system called the Cordillera Marianica, which also takes in smaller Spanish ranges and the mountains of southern Portugal. Its mean height is about 2,500 feet, and its breadth is not less than forty miles.

The range runs east as far as the steppe region of Albacete, and west to the valley of the lower Guadiana. Its line is often broken, above all in the west. In the east and middle it is made of many ridges set in no clear order, and many of these bear names of their own. The easternmost and loftiest is the Sierra de Alcaraz, at 5,900 feet, while some ridges in the far west are grouped as the Sierras de Aracena.
britannica-1911-solent-the:
Solent is a strait of the English Channel, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It lies between the mainland coast of Hampshire and the north western coast of the Isle of Wight. It forms the western entrance to Southampton Water, with Spithead as the eastern entrance. Its length is 15 miles, from Southampton Water to the Needles rocks.

Its general breadth is from two and a half to three miles in its course. At one point it narrows to one and three quarter miles between the two coasts. A great shingle bank springs from the mainland north of the Needles for near two miles. It reduces the breadth of the Solent to a little over three quarters of a mile at its end. On that end stands Hurst Castle, a fort from the time of Henry the Eighth. Charles the First was imprisoned there in 1648, the text notes.
britannica-1911-strophe:
Strophe, a Greek word from a root meaning to turn, is a term of verse making treated in this 1911 Britannica article. In its strict sense for choral song, a strophe was a set section in the build of an ode. Milton's phrase is quoted, in which strophe, antistrophe, and epode were a kind of stanza framed only for the music.

In a wider sense the strophe is a set of verse periods of varied kinds joined into one unit. In modern poetry the strophe is in most cases the same as the stanza. The placing and return of the rhymes give it its character. The ancients, by contrast, called such a joining of verse periods a system. They gave the name strophe to it only when it was repeated once or more in unaltered form.
britannica-1911-theroigne-de-mericourt-a:
Anne Josephe Theroigne de Mericourt, born in Luxembourg in seventeen sixty two, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She took her name from Marcourt, the small town where she was born. Her father was a well off farmer.

She was raised in a convent school and was quick, bold, and a strong speaker. The entry clears her of a tale that she sought revenge on nobles for a wrong done to her. She left home after a row with her step mother. She sang in concerts and lived in London, Paris, and Genoa. Back in Paris in seventeen eighty nine, she drew a circle of known men of the French revolt.
britannica-1911-thessalonians-epistles-t:
The Epistles to the Thessalonians are two books of the New Testament. They were writ to the church in a Greek port city. That flock was founded by Paul and two mates. The founding came just before their trips to two great Greek cities. The 1911 Britannica entry sets out the faith they preached there.

It held the one God and faith in Christ as Lord. It held the near day of doom as well. It held too the mark of Pauls own teaching. The Christ who dwells in the heart is a pledge of a clear name at the last day. He is a pledge of life with Christ for ever. The new flock met harsh treatment from the start. Its folk were chiefly Gentiles who worked with their hands.
britannica-1911-tichborne-claimant-the:
Roger Charles Tichborne was an heir whose loss at sea sparked a famed fraud case. His story entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest grandson of Sir Edward Tichborne, the ninth baronet. His Hampshire family was old, rich, and Roman Catholic in faith.

Roger was born in Paris in eighteen twenty nine and raised as a French boy. He joined the Sixth Dragoon Guards in Dublin in eighteen forty nine. He sold out in eighteen fifty two and sailed for South America next. In eighteen fifty four his ship Bella sank with all hands on board. An impostor in eighteen sixty eight claimed to be Roger and sought his estate.
britannica-1911-topffer-rodolphe:
Rodolphe Topffer, who lived from 1799 to 1846, was a Swiss teacher famed for schoolboy walking tours. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his birth at Geneva to an artist father. He meant to paint like his father, but weak eyes in 1819 ended that plan. Paris study turned him toward the schoolmaster path for his life work.

He ran a private school, then founded his own in 1824 after his marriage. Foot journeys in the Alps with his pupils began in 1823 as trials. From 1832 they became a yearly custom loved by boys and readers alike. His zigzag voyage books, with his own sketches, told those tours each year.
britannica-1911-tower-of-london-the:
Tower of London is a fortress article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Tower is an ancient stronghold on the east side of the City of London. It stands on the north bank of the River Thames. A British stronghold first held the site, guarded by river, marsh, and woods.

Tradition named Julius Caesar as the Tower's founder, and Roman remains have been found below the site. The entry describes the fortress as it stood in 1911. It holds barracks and keeps the regalia, the crown jewels of the realm. A ditch, once fed by the Thames but now dry, rings its walls. Gardens lie to the north and west, an embankment along the river. Two lines of walls enclose the inner court and its great White Tower. That keep, flanked by four turrets, crowns the whole place.
britannica-1911-vatican-council-the:
The Vatican Council of 1869 and 1870 is the subject of a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry calls it the last general council of the Roman Catholic Church at that time. It ranks the event as the most important in that church's growth since the synod at Trent. The early steps toward it were kept in close secrecy.

Inside, the article says Pius the Ninth asked cardinals in Rome for their views at the end of 1864. Most favoured the plan, and by March 1865 the call was no longer in doubt. Thirty six bishops of varied lands were asked in private what tasks the gathering should take up. Some urged that papal infallibility be raised to a formal teaching of the church.
britannica-1911-vendee-wars-of-the:
Wars of the Vendée names a rising against the Revolution in western France, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article tells its origins. The revolt spread beyond Vendée into Lower Poitou, Anjou, Lower Maine, and Brittany. The district was peasant country with few large towns. Its people were slow to take up the ideas of the Revolution. In 1789 the events that stirred the rest of France left them cold.

Discontent soon showed itself. Priests who refused the Civil Constitution of the Clergy moved through these remote districts. They branded the revolutionists as heretics. In 1791 officials warned the Convention of the region's unrest, and a royalist plot was exposed. The spark for a wide rising was conscription. In February 1793 the Convention decreed a levy for the depleted armies. Rather than comply, the Vendée broke out in revolt on the eve of the ballot.
britannica-1911-wash-the:
The Wash is a shallow bay of the North Sea on the coast of Lincolnshire and Norfolk. It is roughly square in shape, cutting twenty two miles into the land. It is twenty miles wide at its head and twelve at its mouth. Sandbanks fill its bed, with two main channels cut through them. One channel is kept open by the Witham and Welland rivers.

The other channel gives passage to the Nene and the Great Ouse. The Wash is the remnant of a much larger bay that once covered the Fens. It is filling slowly with silt brought down by its rivers. Small parts are reclaimed from the sea from time to time. Flat lands round it are guarded by sea walls against the tide. King John lost his baggage wagons in its marshes in twelve sixteen.
britannica-1911-weald-the:
Weald is a district in the south-east of England, spread across parts of Sussex, Kent, and Surrey. The 1911 Britannica article sets it between the North Downs and the South Downs. Its rocks are of an older chalk age than the hills that ring it. The district runs from the Hampshire border to the Channel shore between Folkestone and Eastbourne. Its rivers cut gaps in the Downs as they flow north and south.

Long ago a great forest, Andredsweald, covered the whole tract. It ran one hundred and twenty miles long and some thirty miles wide. Ashdown and Saint Leonards forests are its chief remains. Place names with hurst, the word for wood, mark its old reach. The woods fed the iron works of the district for fuel. That trade, worked by the Romans and at its peak in the sixteenth century, ate the forest down.
britannica-1911-west-indies-the:
West Indies is a region study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a chain of islands in the Atlantic. The chain sweeps in a rough arc from Florida and Yucatan down to Venezuela. It rings the Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico.

The article gives the land of all the islands as near 100,000 square miles. The people of the chain are put at about six and a half million. Three groups sort the islands by size and place. The Bahamas stand apart, then the Greater Antilles, then the Lesser Antilles. The Lesser group splits in turn into Windward and Leeward isles. In rock terms the chain is the crest of a drowned range of hills. One band of isles is wholly of volcanic birth, with fresh cones still standing.
britannica-1911-whisky-insurrection-the:
Whisky Insurrection is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a rising in Pennsylvania. It broke out in the west of the state in 1794. The cause was a bid to enforce a tax on home-made spirits. Congress had passed that tax law in March 1791.

Hate of excise ran strong in the west, where small stills were many. Albert Gallatin voiced the protest in lawful form at first. Under David Bradford the mood turned to riot and force. Tax men were tarred and feathered in some of the attacks. In September 1794 Washington sent a large militia force west. The rebels then gave in with no blood shed at all.
britannica-1911-zouche:
Zouche is the name of an English family traced from Alan la Zouche, a Breton settler. A 1911 Britannica entry says he came in the reign of Henry the Second. Marriage won him Ashby in Leicestershire, called Ashby de la Zouch after his house. His grandson Alan served as justice of Chester and of Ireland under Henry the Third.

That Alan stayed loyal in the barons war, fought at Lewes, and helped make the Kenilworth peace. A land quarrel with Earl Warenne ended in blood in Westminster Hall itself. Attacked there by the earl men, he died of his wounds in August 1270. His line split, and one barony later fell into abeyance for good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-absinthe:
Absinthe here is not the liquor but the biblical plant wormwood, Hebrew la'anah, known for repulsive bitterness. Scripture cites it in Jeremiah, Deuteronomy, Lamentations, and Proverbs. As a figure it denotes curse or calamity, and injustice in Amos. In Apocalypse 8:11 the Greek equivalent names the star that dropped into the waters, turning them bitter.

Jerome's Vulgate gives absinthium for the Hebrew word, except in Deuteronomy 29:18, where it gives amaritudo. The biblical plant seems identical with Artemisia monosperma, Artemisia herba-alba, or Artemisia judaica. The entry points readers to its companion piece on plants in the Bible and cites Hagen, Vigouroux, and Tristram.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alanus-de-rup:
Alanus de Rupe, sometimes Alain de la Roche, was born about 1428 and died at Zwolle in Holland on 8 September 1475. Some claim him German, others Belgian, but his disciple Cornelius Sneek says he was born in Brittany. Entering the Dominican Order early in life, he distinguished himself at Saint Jacques, Paris, in philosophy and theology.

Teaching from 1459 to 1475 took him to Paris, Lille, Douay, Ghent, and Rostock, where in 1473 he became Master of Sacred Theology. Sixteen years of teaching made him a renowned preacher. Indefatigable in his special mission, preaching and re-establishing the Rosary, he succeeded across northern France, Flanders, and the Netherlands. Dated 1460 is his vision of restoring the Rosary. He published nothing in life, but after his death his province's brethren collected his writings. His relations of St. Dominic's visions and sermons, supposedly revealed to Alanus, count as unhistorical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-ant:
Alexandre-Antonin Taché was the first Archbishop of St. Boniface in Manitoba, a missionary, prelate, and writer of Canada, born at Fraserville in Quebec in July 1823 and dead at St. Boniface in June 1894. His father belonged to a Canadian family, and through his mother he descended from La Vérendrye, the explorer of the country of his life's work. He studied at the College of St. Hyacinthe, joined the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, and reached St. Boniface in August 1845.

Taché was ordained a priest at St. Boniface in October 1845 and laboured in the north. He learned Saulteux, then Chippewayan, at Ile-à-la-Crosse. After Bishop Provencher's death in 1853 he carried on his missions. A later division let him attend to the missions and parishes of Assiniboia, now Manitoba. Called home from the Vatican Council, he saw the promised amnesty refused after Scott's execution, a blow to his standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-campeche:
Campeche is a diocese in Mexico, under Yucatán, created on 24 March 1895 by dividing the Diocese of Yucatán. Its land covers the western Yucatán peninsula, with plains in the north, broad savannahs and dense forests, and a well-watered south. Spaniards found a Maya seaside village called Ah Kin Pech in 1517. In 1540 Captain Montejo founded a seaport town there, starting at once the church of Santa Maria de la Concepción, now the cathedral.

The first bishop to visit Campeche was Bartolomé de las Casas, driven ashore by a storm, and its first missionaries were Franciscans, followed by Jesuits in 1715 until their expulsion in 1767. The diocese counts about 100,000 people in twenty-three parishes, and its third bishop, Francisco Mendoza y Herrera, opened a seminary, three colleges, and an episcopal residence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-rothe:
A biographical entry presents David Rothe, Bishop of Ossory in Ireland, born at Kilkenny in 1573 and dead on 20 April 1650. Schooled at Douai and Salamanca, he took a doctorate in civil and canon law. Ordained in 1600, he then served at Rome, teaching theology and acting as secretary to Archbishop Lombard. Made vice-primate of Armagh in 1609, he reached Ireland in 1610. He held synods at Drogheda in 1614 and 1618.

Appointed Bishop of Ossory in 1618, penal laws forced him to seek consecration at Paris in 1620. His Analecta, first issued in 1616 and completed at Cologne, remains a famed defence of Irish Catholic history. He published lives of Saint Brigid and Irish histories, presided at Kilkenny in 1624, joined the Confederates in 1642 and greeted the papal nuncio Rinuccini in 1645.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doliche:
Doliche, a small city on the Germanicia-to-Zeugma road, was a titular see of Commagene. Its temple of Zeus Dolichenus brought it fame, and it minted coins of its own from Marcus Aurelius down to Caracalla. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets its ruins at Tell Duluk, three miles northwest of Aintab in the region of Aleppo. At an early date it became a bishopric answering to Hierapolis.

Lequien names eight Greek bishops, from Archelaus at Nicaea in 325 to Philoxenus in later councils. One bishop, Abibus, a Nestorian, was deposed in 434. In time Doliche itself rose to the rank of metropolis, and fourteen Jacobite bishops of the eighth and ninth centuries are also listed. The entry packs a long church history into a small city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elishe:
Elishe was a famous Armenian historian of the fifth century, dead in 480, whose birthplace and birth date are unknown. Some make him Elisha, Bishop of Amaduni, at the Synod of Artashat in 449. The commoner tale says he served General Vartan as soldier or secretary. That was in the war for religious freedom against Persia's Yezdigerd II from 449 to 451. Afterwards he turned hermit south of Lake Van.

Ancient writers call him vartabed, or doctor. His masterwork is the History of Vartan and of the Wars of the Armenians. David the Mamigonian asked him to write it. It tells how Armenians, Iberians, and Albanians fought together for their faith against Persia. It counts as a masterpiece of old Armenian letters, nearly free of Greek words. Good editions came from the Mechitarists at Venice, and translations exist in English, Italian, and French. An eighth chapter on later martyrs is questioned by scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-pasca:
Etienne-Pascal Tache, a statesman, was born at Saint Thomas, Quebec, on 5 September 1795, and died on 30 July 1865. In the war of 1812 he served as lieutenant of the Chasseurs canadiens. A self-made man, he graduated at Philadelphia as a physician after an elementary course, and later ranked foremost among Canadian statesmen.

Twenty-two years of medical practice came first, and then he entered politics in 1841 as a member of the Legislative Assembly, though he had opposed the Union. Re-elected in 1844, he took the post of adjutant-general of militia in 1846. In 1848 he became chief commissioner of public works in the Lafontaine-Baldwin ministry. Knighted in 1858, he was appointed aide-de-camp to the Queen in 1860, with the rank of colonel. In 1864 he formed the Taché-MacDonald administration and presided over the confederation conference of the British North American provinces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hippolyte-del:
Hippolyte Delaroche, also known as Paul Delaroche, was a French painter born at Paris in 1797 and dead in 1856. He trained first under Watelet, a landscape painter of modest ability, and then under Gros, a great painter but a poor teacher. The entry judges him badly trained, without deep insight into mankind or life and without a novel idea of art or beauty.

Yet Delaroche had a commonplace skill that pleased the public, and he shrewdly chose subjects to make up for what he lacked. His debut at the Salon of 1819 passed unnoticed, but a gold medal followed in 1824. He then settled into a long series of historical anecdotes, mostly from the civil wars of France and England. Multiplied by engraving, those scenes appealed to the bourgeois taste of the Restoration and July Monarchy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-melch:
Publicist Jacques Melchior Villefranche was born at Couzon-sur-Saône on 17 December 1829. He died at Bourg on 10 May 1904. After fine classical studies at Largentière's lesser seminary, he entered the telegraph service. In 1855, during the Crimean War, he directed the Varna telegraph bureau. Varna was the first landing place of Franco-Russian troops. In 1870, as telegraph director at Versailles, he served the Le Mans army's communications.

In 1875 he left the telegraph service and edited the Journal de l'Ain. There he defended religious liberty. His campaigns against school secularization laws were widely noted. His writing activity was very great. His Fables of 1851 and Fabuliste Chrétien of 1875 were welcomed in many schools. Historical and judicial romances from his pen were long read, notably Cinéas, or Rome under Nero. The entry presents a telegrapher turned Catholic journalist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-vegh:
Johannes Veghe was a German preacher and religious writer of the late fifteenth century, praised for his mastery of Low German. Born at Munster about 1435, he studied at Cologne. He entered the house of the Brethren of the Common Life at Munster in 1451. He led the Brethren's house at Rostock and returned to Munster as rector in 1475. Ill health led him to resign in 1481 and become confessor to the Sisters of Niesink, a post he held until his death in 1504.

Leisure for writing brought treatises such as the Spiritual Chase. It turns every detail of a hunt toward the search for God. The Marientrost treats devotion to the Virgin, and the Vineyard of the Soul treats progress toward perfection. His chief work is sermons preached in Low German before the Niesink sisters in 1492. They show keen observation of nature and the human heart in a vigorous, natural style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-beche:
John Beche, also known as Thomas Marshall, was an English Benedictine abbot executed under Henry VIII. Educated at Oxford and doctor of divinity in 1515, he ruled the Abbey of St. Werburgh at Chester and was elected Abbot of St. John's, Colchester, in 1530. With sixteen monks he took Henry's Oath of Supremacy in 1534.

The martyrdoms of the Carthusian priors, John Fisher, and Thomas More in 1535 moved him to speak with reverence for them, and spies reported his words. When he denied a royal commission's right to seize his abbey in 1538, he was sent to the Tower on treason charges, released, and rearrested. Tried at Colchester in November 1539, he stopped pleading against the new order, was convicted, and was executed on 1 December, receiving what the entry calls the crown of martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-peter-:
Julius Peter Garesché was a United States Army officer who died leading troops at the Battle of Stone River. Born near Havana in 1821, he studied at Georgetown College and graduated from West Point in 1841. He served on the frontier, fought in the Mexican War, and became assistant adjutant-general, ranking as captain, in 1855. He took an active part in Catholic life and helped organize Washington's first conference of the St. Vincent de Paul Society.

He also wrote often on Catholic, social, and political questions for the New York Freeman's Journal and Brownson's Quarterly Review. Pius IX made him a Knight of St. Sylvester in 1851. When the Civil War began, he declined a brigadier-general's commission and served instead as chief of staff to General Rosecrans. He was killed by a cannonball on 31 December 1862 while leading a column to regain a lost day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lecoy-de-la-m:
Richard-Albert Lecoy de La Marche (1839-1897) was a French historian. He trained at the Ecole des Chartes in 1861, served as archivist of Haute-Savoie, then of the National Archives' historical section from 1864. For years he also taught French history at Paris's Catholic Institute.

Gifted as writer and scholar, he never split historical truth from religious truth. His masterpiece, La Chaire francaise au moyen age of 1868, won a prize from the Academy of Inscriptions. It remains the standard work, studying medieval French preaching in three parts: preachers, sermons, and society as sermons reveal it. Kings, lords, bishops, priests, monks, burgesses, peasants, men and women pass through it with their traits and faults. Later books cover King Rene, St. Martin, manuscripts and miniatures, and thirteenth-century society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-francoi:
Louis Francois Richer Lafleche was a French-Canadian bishop and missionary, born in Quebec in 1818 and dead in 1898. Ordained in 1844 for the Red River country, he canoed 750 leagues to St. Boniface, then travelled 300 leagues more to La Crosse Island with Father Tache.

He mastered Sauteux, Cree, and Montagnais, and first set Montagnais into grammar. In 1851 he led the defence of sixty Metis against two thousand Sioux near Turtle Mountain, and the attackers withdrew after two days, awed by the missionary in surplice and stole. Later he taught at Nicolet, became Bishop of Three Rivers in 1870, and preached boldly on the social questions of his day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-vehe:
Michael Vehe was born at Bieberach near Wimpfen and died at Halle in April 1559. He joined the Dominicans at Wimpfen, went to Heidelberg in 1506, taught there in 1512, and earned his doctorate in theology in 1513. In 1515 he ran the Dominicans' Heidelberg house of studies as its regent. Cardinal Albert of Mainz later picked him for his theologian and put him in charge of the church at Halle in Saxony.

Called to Augsburg in 1530 to answer the Lutheran Confession, he played a leading part in the Leipzig debate with the Lutherans in 1534. Among his writings are pieces on Communion under one species, on honouring God and his saints, and the Assertio of 1537 on points the Reformers contested. These stand among Germany's best sixteenth-century apologetical treatises. Vehe also brought out a hymn book in 1537, and on 21 February 1559 he was called to the bishopric of Halberstadt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niche:
A niche is a recess for a statue, designed to give it emphasis, frame it effectively, and afford some protection. It hardly existed before the twelfth century, and ranks among Gothic architecture's chief decorative traits. The constant, often lavish use of sculptured saints' images formed an essential part of the great style expressing the Catholic Faith, begun in Normandy through the Cluniac reform.

Once roughly chiselled bas-relief swelled into the round, detached figure, medieval builders learned a lesson Greeks had taught. Figure sculpture turns architectural only when incorporated with its building through surrounding forms harmonising it with the fabric. In Romanesque work the frame was little more than flanking shafts supporting an arch, the statue treated as accessory wherever flat wall appeared. The arrangement's convenience, propriety and beauty were at once apparent, and the niche's development as an independent form was constant and rapid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-maleb:
Oratorian thinker Nicolas Malebranche, born at Paris in 1638, built a philosophy in which God, not bodies, does the real work of sensing and knowing. Frail and home-tutored as a boy, he studied at the Collège de La Marche and the Sorbonne, turned down a canonry, and joined the Paris Oratory in 1660.

A chance reading of Descartes set his course, and his 1674 Search after Truth argued that sense and fancy serve practical need, not knowledge of things as they are. Later books refined that doctrine, and he died in 1715 after long disputes with fellow Cartesians and theologians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olivier-de-la:
Burgundian chronicler Olivier de la Marche, born in Franche-Comté in 1426, served Charles the Bold and his daughter Marie through war and court. Knighted by the count of Charolais in 1465, he became bailiff and captain of guards. Captured at Nancy in 1477 where Charles died, he ransomed himself to serve Marie as master of household.

His Memoirs, covering 1435 to 1492 and first printed at Lyons in 1562, remain singular and vital for the age, despite Walloon phrasing and long fêtes. Verse works include Le Chevalier Délibéré, read as his own life or an allegory of Charles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quiche:
The Quiche, also called Ulateca, were the chief aboriginal people of Guatemala. This encyclopedia entry places them in the great Mayan language stock, beside their neighbours the Cakchiquel, Pokonchi and Tzutuhil, whose four dialects form a single language. They held north-central Guatemala, including the present districts of Quiche and Totonicapan and part of Quezaltenango. Their traditions suggest a northern or north-eastern origin, and their fairly reliable history reaches back to about AD 700.

Pedro de Alvarado subdued them about 1525, with more than the usual atrocities, and they declined fast under slavery and heavy tribute. That decline came despite papal warnings and humane laws proclaimed by the Spanish crown. Brasseur de Bourbourg's studies of native languages, including the Popol Vuh, supply one source. Sahagún's history of New Spain and Squier's Central America supply others, on a people whose ancient books still speak for a shattered nation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-hyacint:
Saint Hyacinthe is the Quebec diocese, suffragan of Montreal. It was formed from parts of Montreal and Quebec by a bull of 8 June 1852 after a petition from the First Council of Quebec. At first it covered the south side of the Richelieu River and the Eastern Townships, land granted late in the eighteenth century to American loyalists. Later three parishes north of the river were added. It takes in the counties of Bagot, Iberville, Missisquoi, Richelieu, Rouville, and Saint Hyacinthe, with parts of Brome and Verchères.

Its city, a French Canadian town on the Yamaska thirty-five miles from Montreal, had 10,000 people. Jean Charles Prince, coadjutor bishop of Montreal, became its first bishop and took possession on 3 November 1852, turning the seminary into cathedral and residence. Fire destroyed it in 1854. He rebuilt, founded twenty parishes, brought the Sisters of the Presentation from France in 1853, and died on 5 May 1860.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sidron-de-hos:
Sidron de Hossche, in Latin Hosschius, was a poet and priest born at Mercken in West Flanders in 1596 and dead at Tongres in 1653. In youth he followed his father's trade as a shepherd, and at twenty he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tongres. He soon showed a wonderful gift for Latin verse, and his first work, On Christ Suffering, in elegiac verse, appeared in 1635. Its chorus of praise brought him to the notice of Leopold William, Governor General of the Netherlands, who made him tutor to his two sons for two years.

Court life did not appeal to him, and he retired to Tongres until his death. His surviving works include On the Course of Human Life, On the Tears of Saint Peter, and many elegies and occasional verses. His age acclaimed him as worthy of the Augustan age, while sober criticism calls his works elegant versification.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-abban-of-m:
St. Abban of Magheranoidhe was a sixth- and seventh-century Irish saint, nephew of St. Ibar, apostle of Wexford and a predecessor and contemporary of St. Patrick. This entry makes him the son of Cormac, King of Leinster, flourishing between 570 and 620. And founder of many churches across Ui Cennselaigh, a district nearly matching modern County Wexford and the diocese of Ferns.

His chief monastery stood at Magheranoidhe, also rendered Murneave or Murnevin and later called Abbanstown, now Adamstown, while his abbey at Rosmic-treoin, or New Ross, grew famous as a school. He died on 16 March 620, and the entry warns readers not to confuse him with his namesake of New Ross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-richard-de:
Richard de Wyche, bishop of Chichester, rose from a ruined estate to the chancellorship of Oxford and the episcopate. Born about 1197 at Droitwich in Worcestershire, he was second son of Richard and Alice de Wyche. He refused his elder brother's offer of the inheritance. He managed the family's broken property back to health. At Oxford he and two companions shared one tunic and gown between them for lectures.

After Paris and a master's degree, he studied canon law at Bologna and became chancellor of Oxford. Edmund Rich of Canterbury made him his chancellor and friend, and Richard backed the archbishop against the king over vacant sees. Elected bishop of Chichester, he reformed his diocese with energy. He died at Dover on 3 April 1253, famed for learning and sanctity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-didache:
Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, the Didache, is the early Christian manual recovered here. Some Fathers ranked it next to Scripture itself. Bryennios, Greek Orthodox metropolitan of Nicomedia, rediscovered it in 1873 in the codex that in 1875 yielded Clement's full epistles. Manuscript title reads Didache kyriou dia ton dodeka apostolon ethesin, with shorter heading Didache ton dodeka apostolon.

Three parts divide it: Two Ways, of Life and of Death, a ritual for baptism, fasting, and communion, and a section on ministry, with doctrine assumed rather than taught. Eusebius lists it among spurious books after Scripture. Latin version of chapters one to five, found by Schlecht in 1900, and the text's date, origin, and influence close a compact guide to primitive Christian life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-bathe:
William Bathe was an Irish Jesuit whose language primer shaped how Europe learned tongues. Born at Dublin in 1564, he died at Madrid in 1614. He went to Oxford about 1583 and while still a student issued a short guide to music in 1584, followed by a song manual in 1600. His skill on instruments, above all the Irish harp, won favour with Queen Elizabeth, to whom he was kin through the Kildare family, but his bent ran toward religious life.

From court he moved to Louvain for theology, entered the Jesuits at Tournai in 1595, and studied at Saint Omer and Padua. A 1601 mission to Ireland with the papal nuncio stalled in Spain, where he stayed. At Salamanca in 1611 he issued Janua Linguarum, grouping 1330 short sentences with Latin and Spanish face to face, plus a word index. Editions spread it to eleven tongues, and Comenius owned his debt to it in 1631.
conception-control-and-its-effects-on-th:
Conception Control and Its Effects on the Individual and the Nation, by Florence Elizabeth Barrett, examines the birth control question in five chapters. The Problem of To-day opens with history. In the late seventies of the last century, Annie Besant and Charles Bradlaugh republished The Fruits of Philosophy. They meant to ease poor women overburdened by work and weakened by frequent child-bearing.

The demand for knowledge and from whom to obtain it comes next, then methods, then the effect of widespread conception control on national efficiency. Conclusions are summarized at the end. Barrett argues against easy answers: slum women's ill health, she insists, is not child-bearing alone, and to pretend conception control solves the question is a mockery that salves the community's conscience.
creative-chemistry-descriptive-of-recent:
Recent gains in the chemical trades are set out for lay readers by Edwin E. Slosson in Creative Chemistry. The Century Company of New York published it in October 1919, with many pictures. Slosson was literary editor of The Independent and taught in the Columbia School of Journalism.

Chapters move through metals and non-metals and the goods made from them. One long passage tracks rubber, wild and planted, with world output figures for 1907 to 1917. Dyes, fuels, and other war-driven trades get the same plain treatment. The book explains how lab work became factory wealth, in words a non-chemist can follow, soon after the First World War.
cutler-lynch-law-an-investigation-into-t:
A study of lynching in the United States by James Elbert Cutler fills this 1905 book from Longmans, Green, and Company. Cutler taught economics at Wellesley College and had held posts at Yale. A note from W. G. Sumner stands at the front, dated February 1905.

Cutler says his aim is less to write the history than to find the causes. He asks what social states let lynch-law work, and tests the pleas made in its favour. The rise of the Ku Klux Klan at Pulaski gets a full account in the middle. The book is cool and probing on a violent theme. It stands as an early work of American social science on mob killing.
d-ri-and-i-a-tale-of-daring-deeds-in-the:
A tale of the second war with the British, told as the memoirs of Colonel Ramon Bell, fills Irving Bacheller's 1901 novel. Bacheller had won fame with Eben Holden. Twenty-seven chapters carry the story, with pictures named at the front.

An introduction prints a letter from Captain Darius Hawkins, who commends young Bell to the Comte de Chaumont. Bell, a month in the army, rides and fights like a born soldier. D'Ri, the rough guide whose speech names the book, stands beside him. Louise leads the love thread, and Bell owns he could not tell which of two girls he loved the better. The novel is a brisk romance of the War of 1812.
day-symbols-of-the-maya-year-sixteenth-a:
The day signs of the Maya year are studied one by one in this paper by Cyrus Thomas. It first ran in the Sixteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, for 1894 to 1895. The Government Printing Office at Washington issued it in 1897, on pages 199 to 266.

Twenty sections treat the first day through the last, glyph by glyph. Thomas weighs the names in Maya and in Mexican tongues. One sign, he argues, means a row of teeth or a flight of steps, and matches forms in Mexican writing. Dr Brinton's reading of the word eb is set beside his own. Plates show the carved and painted forms. The paper is close, dry scholarship on the Maya calendar.
dick-prescott-s-first-year-at-west-point:
Dick Prescott's First Year at West Point, or Two Chums in the Cadet Gray, by H Irving Hancock, opens the author's West Point series. Hancock's contents name the plebe year's stations. Two Tiny Specks of Nothing introduces the new cadets. The Tyranny of the Cadet Corporal and In the Hands of the Yearling Hazers follow. Greg's Case of Blues, a sudden grind at math, and Plebe Prescott's First Fight keep the pace.

Dick and Greg climb from candidates to class president by the final chapters. A prowler in quarters and a sentry's capture supply the mystery. The Saalfield Publishing Company issued the book in 1910. Hancock wrote boys' military series by the shelf. His West Point is exact about uniforms, demerits, and hazing rituals. Generations of American boys learned the Academy from him first. Some arrived at the real parade ground already knowing where to stand.
disturbances-of-the-heart-discussion-of-:
Oliver T. Osborne, an American physician, gathered his journal series on heart treatment into Disturbances of the Heart, a reference for doctors. A complete section on blood pressure marks the revised second edition. Osborne skips anatomy lectures and goes straight to therapy, how to treat each disorder at the bedside. The Journal's warm reception for the articles prompted the book form.

A classification of cardiac disturbances opens the work, sorting failures of muscle, valves, and rhythm. Blood pressure chapters treat hypertension, high pressure, and hypotension, its low opposite, as guides to action. Pericarditis, endocarditis, and chronic valve disease each receive handling, drugs included. Digitalis and other heart medicines of the era appear with doses and cautions. Diet, baths, acute heart attacks, and heart disease in children and pregnancy fill later sections. Medical historians read Osborne for a clear window on American heart practice just before cardiology tools arrived.
doe-osti-17014359-power-plant-supply-cha:
Argonne National Laboratory study ANL-26/41, by Tisi Barlock and colleagues, assesses supply chains for key power plant parts and large capital gear. Reliable plant building depends on global chains for materials and specialized making, so the team hunted for bottlenecks that could slow near term projects. Natural gas combined cycle plants anchor the detailed work.

Screening covered eleven plant subsystems for foreign dependence, scarce materials, home capacity, and making difficulty. Six subsystems were picked for closer study, then thirteen parts, with five given deep reviews. Risk sat in a few inputs and stages, such as nickel and chromium alloys, turbine blades and vanes, and large forgings.
doe-osti-17019156-a-heavy-metal-radioact:
Richard Hughes of Lawrence Livermore reports in September 2026 on using heavy metal isotopes as radioactive clocks for dating the early solar system and galaxy. Hafnium 182 and rhenium 187 decay at known rates, so their amounts can mark interstellar time spans. The project sought better data on how fast nature produces these isotopes.

Deuterium bombardment of hafnium 180 at Florida State University tested the setup for later tritium beam work aimed at hafnium 182 output. Alpha bombardment of tungsten 186 at the University of Oslo constrained traits tied to rhenium 187 production. Both analyses were nearing completion, and a planning simulation tool for the tritium runs was also delivered.
doe-osti-2583510-ge-nrel-bilateral-colla:
CRADA final report NREL/TP-5000-94081, dated October 11, 2024, covers the GE and NREL collaboration behind AWAKEN, the American Wake Experiment. Patrick Moriarty was NREL's contact. A wind plant is not a row of independent turbines; each machine's wake steals wind from its neighbors and stirs the air for the whole site. AWAKEN was designed as a field campaign to measure those plant-atmosphere interactions properly.

GE Renewable Energy brought what only a manufacturer has: detailed knowledge of its own turbines and models of their operation. Together the partners modeled the experiment in advance, optimizing which sensors to deploy and where to place them. They defined turbine operating strategies to test, including plant-level control schemes, and the atmospheric conditions worth waiting for. The design work this report covers is the unglamorous prerequisite of good field science: deciding, before the instruments go up, exactly what would make the data decisive.
doe-osti-2587889-success-path-method-int:
Vera Moiseytseva, Debra Fredrick, Hyekyung Kim, Sinem Perk, Bruce Hamilton, and Dave Grabaskas of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this guide, ANL-25/39, in August 2025. It introduces the Success Path Method software tool. Argonne pioneered the method to improve risk management for offshore oil and gas operations, with support in this work from Tulane University.

Most risk methods catalog how things fail. The Success Path Method instead maps the steps required for success, then analyzes where a success path can break. The guide explains the tool, its integration with the OpenPRA web editor, and the contrast between success space and failure space. A worked test case builds a success path diagram, then runs qualification and quantification analyses, including a switch into fault tree form with numerical inputs. A full user manual for the tool is attached as an appendix.
doe-osti-2589739-understanding-climate-a:
City College of New York's final report on award DE-SC0023174, by Naresh Devineni and James Booth, studies rainfall extremes around New York City. Work ran from September 2022 to May 2025 under the Department's Biological and Environmental Research program. Hurricane Ida's flooding showed how fast city rainfall risk can outgrow old design numbers.

The project built a framework that blends historical records with climate model output to price extreme rain risk at specific places. One published study found the risk of extreme hourly rainfall for the city rose after Ida. That paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2024 and landed in the top 5 percent of tracked research attention. City planners and insurers can use the framework to test drainage and building standards against a wetter future.
doe-osti-2999881-biologically-influenced:
Juliet Swanson of Los Alamos National Laboratory updates a study of microbes and actinides in LA-UR-25-30181, issued 14 October 2025. If brine ever moves through the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant, microbes riding that brine could carry radioactive actinides with them. Neodymium stands in safely for actinides in the +3 state. Earlier work tested how three salt-loving organisms from the site grab neodymium in two real brines; this report finishes the set with four more isolates.

The added organisms are two archaea and bacteria named Trans-1b, Salinicoccus, Nesterenkonia and Thalassobacillus in the text's roster. All seven organisms lowered neodymium levels in plain salt water and in ERDA-6 brine, though loss ran slower in the brine. In Generic Weep Brine, earlier tests found little biological effect, traced to competition for the metal. Overall conclusions hold steady, and the results feed updated biocolloid values for the 2026 compliance application.
doe-osti-3008436-search-for-a-cloud-phas:
Final technical report for DOE grant DE-SC0021974, by Dan Lubin of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, searches for a cloud phase feedback in the Arctic climate system. The idea: as air near freezing warms past it, mixed-phase clouds lose their ice, changing how much radiation the surface gains or loses.

Analysis used a much larger North Slope of Alaska sample than planned, including radar products carrying secondary ice production properties. The four known weather regimes re-emerged in the longer record, drifting toward the warmer regimes over time. The headline trend is a significant decrease in net surface radiative flux through July and August between 1999 and 2024, driven by cloud liquid changes rather than the hypothesized phase switch.
doe-osti-3008455-spectro-microscopic-inv:
Single atmospheric particles are examined under the microscope to trace their role in the water cycle in a final report for DOE award DE-SC0021977. Alexander Laskin of Purdue and Ryan Moffet of Sonoma Technology led the work. Samples came from the SAIL campaign in the mountains and the TRACER campaign near Houston.

Computer-controlled electron microscopy with X-ray microanalysis measured each particle's elemental makeup. Synchrotron X-ray microscopy probed mixing state and molecular bonding. Snow samples and bulk aerosol added detail on brown carbon, the light-absorbing organic particles from burning. The team tied particle types and mixing states to field readings taken in real time and to how deposits darken snowpack.
doe-osti-3009560-new-particle-formation-:
Final report for DOE grant DE-SC0021208 covers new particle formation in Houston's air during the TRACER campaign. James Smith of UC Irvine led it, with Don Collins of UC Riverside and Jeffrey Pierce of Colorado State. The field phase ran July 1 to August 31, 2022.

Mass spectrometers tracked gas-phase precursors and nanoparticle composition, and a CAGE chamber measured how fast fresh particles grow. Modelling with an enhanced column model, now including volatile chemical products from consumer goods, showed Houston particle formation is mostly a local urban event. Particles nucleate in and around the city, then grow as the air drifts away in the urban plume. Fixed-site readings can mislead about that moving picture.
doe-osti-3009648-development-of-the-e3sm:
Project final report for DOE award DE-SC0022177, covering September 2021 to August 2025, reports Jefferson Keith Moore's work on the marine biogeochemistry inside the E3SM climate model. The ocean module is MARBL, and the goal is fuller biogeochemistry-climate feedbacks.

The next-generation ecosystem carries eight phytoplankton and four zooplankton groups, each with its own elemental recipe. Nitrogen-to-carbon ratios now vary dynamically, joining phosphorus ratios added earlier, and sinking export fluxes follow the same variable stoichiometry. One planned task, nutrient inputs from glacial processes, was dropped for lack of time and ready ice-sheet coupling. Offline inverse models constrained the key fluxes against observations.
doe-osti-3010066-robust-dark-energy-cons:
Dark energy work with the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument is covered by Lado Samushia of Kansas State in a final report for DOE award DE-SC0021165, spanning September 2020 to August 2025. DESI maps millions of galaxies to measure the expansion history of the universe.

Samushia led the forecasting work for the DESI collaboration: the simulations behind target picks and observing plans, which now feed planning for DESI-II. New analysis methods squeeze the bispectrum and three-point correlation functions, measures beyond the standard pair counts. Small-scale three-point signals tightened estimates of how galaxies occupy dark matter halos. Machine learning methods were built to strip imaging systematics from primordial non-Gaussianity readings.
doe-osti-3011863-control-strategies-and-:
Control strategies for hybrid power plants are set out and validated in a National Renewable Energy Laboratory report by Genevieve Starke, Jonathan Martin, Kaitlin Brunik, and Parangat Bhaskar. The Hybrid Optimization and Performance Platform, HOPP, dispatches combined wind, solar, and storage assets. Modes include meeting a load demand at minimum operating cost and a hydrogen dispatch mode.

Checks compared HOPP output against the HOMER tool at unit scale. Photovoltaic error breakdowns and a 1.5 megawatt wind turbine case supplied the checks. A close match to HOMER led the team to count HOPP's PV model as proven. The report also records how loss factors were tuned for the checks.
doe-osti-3012595-study-of-quadrupole-fri:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-229299-2025-TECH, by F. Willeke, dated December 2025, studies fringe fields in the interaction region of the Hadron Storage Ring of the Electron-Ion Collider. Quadrupole magnets focus the beam, but their fields spill past the magnet ends. Those fringe fields bend particle paths in ways that shift the beam's tune, its oscillation rate around the ring.

Willeke worked through the magnet physics mathematically and computed the tune shift terms for every interaction region quadrupole. He then compared them with the shifts caused by the ring's sextupole magnets. The fringe field shifts were about one order of magnitude smaller than the sextupole shifts, though of a similar scale. His verdict: the effect is not threatening, but it is not negligible either, so designers should keep it in the calculations.
doe-osti-3017513-assessment-of-the-loss-:
Daniel L Flowers, Jacob D Glesmann, and Matthew J McNenly of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this January 2026 assessment of the TEX experiment assembly. TEX works with plates of highly enriched uranium, including the Jemima plate assembly. The question: if the vacuum around the assembly is lost abruptly, how much do local metal temperatures change?

The team attacked the problem four ways, with analytical methods and semi-analytical simulation tools. Their answer: the maximum temperature variation in the assembly stays under ten kelvin in an abrupt loss of vacuum. Under the most realistic conditions, the variation is likely one to four kelvin. A parametric Comsol simulation checked the unsteady response, assuming incoming air at the maximum speed the choked flow restriction allows. Criticality experimenters get a bounded, checked answer to a what-if that safety reviews always ask.
doe-osti-3018639-thermal-analysis-of-the:
Silvia Picchi of the University of Pisa analyzed bus bar heating for Fermilab's PIP-II era in FERMILAB-TM-2882-STUDENT. Victor Grzelak supervised the 2023 summer school work. PIP-II will inject protons at 800 MeV, and the bus bars feeding the magnets must carry the new currents without overheating. Picchi attacked the problem at three levels. Lumped calculations came first, for one bar and then for pairs. 2D COMSOL simulations followed, checked against ampacity tables. 3D COMSOL models closed the study.

The models compared present conditions against PIP-II conditions, for both the existing assembly and a new one. In the tunnel sections, polyethylene beads around the bars act as insulation, and the peak temperature sits there. Magnet engineers get a direct answer: which assembly keeps the bars within limits at the new currents. The staged method, hand calculation to 3D model, is a template for student thermal work.
doe-osti-3020942-photovoltaics-and-energ:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-17369R, issued as IEA-PVPS report T13-40:2026, examines solar power in a place planners usually ignore: the greater Arctic region above 60 degrees north latitude. Few large solar installations exist there now. The authors, working under the International Energy Agency's Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme, argue that the region's geography, climate, and energy needs deserve a closer look.

The Arctic offers cold temperatures that raise panel efficiency and bright snow that reflects extra light onto modules. Against that stand months of winter darkness, low sun angles, and heavy snow loads. Northern Europe's grids reach far north, while North American Arctic communities often depend on isolated microgrids and shipped-in diesel. The report weighs utility-scale plants and village systems separately, and judges photovoltaics a real contributor to Arctic energy security.
doe-osti-3022206-bluecrab-domain-overlap:
INL report INL/RPT-25-87558 documents the theory and verification of domain overlapping coupling in BlueCRAB, the NEAMS multiphysics framework. The authors are Victor Coppo Leite, David Reger, Ramiro Freile, Mauricio Tano, Vasileios Kyriakopoulos, and Lise Charlot. The method lets two codes with overlapping domains, here the SAM systems code and the Pronghorn porous-media code, exchange conditions without sharing a mesh boundary.

Verification cases test whether the coupling conserves energy and transports scalar species faithfully. The numerical scheme adds corrections for inertial and convective effects so net thermal effects survive the handoff. The scalar formulation was checked against an experiment on tracer mixing between two piping loops joined by a double-T junction. Practical findings include placing the branch at the center of the reference plane to represent buoyancy correctly in natural circulation problems.
doe-osti-3022926-remarks-on-the-thesis-o:
Luiz C Leal wrote these remarks as a PhD committee report on the thesis of Aitor Bengoechea Fernández, done at Aix-Marseille Université in doctoral school ED 352 and hosted at CEA Cadarache. The thesis tackles a gap in how neutron scattering in nuclear materials is modeled, where crystal lattice effects meet low-energy resonances. The report is printed in English and French side by side.

Leal sums up the nine chapters and annexes, then judges the work. The thesis extends thermal scattering laws, written S(α,β), with higher-order correlation functions and a phonon expansion method, and it generalizes the nuclear interaction kernel. He credits the checks of the model across several codes and physical regimes, and calls the approach rigorous and creative.
doe-osti-3029612-development-of-high-thr:
Mark A. Kasevich of Stanford University reports final results for award DE-SC0021976, which ran from August 2021 to August 2025. The project, shared with Soichi Wakatsuki of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, built a faster way to image living chemistry. Its tool pairs light-sheet microscopy, which lights one thin slice at a time, with electro-optic fluorescence lifetime imaging. Lifetime data add chemical contrast that plain brightness cannot give.

Early tests showed speed gains near 100,000 times over older lifetime methods, per the report. The team built wide-field, light-sheet, and two-photon versions of the microscope, reaching a light sheet as thin as 4 micrometers. Images include fluorescent beads and a beating zebrafish heart. The goal was three-dimensional views of metabolic paths in plants and microbes, and of plant roots meeting microbes.
doe-osti-3342900-estimating-residual-gas:
Frank Rathmann of Brookhaven National Laboratory models a slow leak of beam quality in technical note BNL-229699-2026-TECH, dated April 2026. Even a good vacuum leaves stray gas in a storage ring, and beam particles that hit gas molecules are lost. The note treats the AGS Booster, a ring of 200 meters around. Magnetic rigidity ramps in a straight line from 1.25 to 9.50 tesla-meters over a 1.00 second cycle.

Three loss routes are tallied: nuclear inelastic hits, single Coulomb scattering, and charge exchange. Cross sections mix standard tables with fitted forms, then get integrated in the team numerical tools. The payoff is practical: a carbon target polarimeter chamber can sit behind an ultra-high vacuum valve, opened only for polarized light-ion runs, so heavy-ion vacuum stays clean.
doe-osti-3365791-innovative-remediation-:
Sandia National Laboratories' 2026 R&D 100 award submission, from Jessica Kruichak-Duhigg's team, presents a mesoporous carbon material that strips PFAS chemicals from water. PFAS, the persistent fluorinated pollutants nicknamed forever chemicals, resist ordinary treatment. Sandia's carbon is modified with aliphatic quaternary amines that grab the PFAS. The loaded sorbent can then thermally degrade what it captured. That closes the loop instead of moving the problem to a landfill.

The submission prices the sorbent at roughly 3 to 5 dollars per kilogram when made from biomass-derived carbon, and the product was introduced between January 2025 and March 2026.
