Support letters from outside researchers describe the scale of PFAS contamination in soils and waters worldwide. As an award entry, the document is part technical brief and part case for impact, organized by the competition's product categories.
doe-osti-3366744-nuclear-balance-of-plan:
Argonne National Laboratory report, dated May 29, 2026, models the balance of plant for several advanced reactor concepts. Anton Moisseytsev and Nicolas Stauff wrote it, with Iza Lantgios and Logan Williams of Idaho National Laboratory. The balance of plant is everything past the reactor itself: turbines, steam lines, and heat exchangers that turn reactor heat into electricity or industrial steam. Vendors quote core performance; owners live with plant performance.

Rankine cycle models were built per concept, starting with a sodium-cooled fast reactor. One experiment bleeds steam off to an external process, representing industrial heat sales, and increases the bleed until feedwater heating can no longer be sustained. Electrical output and cycle efficiency fall as heat sales rise, exactly the trade a cogeneration customer must price. The models give reactor designers plant-level numbers early.
doe-osti-3388175-research-and-developmen:
Research and Development Related to the Commercialization of Perovskite Radiation Detectors, CRADA final report NLR/TP-5K00-100238 from July 2026, closes agreement CRD-22-22690. Five National Laboratory of the Rockies contacts are printed: Kelly Schutt, Joseph Berry, Axel Palmstrom, Marc Migliozzi, and Kylie Thompson. Funding came from the Solar Energy Technologies Office, an office that knows perovskites from solar cells.

Perovskite crystals, the same family chased for cheap solar panels, also stop radiation well, which makes them candidates for detectors. A detector business needs more than a good crystal: repeatable growth, contacts, and readout that survive production. Commercialization research and development is that bridge work, and this report is the agreement's final record, summarizing the laboratory's contribution at the level the partners cleared.
doe-osti-3409075-expanding-scientific-ca:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-230020-2026-TECH, by H. Oh and dated July 2026, asks whether the Electron-Ion Collider could also hunt light dark matter. The idea uses synchrotron beam dumps: beams are thrown away in dumps, and those dumps could birth rare particles. The note comes from the collider team at Brookhaven.

Dump design must handle fierce heat loads. The 10 GeV beam layout holds 320 kilojoules in total. That energy lands within a few microseconds, giving several gigawatts of beam power. Beam spots span only a few millimeters. Any dark matter search must first survive those hard physics facts.
droste-hulshoff-die-judenbuche:
A murder under a beech tree haunts a Westphalian village for decades in Annette von Droste-Huelshoff's Die Judenbuche, given here in German. The Jew's Beech opens with a killing, a vanished suspect, and a tree that becomes a place of dread and memory. Part crime story and part moral reckoning, the novella unfolds slowly and lands hard.

Droste-Huelshoff builds her mystery from village gossip, guilt, and the pressure of an unsolved wrong. The famous ending turns the whole tale over like a stone. Atmospheric and psychologically deep, the book is often called the greatest German novella of the nineteenth century. Its quiet devastation has lost nothing with time. Readers who finish it tend to start it again at once.
english-literature-its-history-and-its-s:
William J. Long wrote English Literature as a school text-book, telling the story of English writing from Beowulf to his own century. Eleven chapters divide the field: Anglo-Saxon, Anglo-Norman, the Age of Chaucer, the Revival of Learning, Elizabeth, the Puritans, the Restoration, the eighteenth century, Romanticism, and the Victorian Age. Each chapter ends with a summary, bibliography, questions, and chronology.

Long opens by asking what literature means, with the shell and the book as his figure. He praises variety in the romantic writers against the polished sameness he finds in Pope. Long, who held a Heidelberg doctorate, wrote from Stamford, Connecticut, for American schools. His textbook sold widely and taught two generations their Chaucer, Spenser, and Tennyson in one steady narrative.
everybody-s-guide-to-money-matters-with-:
William Cotton, a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, wrote Everybody's Guide to Money Matters for cautious British savers who feared the stock exchange. Cotton begins at the beginning: what money is, how to open a bank account, and how to draw a cheque. He then explains deposits, bills of exchange, and the London banks in plain order.

Longer chapters describe investments one by one: government funds and consols, mortgages, railway shares, colonial and foreign stocks, gas, water, mines, and breweries. A stock exchange chapter translates the slang of bulls, bears, contango, and backwardation, and warns against advertising swindles and gold-mine traps. Tables of interest close the book. It is Victorian personal finance, careful to the last coupon.
faust-a-tragedy-part-1-translated-from-t:
Goethe's Faust, Part 1 appears here in Charles T. Brooks's verse translation. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe wrote the tragedy in German. This seventh edition was printed in Boston in 1868. Brooks entered his translation for copyright in 1856.

In his preface Brooks apologizes for adding one more Faust to many. Prose and metrical versions already numbered twenty or thirty, he notes. None, he claims, had tried the original's exact, ever-changing metre. Lesser versions neglect the planned mix of male and female rhymes. Those rhymes fall on the last syllable or the one before it. A careful student can see Goethe's order in that pattern, Brooks argues. His version aims to carry that music into English.
govdocs-archive_org-lifschultz-1979-bang:
Lawrence Lifschultz, a correspondent for the Far Eastern Economic Review, wrote Bangladesh: The Unfinished Revolution in 1979. His subject is the new country of Bangladesh, born in the 1971 war with Pakistan and already in turmoil within a few years of independence.

Lifschultz reports on the politics of the young state, the assassination of its founding leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, and the coups that followed. He argues that the revolution promised at independence was left unfinished, its hopes captured by soldiers and elites. The book is on-the-ground history of a country's hardest decade, by a reporter who was there.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AssassinationJF:
On November 20, 1988, the Los Angeles Herald Examiner ran Associated Press writer Mike Cochran's look back at Dallas, twenty-five years after the Kennedy assassination. Its headline reported that the Kennedy mystique and conspiracy theories thrive, a quarter century later.

Cochran surveys why the case would not close: the books, the researchers, and the public's lasting refusal to accept the lone-gunman account. Anniversary journalism like this measures a country's memory at a fixed date. The piece records both the evidence as it stood in 1988 and the mood of a nation still arguing with 1963.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CouncilorThe_Co: Nsia-CouncilorThe Councilor The: the made public government document, captured as titled, subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued, an obscure item, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CubaProjectThe_: Book publishing announcements survive here only as a fragment, and the publication they came from is not identified. Among the titles announced is one about an alleged conspiracy joining the Mafia, the CIA, and Cuban exile groups to assassinate Fidel Castro. The fragment preserves that announcement without the surrounding pages, so the book's author, publisher, and date cannot be confirmed from this record alone.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DefenderThe_Def: One issue of The Defender, volume 18, number 5, dated September 1943, was edited by Gerald B. Winrod. Winrod, a Kansas evangelist, used the magazine to spread his religious and political views during the Second World War. The surviving record identifies the issue and its editor but does not list its articles, so the number stands here as a dated wartime issue of his publication.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ProgressiveThe_: A writer sent this letter on December 24, 1986, to Erwin Knoll, the editor of The Progressive magazine. The writer describes himself as handicapped. He writes about representing himself in a matter where he had previously had ACLU counsel. His name cannot be recovered from the text. The letter belongs to the mail a political magazine receives from readers in legal trouble, part grievance and part request for a hearing in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SawyerJHerbertI:
Harold Weisberg wrote this critical analysis of Dallas Police Inspector J. Herbert Sawyer's Warren Commission deposition. The deposition was taken by David Belin and appears at 6H315-25 in the hearings. Weisberg argues that the questioning was incompetent. He argues further that the missing answers show collusion between the Commission's staff and the police.

Sawyer was the inspector who broadcast the suspect description on police radio, a hinge point of the afternoon. His deposition should have been handled with care, in Weisberg's view, and was not. The analysis works the transcript line by line. It preserves one critic's method at its most exact: the official record, read against itself, with the lawyer's questions treated as evidence too.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ScallyChristoph: Note to Mr Weisberg (Fragment): the fragment of a handwritten note to Weisberg, dated 1964, illegible beyond the salutation. A scrap, kept. A single fragment, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-wargovUFO_DOW_UAP_D_:
Research Triangle Institute delivered a final report to the Department of the Air Force in September 1996. Its subject is narrow and technical: modeling unlikely space-booster failures in risk calculations for launch operations.

Launch risk studies must price disasters that almost never happen, because a single booster failure over a populated area can be catastrophic for people on the ground. The report works out how to fold those rare events into honest numbers instead of ignoring them. It is a United States government document, and the full text shows the mathematics and the assumptions behind official launch safety figures.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_china-nu:
Would China help Pakistan build a nuclear bomb? That was one of several sharp questions American intelligence officers asked in the 1960s. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 549, published in May 2016. It collects recently declassified reports from the State Department's intelligence bureau, known as INR.

The reports, written between 1959 and 1967, also asked whether Sweden would go nuclear. They weighed whether West Germany wanted to wreck the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty. Read together, they show how early and how widely officials feared the bomb would spread beyond the first nuclear powers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_climate-: Spying on Climate: Inside the Intelligence Community's Environmental Programs - the the Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records. Well documented and clear.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Osc:
James Donovan negotiated the release of captured pilot Francis Gary Powers, a story told in the film Bridge of Spies. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, posted in February 2016, as a kind of sequel. White House and CIA records show Donovan then did something fewer people know about.

With covert CIA support, Donovan conducted the first secret negotiations ever held with Fidel Castro. The talks grew out of his work freeing prisoners after the Bay of Pigs. The posting uses the Oscar-nominated movie as a doorway into real records, and the real sequel turns out to be diplomacy, not espionage alone.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuban-mi:
American Jupiter missiles based in Turkey sat at the hidden center of the Cuban Missile Crisis settlement. This briefing book covers their role in the endgame, sixty years on. Turkey's defense minister warned that removing the Jupiters would hurt confidence in the United States.

He also predicted a depression in morale if the missiles came out. Henry Kissinger later noted that almost everyone in Italy's leadership believed a secret United States-Soviet agreement covered the Jupiters. The records show allies worrying in private about a bargain they were not meant to know existed, one that traded their missiles for peace.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Rum:
Nate Jones edited this briefing book, number 615, published in January 2018, on Donald Rumsfeld's snowflake memos. A freedom of information lawsuit by the Archive won monthly releases of the memos. Law firm Skadden Arps represented the Archive for free in that case.

One memo records a striking judgment. On September 10, 2001, the day before the attacks, Rumsfeld named the Pentagon bureaucracy itself as the biggest threat. The snowflakes as a whole give a secretary of defense thinking on paper: orders, complaints, and questions fired off in short bursts across his years running two wars.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_henry-ki:
Henry Kissinger's telephone calls were transcribed by his staff, creating a record called the telcons. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in February 2024, on the legal fight over those transcripts. State Department lawyers had advised Kissinger that the telcons were his personal papers.

Because they were personal, the lawyers said, the transcripts were not subject to disclosure under freedom of information law. That advice kept a verbatim record of American diplomacy out of public reach for years. The posting tells the story behind the story: how the classification of a phone log decided what history could be known.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
John Prados, Wendy Valdes, and Tom Blanton edited this briefing book, number 626, published in May 2018. It concerns the CIA's black sites program, the secret overseas prisons where detainees were tortured. Its occasion was the Senate confirmation fight over Gina Haspel as CIA director.

The posting asks one sharp question: will the hearings fill in the redacted blanks in the record? Much of the black sites story was still blacked out in released documents. Confirmation hearings offered a rare chance to force answers on the record. The set preserves what was known, and what was hidden, at that decision point.

In 1969 the State Department finished a top secret study of the Vietnam War while the war was still being fought. Tom Blanton edited this briefing book, posted in December 2020, which updates a 2004 electronic book on that study. The study remains landmark but little known.

An official history written mid-war, by the department running diplomacy, is a rare artifact. It can show what analysts understood about the war's course before the outcome was settled. The posting's second part returns attention to a document that historians of intelligence regard as unusually honest for its time and place.

Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book on American covert action in Chile and the Senate investigation that exposed it. The Church Committee's report on Chile became one of the defining documents of 1970s oversight. Fifty years on, the posting asks what those revelations still mean.

Evidence here is limited to the editor and subject. Even so, the focus is clear: the Chile case taught Congress and the public how far covert action had gone, and Kornbluh is the Archive's leading Chile specialist. The set belongs with the Church Committee anniversary records on assassination plots and agency reform.

America's Bicentennial in 1976 gave the CIA and the Ford administration a patriotic stage. Arturo Jimenez-Bacardi edited this briefing book, number 925, published in July 2026. It argues that officials used the celebration to justify covert intelligence operations.

The other actor in the story is the Church Committee, which was then investigating intelligence abuses. Defending covert action as part of the nation's founding story was a public relations move in that fight. The posting shows patriotic symbolism being put to bureaucratic work, and it preserves the documents of that campaign fifty years after the fact.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran-nuc: Republics of Myth: National Narratives and the US-Iran Conflict - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
President Richard Nixon cultivated a madman image, hoping Hanoi would believe he might do anything, including using nuclear weapons, to end the Vietnam War. This Archive posting pairs that strategy with its domestic counterpart: the mass antiwar movement. It features declassified documents and a PBS documentary.

The pairing is the insight. The madman performance was aimed partly at the enemy and partly shaped by protest at home, which limited Nixon's real options. Documents let readers see the threats drafted in secret while marches filled American streets. Few postings join a war strategy and the movement against it in one file.

NATO was founded to contain the Soviet Union, but early documents show a second purpose: containing Germany too. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 652, published in December 2018. French officials told Washington that West Germany could join NATO only with no independent Wehrmacht.

State Department intelligence described the alliance as a place where West Germany could satisfy reasonable aspirations. The same structure would contain any unreasonable ones. That double design explains much about NATO's odd shape, an alliance that armed a recent enemy inside itself. The documents let readers see the founders state the German purpose plainly, in private, at the creation.

The nuclear football is the briefcase that shadows the president, holding the tools to order a nuclear strike. William Burr edited this briefing book on presidential control of nuclear weapons, first posted in July 2018 and later updated. The update adds discussions between Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin about the football.

Two former rivals talking about each other's launch briefcases is a rare window into how the system looked from the top. Control of the arsenal is at once a legal chain, a physical object, and a personal burden. The documents show presidents and their staffs treating all three aspects with a seriousness that public debate rarely matches.

William Burr edited this briefing book, number 849, published in December 2023, as a scorecard of recent nuclear releases. He sorts them into the good, the bad, and the ugly. The good includes new documents on the Cuban Missile Crisis, Kennedy and Germany, South Korea, and Taiwan.

The bad and ugly are Defense Department denials. Requests on Dimona in 1963 and on American aid to British submarine missiles were refused. The Strategic Air Command censored a film on airborne command posts. A mixed scorecard like this teaches researchers where the walls still stand, which is nearly as useful as the documents that come through them.

Strategic Stability and Instability during the Middle Years of the Cold War: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers.

From the late 1960s until the late 1980s, Taiwan pursued a nuclear weapon while depending on American protection. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in January 2019, on that twenty-year quest. It publishes declassified records of the program and of Washington's knowledge of it.

Evidence here is brief beyond the dates and editor, so the shape is what can be told. An ally building a bomb in secret puts its protector in an impossible spot, and the United States eventually forced the program shut. The record belongs beside the South Korean case: two partners, two hidden programs, and one superpower determined that its allies would not go nuclear.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Nikita Khrushchev's meetings with Fidel and Raúl Castro, before the missile crisis, are the subject of this Archive posting. It draws on a newly available transcript of the Soviet leader getting to know the Cubans. Raúl Castro, the posting notes, wanted detailed Soviet security assurances for the island.

That transcript helps explain Khrushchev's 1962 determination that defending Cuba required drastic steps. He concluded that only a massive Soviet military base, with nuclear weapons on the island, would do. Reading the earlier conversations shows the commitment forming in person, between leaders, rather than appearing suddenly as a gamble. The Cuban side of the crisis story gains a documentary voice here.

Llewellyn Thompson, known throughout Washington as Tommy, served twice as American ambassador to the Soviet Union and became the State Department's most trusted reader of the Kremlin. A National Security Archive briefing book page honors him under the label his colleagues used: the Kremlinologist. Thompson advised presidents from Eisenhower through Johnson, and his cables from Moscow shaped American policy at the Cold War's tensest moments. Only the page capture is preserved in this entry's evidence, marking the Archive's tribute to a diplomat whose judgment steadied more than one crisis.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern: Declassification can be used as diplomacy: a government hands another country the secret files that document its past crimes. Under the heading of lessons learned, a National Security Archive briefing book page collects reflections on the Argentina Declassification Project. That was the American effort to open intelligence records on Argentina's dictatorship. The records were meant for the victims' families and courts. Only the page capture survives in this entry's evidence, so it stands as a signpost to the Archive's case study of releases used as foreign policy.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_National_Sec:
Tom Blanton directed the National Security Archive for decades, and in October 2024 he sat for Peter Bergen's podcast In the Room. The Archive's posting announces the episode, in which Blanton looks back on forty years of work, in his phrase, to dislodge and declassify United States government secrets.

Bergen, a CNN national security analyst, built the show around long conversations with people who were present for major events. Blanton's presence was of a different kind: not in the room where decisions happened, but in the archives afterward, forcing the records of those rooms into daylight. The posting will interest readers who want the short version of how the Archive works and why its director believes secrecy, more than any single scandal, is the standing problem.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_mexico-ayotzinapa: The Ayotzinapa case, the 2014 disappearance of forty-three Mexican students after a police attack in Iguala, turned on what Mexico's military knew and when it knew it. A National Security Archive briefing book page reports that Mexican military archives have produced revelations in the case. Sealed files on the army's role that night began to open. Only the page capture is preserved in this entry's evidence. Its subject is the evidentiary heart of Mexico's most painful open case: the soldiers' records, read against the official story.
grisly-grisell-or-the-laidly-lady-of-whi:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Grisly Grisell, or The Laidly Lady of Whitburn, is a tale of the Wars of the Roses. Yonge prefixes Chaucer's lines on women steadfast in humility, setting the tone for a heroine whose patience is tried by war and family fortune.

Contents open with an explosion, a broken match, the mirror, parting, Sister Avice, the proctor, and the pilgrim of Salisbury. Old playfellows, the king-maker, a cold welcome and Bernard carry Grisell through the Yorkist and Lancastrian struggle. Readers who enjoy Yonge's historical tales for young people will find Grisell brave, patient and very much of her troubled age.
happy-little-edward-and-his-pleasant-rid:
Happy Little Edward, printed in 1850, is a small tale for young children. Edward Jones is about four years old, a good and therefore happy little boy, who lives in a beautiful city in Connecticut with his parents, brothers and sisters, and a dear aunt. His mother has a sister in Massachusetts, the wife of a farmer. One beautiful spring morning his parents resolve to pay her a visit and take Edward with them.

The ride to the country and the rambles there fill the little book: farm sights, animals, and the wonders of a world beyond the city streets. Verses scattered through the prose call little children to wake and take a peep at the country. The moral is gentle and constant, that goodness and happiness go together. Such books were the first reading of many children of 1850, and this is a sweet, plain survivor.
history-and-ecclesiastical-relations-of-:
John Van Nest Talmage, a Reformed Dutch missionary, wrote this account, printed at New York in 1863. Its subject is the churches of presbyterial order at Amoy, in China. Talmage addresses the ministers, elders, and members of his home church. He says the order of churches raised on mission fields is a grave, unsettled question.

Talmage argues that missionaries are evangelists, not pastors, by office. Their tie to the church that sent them should match that office, he holds. He weighs practice in India and other fields as he goes. Church readers get a working missionary's plea for clear, honest order abroad.
history-of-egypt-chaldea-syria-babylonia:
L W King and H R Hall, both of the British Museum, wrote this history in the light of recent discovery. It was copyrighted in 1906. Both men worked in the lands they describe. Most of the photographs in the book are their own.

The volume retells Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia, and Kurdistan through fresh finds. A mace-head in the Museum records a governor's conquest of Elam. Such objects are made to speak for whole reigns. Plates borrowed from De Morgan's works add French dig results. Readers of the time got ancient history rewritten by the spade, year by year.
home-scenes-and-home-influence-a-series-:
T. S. Arthur's Home Scenes and Home Influence, issued in Philadelphia in 1854, is the fifth volume of Arthur's Library for the Household. His preface stresses the mother's influence with her children. A few tales treat the marriage relation, and a few give other domestic pictures. Home, he argues, is the centre of good and bad influence alike.

Taking Comfort opens with a young husband who goes in for comforts on a small income. Losing One's Temper and Trouble with Servants supply the friction. The Mother and Boy, A Mother's Influence, and The Power of Patience state the book's creed. Other sketches ask Is She a Lady and follow an old man's recollections. Arthur writes household fiction as moral housekeeping, scene by scene.
in-the-yule-log-glow-book-ii-christmas-t:
Harrison S. Morris edited Book II of In the Yule-Log Glow, issued at Philadelphia in 1900. Contents list Christmas with the Baron by Angelo J. Lewis and A Christmas Miracle by Morris. Daudet's Salvette and Bernadou comes in Morris's rendering from the French. Juliana Horatia Ewing gives The Peace Egg and Melchior's Dream.

Agnes Repplier tells a story of Nuremberg, and Vernon Lee treats a Nativity picture by Fra Filippo Lippi. Playful chapters show children locking each other in rooms for frivolous complaints and sentry duty. Book II mixes tale, art, and mumming for the season.
la-grande-breteche:
Honoré de Balzac's short tale La Grande Bretèche is read here in English. Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell translated it. The story is framed as one told late at night among friends.

A doctor warns that he keeps appalling stories in his collection. The hostess urges him to tell one, since the hour fits. Talk of champagne and earlier tales sets the mood. Balzac then unfolds a dark story tied to a great house, told with his usual sharp eye for motive. The frame shows Balzac's love of stories told after midnight. Suspense builds before the buried secret of the house emerges.
manual-of-gardening-second-edition-a-pra:
The Manual of Gardening, by L. H. Bailey, guides the making of home grounds. This second edition dates from 1910. Bailey treats flowers, fruits, and vegetables grown for home use. His first chapter asks what a garden truly is.

The plan of the place comes next, as a picture in the landscape. Planting is part of the design, not an afterthought. Bailey weighs lawn flower-beds against honest flower borders. Birds, cats, lawns, and odd trees all find their place. He values foliage and form as much as bloom. Bailey was America's great teacher of horticulture. His manual still shapes how home gardens are planned.
moorish-literature-comprising-romantic-b:
René Basset, of the University of France and director of the Académie d'Alger, introduces this anthology of 1901. Its subtitle promises romantic ballads, tales of the Berbers, and stories of the Kabyles. Folklore and national traditions fill out the volume. The works are translated into English for the first time.

Basset's introduction maps the word Moor across North Africa. The region runs from Egypt's frontier to the Atlantic, and south to the Niger. Berbers, Arabs who brought Islam in the eighth century, and Spanish Muslims share the name. Keeping those peoples distinct, he argues, gives the divisions needed to study their literatures.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner follows the Delaware River in this third volume. The Phantom Dragoon opens it on Iron Hill near Newark. British tents crowded that hill as Howe advanced to Brandywine. A white-robed rider charged one lone American picket.

The sentry begged never to hold that post again. Other tales tell of Valley Forge and the last shot at Germantown. A blacksmith at Brandywine and Marion share the list. Lenni Lenape lore stands beside Revolutionary ghosts. Skinner blends settler and Native tales into one mid-Atlantic treasury, eerie and charming by turns.
narrative-of-a-journey-to-the-shores-of-:
John Franklin tells of his first Arctic land journey in this volume. The title dates the trek to 1819 through 1822. His party crossed the Canadian north toward the Polar Sea. This text keeps old spellings like Saskatchawan and Winipeg.

Transcribers note that the third edition added many small errors. Names with Mc were fixed by hand through the file. Franklin's men mapped rivers and coasts in brutal cold. Hunger and hard travel marked the road to the sea. The narrative is a founding record of Arctic exploration, valued for its plain detail on lands then unknown to Europeans.
narrative-of-captivity-in-abyssinia-with:
Dr. Henry Blanc, a Bombay Army surgeon, tells of captivity in Abyssinia. Emperor Theodore held European envoys and missionaries in chains. The contents trace Theodore's rise, conquests, army, and rule. His looks, household, and private life get close study too.

Later chapters tell how Consul Cameron was seized and chained. Hormuzd Rassam was sent to free the captives, with Blanc beside him. Their road ran from Massowah through Kassala toward Gondar. Delays and hard talks with Theodore fill the middle. Blanc writes as doctor, envoy, and prisoner, in a rare inside view of a proud, falling empire.
nasa-tm-19640009696-inferences-of-strato:
G. Warnecke and W. Nordberg of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper in January 1964. It infers how air moves high above Earth from rocket tests. The layers studied are the stratosphere and the mesosphere. Weather balloons cannot reach those heights, so rockets must probe them.

The abstract points to rocket grenade tests at Wallops Island. In such tests, grenades burst at set heights during the fall. Their sound waves reveal wind and temperature on the way down. From those traces the authors sketch broad circulation systems. The work gave early maps of winds tens of miles up, where few direct measures existed.
nasa-tm-19640018157-geomagnetic-control-:
S. Chandra and R. A. Goldberg of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper. It was set to appear in the Journal of Geophysical Research in August 1964. Their subject is how Earth's magnetic field steers gas spread high up. That spread is called diffusion in the upper atmosphere.

The abstract treats papers that try to explain the geomagnetic anomaly. It says match with measured data has come from motion equations for electrons and ions. A boundary condition taken from observation helps that match. The work links the field's shape to how charged gas thins and drifts. Such links matter for radio, satellites, and the air glow itself.
nasa-tm-19650020212-the-reflection-of-so:
J H Underwood, of the University of Leicester in England, measured how well soft X-rays reflect from polished glass and steel in May 1965. At very shallow angles, even soft X-rays can bounce off a smooth surface. His tests used a vacuum reflectometer fitted with a mica crystal device. The test surfaces were polished flats, one of Pyrex glass and one of stainless steel.

Reflection data decide whether X-ray telescopes can use such materials. A poor surface scatters the rays and blurs the image. Underwood reports the reflection efficiency he measured for both materials. That kind of bench data guides the design of instruments meant to focus the faintest rays from space.
nasa-tm-19660001141-neutral-hydrogen-in-: Neutral hydrogen in Earth's atmosphere above one hundred twenty kilometers is the stated subject of this NASA report. The catalog note says the work covered the spread of that hydrogen, and its relative and absolute amounts, in the zone between the lower thermosphere and the exosphere. The hosted sample preserves no readable body text beyond the title, so no author, center, date, or findings can be grounded from it.
nasa-tm-19660006070-n2-temperature-and-d:
N W Spencer of Goddard and the University of Michigan, with G R Carignan and D G Taeusch of Michigan, report measures of molecular nitrogen high above Earth. Their data cover heights from one hundred fifty to three hundred kilometers. Both the density of the gas and its temperature are given. The readings came from a thermosphere probe, the catalog note says.

The thermosphere is where satellites first feel air drag. Nitrogen density there decides how fast an orbit decays. Temperature shapes the whole structure of that region. The authors also draw out what their data imply. Such profiles became basic input for the first standard models of the upper atmosphere.
nasa-tm-19660012886-the-possibility-of-r:
Small red spots had been reported near the Aristarchus crater and a few other places on the Moon, and this paper asks whether they might give off radio noise. The spots are well attested but hard to explain, the author begins. A spectrogram by Kozyrev is the key evidence. It showed lines of molecular hydrogen at the spot near Aristarchus, which points toward water breaking apart in vacuum.

Exciting that gas with sunlight seems very hard to arrange, the author argues. Yet the red glow sits against the bright lunar disk. Static electric discharges and radio noise from craters frame the catalog note. The paper weighs a strange observation with care, keeping open a question that later missions would revisit.
nasa-tm-19660014447-measurements-of-ante:
R G Stone, J K Alexander, and R R Weber measured the impedance of a short antenna inside the ionosphere, in this March 1966 paper. Part two covers observing frequencies above the electron gyro frequency, a natural rate set by Earth's magnetic field. Impedance is how strongly an antenna resists the current driven through it. In a plasma, that value changes with the local conditions.

Measuring it turns an antenna into a probe of the ionosphere itself. The work was sent to a planetary and space sciences journal. Radio astronomy from satellites depended on such knowledge. An antenna that behaves as modeled gives cleaner data, whether its job is listening to Jupiter or sounding the charged air around Earth.
nasa-tm-19660015356-monochromatic-pictur:
Kerstin Fredga, a research associate from Stockholm working at Goddard, took pictures of the Sun in a single color of ultraviolet light in February 1966. The color is the magnesium line at a stated wavelength in the solar ultraviolet spectrum. Pictures in one narrow line show the Sun's face as that one gas layer sees it. The catalog note calls them filter heliograms, taken from an Aerobee-Hi rocket.

Above the air, the rocket camera could catch light that never reaches ground telescopes. Fredga prepared the note as a letter to an astrophysics journal. Such images reveal patterns in the Sun's outer layers that white-light pictures hide. They helped build the case for permanent solar observatories in space.
nasa-tm-19660021064-spectral-degradation:
E H Johnson and T E McGunigal evaluated how much a frequency synthesizer's clean signal degrades in practice, in this Goddard report. A synthesizer builds exact radio frequencies from a single standard. Ground stations and spacecraft radios depend on that exactness. Degradation means the output carries unwanted extra tones and noise, which can foul a clean channel.

Their evaluation aimed to state the amount of degradation a user should expect. A system planned around ideal figures alone would fail in service. Measured limits let engineers set honest margins for Apollo-era communication gear. The report belongs to the test work that kept the growing tracking network speaking clearly to spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19670008915-whole-rock-rubidium-:
Michael L. Bottino and Paul D. Fullagar, both linked with Old Dominion College in Virginia and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this geology paper. It uses whole-rock rubidium-strontium dating to pin down the age of the Silurian-Devonian boundary in northeastern North America. That boundary marks a major turning point in the history of life on land.

The authors dated volcanic rocks from the Eastport Formation near Eastport, Maine, and the Hedgehog Formation near Presque Isle, Maine. Whole rocks, they explain, lose less radiogenic strontium than single minerals, so a whole-rock age records when the rock solidified. The volcanic layers sit interleaved with fossil-bearing sediments, which ties their ages tightly to the fossil record. Separate sections treat each formation, and an appendix lists the sample localities.
nasa-tm-19680003902-the-plasmapause-and-:
H. G. Mayr, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in November 1967. It connects two features of near-Earth space. One is the plasmapause, the sharp outer edge of the plasmasphere's cold plasma. The other is the ion makeup of the topside ionosphere. That changing mix is the central question.

At high latitudes, the level where oxygen ions give way to hydrogen ions sits high, and the plasmapause shows a flat density plateau. Mayr argues both features share one cause: protons streaming upward and escaping along open field lines. That escape thins the hydrogen ion density and drives diffusion across field lines, building the plateau where open and closed regions meet. Ordinary collision-driven diffusion would sharpen the boundary to a few meters, which observations rule out. A turbulent diffusion coefficient instead describes the plasmapause well.
nasa-tm-19680010139-lubrication-and-bear:
Edmond E. Bisson, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a friction conference in Paris, France, in December 1966. He spoke in French at the meeting. His subject is lubrication and bearing problems in the vacuum of space. There, ordinary oils evaporate quickly. Clean metal surfaces, starved of oxygen, can seize or weld together.

Bisson lists the peculiarities of the space environment that drive the problems. They include very low pressure, radiation, and no gravity. Atomic species unlike Earthly molecules also play a part. Mechanisms such as horizon seekers, star finders, and radar antennas must usually work exposed to that vacuum. Sealing them hermetically avoids the exposure but adds considerable complexity and weight. The catalog record describes the paper as covering experiments and engineering measures, the practical countermeasures developed for bearings that must live in space.
nasa-tm-19680010283-experimental-stabili:
Robert E. Cunningham, David P. Fleming, and William J. Anderson, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a gas lubrication symposium in Las Vegas, Nevada, in June 1968. It reports experimental stability studies of the herringbone-grooved gas lubricated journal bearing. Spiral grooves pump gas under a spinning shaft so it floats on a gas film, with no oil and no contact.

Gas bearings suit closed-loop Brayton cycle turbomachinery, where the working gas doubles as lubricant and must stay clean for thousands of hours. Their weakness is a self-excited whirling instability, in which the shaft orbits the bearing center at about half its rotation speed. Predicting that whirl's onset from theory is unreliable, because the governing flow equation demands simplifying assumptions. The Lewis experiments therefore measured stability directly, with herringbone groove geometry as the variable under study.
nasa-tm-19690027306-photoelectron-flux-a:
B. C. Narasinga Rao and E. J. R. Maier, of Goddard Space Flight Center's Laboratory for Space Sciences, wrote this preprint, X-615-69-301. They study how photoelectrons stream and heat the protonosphere at conjugate sunrise, using selected Explorer 31 data. Sunrise at one foot of a magnetic field line frees electrons there. Some stream along the line to the far, still-dark end and warm it.

On low latitude passes high above Earth, night-side electron temperature climbed steeply at conjugate sunrise, they report. Ion temperature rose with it, and the flow of energetic electrons jumped several times over. A notable return flow ran back toward the sunlit side as well. Theory for the electrons' energy loss along the line is compared against the readings.
nasa-tm-19700021850-the-potential-temper:
George H. Fichtl and Julian F. Nelson of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on April 27, 1970. It gives the potential temperature profile in the planetary boundary layer. That layer is the lowest part of the air, where the ground shapes wind and the flow of heat.

The pair analyze nineteen temperature profiles gathered at NASA's tall meteorological tower. Readings came from six heights in the lowest stretch of air, and each test ran from about fifteen minutes to an hour. They test the idea that the temperature gradient, written in dimensionless form, depends on a few surface quantities. Stability length, surface friction values, and Earth's spin all enter that test.
nasa-tm-19700023361-electric-field-hyste:
Louis Melamed and David Rubin of the Electronics Research Center wrote this report on liquid crystals. It studies how an electric field leaves a lasting mark on the crystals. After the field acts, the way the material passes light changes and stays changed.

Certain liquid crystals at room temperature show this memory effect, the authors state. The change in light transmission slowly decays once the field is gone. In many cases it lasts at least several days, they found. A material that remembers a past signal could store information. That promise is what makes this odd behavior of the crystals worth close study.
nasa-tm-19700026399-estimation-of-percen:
F. M. Speed and A. H. Feiveson of the Theory and Analysis Office prepared this statistics paper for NASA. It treats the estimation of percentage points and the building of tolerance limits. Such limits state the range a measured value can be trusted to fall in, a key question in reliability studies.

The authors open with a common error: assuming data follow a normal distribution when they do not. That mistake, they warn, can make tolerance limits worthless and even lead to dangerous conclusions. Their first section shows false results drawn from the wrong assumption. Four theorems then let a researcher work when the true distribution is not normal, or is unknown altogether.
nasa-tm-19710022673-imp-5-magnetic-field:
D. H. Fairfield and N. F. Ness of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this report in July 1971, numbered X-692-71-295. It presents magnetic field measurements from the IMP 5 satellite in the high-latitude outer magnetosphere. The satellite crossed the region near the noon meridian, the sunward side of Earth's magnetic bubble.

The measurements reveal a broad region of weakened field, centered on the polar or dayside cusp, that is always present. Field strengths there run far below what a simple dipole field would give. The boundary toward the magnetosheath showed strong fluctuations and no clear magnetopause. The authors note perturbations pointing roughly across the average field, suggesting currents flowing along field lines, with sizes matching low-altitude polar spacecraft data.
nasa-tm-19710029282-aerodynamic-heating-:
Theodore R Creel Jr and Robert Miserentino of the Langley Research Center measured heating on inflatable decelerators at Mach 8. An attached inflatable decelerator is a balloon like brake that slows a craft during entry. Four shapes were tested in the Langley Mach 8 variable density tunnel. A meltable coating that turns clear at a known heat revealed the heating pattern.

Heating on the air inlets and the burble fence ran up to five times the smooth body level. Moving the inlets toward the rear cut heating just behind them. That same move raised heating on the burble fence. Faster flow raised heating mainly on the fence as well. Designers needed such maps to protect the fabric brake.
origin-of-the-anglo-boer-war-revealed-th:
C. H. Thomas wrote Origin of the Anglo-Boer War Revealed to blame the war of 1899 on a conspiracy. He describes himself as a Belfast man of the Transvaal. He had also been an Orange Free State burgher. In the notice opening this second edition of 1900, he explains the book's delay. It was meant to appear in South Africa before the end of 1899. Passports and permits blocked him there, so he sailed for London to publish.

His argument acquits ordinary Boers as dupes and victims. It aims instead at instigators he calls a Dutch coterie in Holland. They sacrificed South Africa's peace for advantage, he charges. Along the way he promises practical information about the Boers and South Africa. Emigrants and the uninformed are his named audience. The book is a partisan wartime pamphlet in full dress.
personal-reminiscences-of-early-days-in-:
Stephen J. Field dictated his Personal Reminiscences of Early Days in California to a stenographer at San Francisco in the summer of 1877. A prefatory note says the sketches were printed for a few friends, not published. Field, by then a United States Supreme Court justice, tells how and why he came to California and of his first experiences in San Francisco.

The index promises his election as first alcalde of Marysville and his work on the bench. George C. Gorham adds the story of Field's attempted assassination by a former associate on the state supreme bench. The volume is gold-rush law told by a man who made it.
personal-sketches-and-tributes-part-2-fr:
Part 2 of Whittier's Personal Sketches and Tributes, from volume 6 of his works, opens with The Funeral of Torrey. Charles T. Torrey, a young Congregational clergyman, died in a Maryland prison in 1846 for aiding slaves to escape. Whittier recalls seeing him seven years before, his young wife on his arm, and bends over his Boston coffin with bitter indignation.

The contents add sketches of Edward Everett, Lewis Tappan, Channing, Lydia Maria Child, Holmes, and Longfellow, with the death of President Garfield. These are an abolitionist poet's memorials of the people and causes that filled his public life.
podcast-dannyjones-6ktulVa8XHE:
Barrett Brown is a journalist who was imprisoned over his work with the hacker collective Anonymous, and he joins Danny Jones as an ex-insider warning about the future of cyber warfare. Brown discusses how states, corporations, and freelance hackers now blend into one battlespace.

His authority comes from proximity: he chronicled private intelligence firms and paid for it with a prison term. Jones asks what comes next, mass surveillance, infrastructure attacks, information operations, and Brown answers from experience of both the underground and the prosecution that followed him out of it. The episode will interest listeners who want the hacker wars explained by a participant rather than a vendor. Brown's politics color everything he says, and the recording keeps that color visible.
podcast-dannyjones-USxH2S0mrhE:
Under the shortest title in this series, Was God an Astronaut?, Danny Jones hosts a conversation on the ancient astronaut thesis itself. The claim, popular since the 1960s, is simple to state. The gods of old religions were visitors from the sky. Ancient people, in this reading, recorded their technology as miracle.

Without a single named guest in its billing, the episode works as a survey of the whole framework. It covers the texts, carvings, and flight stories its believers cite. It also covers the answers its critics give. Jones guides the tour through the theory's greatest hits and its weakest joints. The thesis remains outside every relevant field's consensus, and the recording presents the case as its advocates make it. For listeners, it is a compact primer on an idea that shaped this entire archive's imagination, stated plainly enough to judge whole.
podcast-tuckercarlson-GoD8yx0xbhE:
Pastor Billy Cerveny joins Tucker Carlson to discuss spiritual attack as a daily reality. The subjects include Satan's assaults and the fight over transgender ideology. They also include Cerveny's own experiences of seeing the supernatural and hearing God's voice. The conversation treats the unseen world as the main arena of modern life.

Cerveny speaks as a pastor to addicts and strugglers, and his stories come from that work as much as from theology. Carlson shares the premise that material explanations miss the real action. Listeners outside the faith will hear a worldview stated whole; listeners inside it will hear their own convictions given a national platform. The episode preserves a strand of American Christianity that reads politics as spiritual war, explained by one of its pastors in plain, personal terms.
psyche:
Molière's tragedy-ballet on the love of Cupid and Psyche appears here in English prose translated by Charles Heron Wall, with short notes. Molière sketched the plan and wrote the prologue and early acts before the king asked for speed.

Pierre Corneille, then sixty years old, finished the remaining scenes in a fortnight, and Quinault wrote the songs. Jupiter, Venus, Love, and Zephyr head the cast, with Psyche loved by two princes and served by the Graces. Molière himself played Zephyr. Readers get a court spectacle of gods, envy, and love tested by trials.
scaramouche: Rafael Sabatini wrote Scaramouche, headed as a romance of the French Revolution from 1921. The contents divide the novel into books. Book I lists The Republican, The Aristocrat, The Eloquence of M. de Vilmorin, The Heritage, and The Lord of Gavrillac. Later Book I chapters include The Windmill, The Wind, Omnes Omnibus, and The Aftermath. Book II opens with The Trespassers, The Service of Thespis, The Comic Muse, and Exit Monsieur Parvissimus, and the list shown here runs on to Enter Scaramouche and Climene.
she:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this tale of a deathless queen in 1887, in a white heat of work. He said the tale came to him whole, and he wrote it in a few short weeks. 'She' of the title is Ayesha, who must be obeyed, as her folk name her.

Two English men trek to a lost realm in Africa, ruled by a queen two thousand years old. Ayesha waits for the reborn form of the man she loved and slew in a past age. The book is the root work of the lost world tale, and a peak of its kind.
sutherland-birth-control-a-statement-of-:
Halliday G. Sutherland, a doctor of medicine from Edinburgh, published Birth Control at New York through P. J. Kenedy and Sons in 1922. The subtitle states the book's whole errand: A Statement of Christian Doctrine against the Neo-Malthusians.

Sutherland writes as a Catholic physician against the birth control movement then gaining public ground. He sets the teaching of the Christian church, as he holds it, against the claim that limiting families is a duty of prudence and progress. The book argues doctrine, morals, and medicine together, warning of what he saw as the movement's effects on marriage and the nation. It became one of the best-known answers to the campaign for contraception in its day.
the-bible-book-by-book-a-manual-for-the-:
J. B. Tidwell, professor of biblical literature at Baylor University in Waco, Texas, published a study manual in 1916. A preface to the second edition explains changes: descriptive matter now runs in paragraphs, analyses are shorter, and Old Testament lessons are folded into study topics.

Tidwell thanks readers that the first edition sold out so soon. His stated aim is to give Bible students an outline that builds familiarity with the contents, book by book. The manual was meant especially for academy students. Each book can thus be grasped in outline before closer reading, with topics set for study rather than a full commentary.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-29-lamentati:
Lamentations, in Douay-Rheims English, translated out of the Latin Vulgate and later revised by Bishop Richard Challoner (1749-1752). The Old Testament first came from Douay, in 1609 and 1610; the New Testament from Rheims, in 1582. A preface note says a sorrowful prophet sat weeping over Jerusalem, sighing and moaning as he spoke.

That preface, the note adds, was not written by Jeremias himself. Seventy translators added it to show the occasion on which the lamentations were published. Grief over a ruined city drives the poems that follow. Readers should expect mourning in verse form, not history in order, and a voice that treats loss as both punishment and pain.
the-botanist-s-companion-volume-ii-or-an: William Salisbury, of the Botanic Garden in Sloane Street, wrote The Botanist's Companion, Volume II. It is a guide to the uses of plants, wild in Great Britain or grown for farming, drugs, and the arts. The list for this book starts with plants of use in farming. Grass seeds, sown grasses, fodder from leaves and roots, and grains come first. Then come British trees, drug plants in the London, Edinburgh, and Dublin drug books, food plants, and dye plants. A part on rank plants closes the list.
the-boy-allies-with-the-victorious-fleet: Ensign Robert L. Drake wrote The Boy Allies with the Victorious Fleets, or The Fall of the German Navy,. The pages shown are a list of Drake's navy set, not the tale itself. The set starts with The Boy Allies on the North Sea Patrol. Under Two Flags and With the Flying Squadron come next. With the Terror of the Seas, In the Baltic, and At Jutland fill the mid list. Under the Sea and With Uncle Sam's Cruisers close the named books.
the-campaign-of-1760-in-canada-a-narrati:
The Campaign of 1760 in Canada is a narrative attributed to the Chevalier Johnstone. It was printed at Quebec at the Morning Chronicle office in 1887. The Literary and Historical Society of Quebec issued it. It opens with a reflection on hope as the great sweetener of life, the counterpoise to affliction that kept whole nations patient under hard government.

Applied to the Canadians, that hope meant retaking Quebec. The narrative states their case plainly. They had neither artillery nor stores for such a siege. Yet the wish was father to the thought. They had persuaded themselves the town must surrender without opposition. The work thus begins as both testimony and meditation, a participant's memory of a campaign undertaken on longing rather than means.
the-christian-home-as-it-is-in-the-spher:
The Rev. S. Philips, A.M., wrote this handbook on the Christian home, published in 1865 by Gurdon Bill of Springfield, Massachusetts, and H. C. Johnson of Detroit. Its long title promises the mission, duties, influences, habits, and responsibilities of home life. It also covers home education, government, and discipline, with hints on match making and on how parents should regard a child's choice in marriage.

The preface grants a fault at once: the Christian family, as a formed body, is less developed than it should be. In an age of extreme individualism, Philips argues, the mission of home as the first form of society has been lost from view. Its interests go unvalued, its duties and privileges neglected. Husbands and wives, he says, miss their moral relation to each other, parents give up authority, and children grow up in loose order.
the-circus-boys-in-dixie-land-or-winning: Edgar B. P. Darlington wrote this boys' circus story, subtitled Winning the Plaudits of the Sunny South, issued as a Project Gutenberg text in January 2001. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, with its standard notes on copyright, donations, and public domain status. Greg Berckes is credited with preparing the text.The work's own pages are not present here.
the-conquest-of-the-old-southwest-the-ro:
Archibald Henderson, who held a Ph.D. and a D.C.L., tells the story of the early pioneers who pushed into Virginia, the Carolinas, Tennessee, and Kentucky between 1740 and 1790. The Century Company printed the book in New York in 1920, and Henderson dedicated it to the historian Frederick Jackson Turner. Quotes from Richard Henderson and Lord Dunmore stand before the introduction.

Henderson calls the southward and westward movement of European settlers across the 1700s the growth story of American democracy. In the wilderness, he argues, a settler's survival rested on his own skill and his power to adapt to harsh new conditions. Hardship and daring, in his telling, forged a new society on the continent.
the-elements-of-general-method-based-on-:
Charles A. McMurry's The Elements of General Method, a second edition printed at Bloomington, Illinois, in 1893, rests on the principles of Herbart. McMurry's preface says the Herbart school had stirred Germany for thirty years, with a thousand or more keen teachers among its followers. American teachers who met its ideas, he adds, came away fired with new zeal.

He gives the school's lead ideas in plain form, not full science, and fits them to American schools. The Formal Steps of teaching get their own chapter. Herbart's plan shaped a age of normal schools.
the-fifth-leicestershire-a-record-of-the:
Captain J. D. Hills wrote The Fifth Leicestershire as the war record of the 1/5th Battalion of the Leicestershire Regiment, printed at Loughborough in 1919. Lt.-Colonel C. H. Jones adds an opening word.

Hills claims no fine writing for the book and calls it a diary in aim. It traces the battalion's years from 1914 to 1919, the men, the trenches, the losses, and the joys. The book is given to the Duke of Rutland, who watched over the unit. Such home-printed records held the shared past of a town's own soldiers.
the-fight-for-a-free-sea-a-chronicle-of-:
Ralph D. Paine wrote The Fight for a Free Sea as a tale of the War of 1812, volume seventeen of the Chronicles of America, printed in 1920. A picture of the old frigate Constitution in Boston Navy Yard faces the title page.

Paine moves from the rush to invade Canada to Perry's win on Lake Erie and the frigate duels on blue water. One head quotes the famed cry, Don't give up the ship. The Essex's last cruise and the win on Lake Champlain close the war at sea. The book praises a young navy that held its own against Britain.
the-first-landing-on-wrangel-island-with:
Irving C. Rosse, a doctor, tells of the first landing on Wrangel Island in the Arctic, made from the revenue steamer Corwin in 1881. The ship sailed from San Francisco on May 4 of that year.

The cruise had charge of revenue work, plus a search for two lost whalers and the missing yacht Jeannette. Hail, snow, and blind storms slowed the ship past the Aleutian chain. Wrangel Island itself was a puzzle: a Russian admiral heard of it from Siberian folk but never found it, and whalers' tales made men doubt it stood on any map. Rosse tells how the Corwin at last saw and reached it.
the-forest-exiles-the-perils-of-a-peruvi:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Forest Exiles as a tale of a Peruvian family lost in the wilds of the Amazon, first framed here by a warm address to his boy readers. He calls the Amazon forest the biggest wood in the world.

Reid vows a sharp change from his last tale of the cold north: palm huts, hammocks, snakes, great ants, and bright birds under the Southern Cross. He lists the strange trees ahead, from the cow-tree that gives milk to the bark that cures fever. A line drawn through this forest, he says, would run two thousand six hundred miles. Adventure and natural history march side by side.
the-haunted-house-a-true-ghost-story-bei:
Walter Hubbell wrote The Haunted House: A True Ghost Story, published at Saint John, N.B., in 1879. The title page describes strange events said to have taken place around Esther Cox, a young girl at the center of what became known across the Dominion as the Great Amherst Mystery. Hubbell states that he lived in the house and saw the events himself.

The introduction lists what was reported. Fires started with no clear cause, the house shook, loud knocks sounded on the walls, and furniture moved in broad daylight with no hand seen to move it. Hubbell notes that men of science from Canada and the United States looked into the case and failed to explain it.
the-history-of-puerto-rico-from-the-span:
R. A. Van Middeldyk wrote The History of Puerto Rico. The book runs from the Spanish discovery to the American occupation. Martin G. Brumbaugh edited the volume. The copyright is dated 1903. An editor's preface frames the island as a paradox. Puerto Rico was the latest United States possession then. It was also the oldest in European occupation.

Columbus discovered the island in 1493, the preface says. The United States Army occupied it at Guanica on July 25, 1898. Spain left on October 18, 1898. Civil government began on May 1, 1900. Brumbaugh says Spanish rule had never been well told in English. Van Middeldyk used the island's own records for his narrative. He was librarian of the Free Public Library of San Juan.
the-history-of-rome-book-iii-from-the-un: Theodor Mommsen wrote The History of Rome, Book III. The book covers the span from the union of Italy onward. It ends with the subjugation of Carthage and the Greek states. William Purdie Dickson translated it with the author's sanction. Dickson was a professor of divinity in Glasgow. The German original is named as Roemische Geschichte, Drittes Buch. Only the title page is present here. A preparer's note on marking foreign words also appears.
the-light-in-the-clearing-a-tale-of-the-: Irving Bacheller wrote his tale of the north country in the time of Silas Wright and published it in 1917, illustrated by Arthur I. Keller. Only the title page, a dedication to Thomas R. Proctor of Utica, and the start of the contents for book one are present here. Bacheller other books named on the page include Eben Holden. The chronicles of his hero and of northern New York democracy are not included in this record beyond those front pages.
the-london-bawd-with-her-character-and-l:
The London-Bawd, printed in London for John Gwillim in 1705 in its third edition, promises to discover the various and subtle intrigues of lewd women. Chapter one gives her character in the plain, abusive style of the period. A bawd, it says, is the refuse of an old prostitute. Burned herself, she helps set greener wood on fire. She is a daughter of Eve who first undid herself, then tempts others to the same destruction.

The sketch continues in that prosecutorial tone, treating its subject as one of nature's errors. Readers get an early example of the character pamphlet: part satire, part warning, and part scandal sheet. Its value now lies in the language and attitudes it preserves, not in any fairness toward the women it attacks.
the-marriage-of-william-ashe: Mrs. Humphry Ward's The Marriage of William Ashe, dated 1905 with illustrations by Albert Sterner, is inscribed to the author's daughter and friend, D. M. W., in March 1905. Only the title page, contents, dedication, and list of illustrations are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The contents divide it into five parts with page numbers: Acquaintance, Three Years After, Development, Storm, and Requiescat. The frontispiece shows Lady Kitty Bristol, and other illustrations name Lady Tranmore and Mary Lyster, pointing to the woman at the marriage's center.
the-meadow-brook-girls-under-canvas-or-f: The Meadow-Brook Girls Under Canvas, subtitled Fun and Frolic in the Summer Camp, was written by Janet Aldridge and published by Henry Altemus Company in 1913. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters begin with Crazy Jane's wild drive and something that happened to Tommy. Then the girls take the trail to Camp Wau-Wau, settle in the heart of the forest, and face troubles that multiply.
the-motor-girls-on-waters-blue-or-the-st:
Margaret Penrose's The Motor Girls on Waters Blue, subtitled The Strange Cruise of The Tartar, opens with Chapter I, News. A big car crunches up a gravel drive and stops at a side entrance with brakes whining and screeching. Its driver, a girl bronzed by summer sun, sits a moment with gloved hands fallen from the wheel.

She has driven fast and alone on a glorious October day, sorry that none of the girls could be reached by telephone to share it. On the porch she pauses against white pillars, watching the valley turn gold in the sinking sun. Then Cora Kimball, named at last, scolds herself back to business: her mother will want the worsted, and bridge is planned for the evening.
the-mystic-will-a-method-of-developing-a:
Charles G. Leland's The Mystic Will is present here only in title page, a memorial leaf, and the start of a publisher's notice, so the method itself does not appear. The subtitle promises a way of developing and strengthening the faculties of the mind through the awakened will, by a simple scientific process open to any person of ordinary intelligence. The Progress Company of Chicago published the American edition.

A memorial records Leland's death at Florence, Italy, on March 20, 1903, aged 79. The publisher's notice explains that the treatise first appeared in England years earlier under the title Have You a Strong Will? It ran through several editions there in large, widely spaced type.
the-outdoor-girls-in-army-service-or-doi: Laura Lee Hope published The Outdoor Girls in Army Service, or Doing Their Bit for the Soldier Boys, in 1918. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents list twenty-five chapters, opening with "I've Volunteered!" and Grim Shadows of War. Later titles name The Powder Mill, A Shot in the Dark, A Slacker?, Honor Flags, The Hostess House, and The Mystery Explained, a wartime tale for girls.
the-raid-from-beausejour-and-how-the-car:
Charles G. D. Roberts pairs two stories of Acadie in one volume. The first follows a raid from Beausejour. Pierre visits the English lines in its early chapters. A midnight march and a surprise attack follow. New Englanders arrive before the close. The tale opens on a cry that Beaubassin must go.

The second story turns from war to household economics. The Carter boys work to lift a mortgage on the family place. Only the title pages are present here. A contents list for both stories appears with them. The tales themselves do not appear on these pages.
the-rover-boys-on-treasure-isle-or-the-s:
In 1909 Edward Stratemeyer published The Rover Boys on Treasure Isle, subtitled The Strange Cruise of the Steam Yacht. It was the thirteenth volume of his Rover Boys Series for Young Americans. His introduction traces the line back ten years to the first three volumes. It also lists the many sequels reader demand produced.

Tom, Dick and Sam have finished their school days at Putnam Hall. They are preparing for college. Before leaving home they take a remarkable cruise on a steam yacht. Their father and a number of friends go with them. They hunt an island where a large treasure is said to be hidden. They lose themselves and their yacht, and some come close to losing their lives.
the-spirit-and-the-word-a-treatise-on-th: Z. T. Sweeney wrote this treatise on the Holy Spirit, published by the Gospel Advocate Company of Nashville, Tennessee, promising a rational interpretation of the word of truth. The pages present here give the title page and table of contents only. An introduction and ten chapters follow the Spirit through the Old and New Testaments. Later chapters treat his personality and divinity, John the Baptist, and Jesus. The apostles, the apostolic church, the world, and Christians follow, so the argument itself does not appear.
the-story-of-rome-from-the-earliest-time:
Arthur Gilman rehearses the story of Rome from its beginnings in myth and fable to the end of the republic, in a preface signed from Cambridge in September 1885. He warns that solid facts shade off by degrees. They fade into the obscurity of unlettered antiquity. At times no line can be drawn between history and legend at all.

Fortunately, Gilman says, the effort is not always necessary: traditions disproved as fact must still be told as story. His volume follows Rome's social and political struggles. It moves through the deeds of heroes who occupy the stage in turn. Gilman hopes to catch the real life of the Roman people. He hopes to catch their true spirit too. He pretends to no philosophy. He gives no episode undue prominence.
the-suitors-of-yvonne-being-a-portion-of: Rafael Sabatini presents this novel as a portion of the memoirs of the Sieur Gaston de Luynes. Only the title page and contents appear in this record. The contents list twenty chapters. A boy drinks too much wine in one. A fight erupts in the horse-market. Mazarin plays match-maker. A whip proves a better argument than a tongue. The Chevalier de Canaples becomes a Frondeur. Gaston's adventures themselves do not appear. A companion record carries the same book and contents.
the-treaties-of-canada-with-the-indians-:
Alexander Morris, late lieutenant-governor of Manitoba, the North-West Territories, and Kee-wa-tin, collected The Treaties of Canada with the Indians in 1880. His dedication letter addresses the Earl of Dufferin. It recalls the earl's interest in winning the alliance of the North-West tribes. It also recalls their giving up natural title to the Fertile Belt on fair and just terms. Morris offers the treaties, and the negotiations behind them, in compact form as a service to the Dominion.

His preface calls the relations between Canada and the Indians a question of great practical importance, the treaty work now completed from Lake Superior to the Rockies. The harder duty, he says, is carrying out the obligations in their integrity and rescuing the Indian population from a hard fate. Morris negotiated several of these treaties himself, making the volume a primary record of Canada's treaty era.
the-winning-of-the-west-volume-1-from-th:
Theodore Roosevelt dedicated the first volume of The Winning of the West, a presidential edition covering 1769 to 1776, to Francis Parkman. Roosevelt credits Parkman with Americans' debt for pride in their pioneer history. A long epigraph from Lowell's verse calls the New World a brown foundling of the woods, nursed by stern men with empires in their brains.

Roosevelt's preface explains the documentary base. Much material rests in American government archives dating from the first Continental Congress in 1774. The earliest sets were published complete to 1777 as the American Archives, the title he will cite throughout. A map accompanies the volume. The history moves from the Alleghanies toward the Mississippi through the Revolution's opening years.
the-winning-of-the-west-volume-2-from-th: Theodore Roosevelt's Winning of the West, volume two, carries the subtitle From the Alleghanies to the Mississippi, with the years 1777 to 1783 given. A library stamp dates this copy's use to December 23, 1910, with a private-use restriction noted. The pages present here give the title page and chapter headings, so Roosevelt's narrative itself does not appear. Seven chapter headings divide the war into campaigns: Washington at Valley Forge, fighting in the North, the southern States, the war on the ocean, and the closing years 1781 to 1783.
the-works-of-john-greenleaf-whittier-vol: A contents list represents volume seven of Whittier's works in this record, without the essays themselves. The Conflict with Slavery gathers his abolitionist writings. Titles include Justice and Expediency and The Bible and Slavery. Reform and Politics covers woman suffrage and Italian unity. The Inner Life and criticism sections follow. Whittier's response to his eightieth birthday celebration is also listed among the pieces.
the-young-engineers-on-the-gulf-or-the-d:
H. Irving Hancock's The Young Engineers on the Gulf opens on a pitch-dark night. Harry Hazelton wishes he had brought his electric flashlight. Tom Reade chuckles that he warned him to bring it. Harry protests he could not foresee such darkness. The contents call their job the dread mystery of the million dollar breakwater. Voices calling in trouble and vanishing figures fill the chapter titles.

Divers, night attacks, and secret captures follow in the list. A foreman named Bascomb grows peevish and hears bad news. Hancock blends engineering work with outright mystery plotting. The Gulf breakwater project gives the boys dangerous water to master. Young readers get sabotage and detection beside surveying and construction.
the-young-trail-hunters-or-the-wild-ride:
Samuel Woodworth Cozzens published The Young Trail Hunters in 1877, recounting adventures of Hal Hyde and Ned Brown. His note to readers recalls loving travel books since youth. Tales set in Indian lands, with danger at every step, fascinated him. Hal and Ned crossed the great southwestern plains with him. Their hair-breadth escapes, he hopes, will entertain and instruct. Customs of the plains tribes come from his personal observation.

Those tribes, Cozzens notes, were fast vanishing in his day. A sequel crossing the quicksands toward the Pacific is promised. Boys of the 1870s craved exactly such frontier narratives. Personal witness lends the hunting and escaping scenes their claim to truth. Adventure and ethnography, however dated, march together here.
the-youth-of-goethe: P. Hume Brown's The Youth of Goethe, published by John Murray in London in 1913, is shown through a dedication letter and opening contents. Brown dedicates the book to Viscount Haldane, the Lord Chancellor. Haldane, he says, was the book's only begetter. A German motto from Friedrich Hebbel follows about a point expanding into a circle. Chapter one covers Goethe's early years in Frankfurt, 1749 to 1765. His birthplace, parents, and sister are treated. The biography itself begins beyond the pages present.
thoughts-on-the-necessity-of-improving-t:
T. Clarkson published his thoughts on improving the condition of enslaved people in the British colonies in 1823, aiming at full freedom in the end. The essay first came out in a journal called The Inquirer. Clarkson's first pages now correct his early hope that things had got much better since the slave trade ended.

He admits he rated that change too high and calls slave life much as it was in its main parts. He notes Dundas put full freedom to Parliament in 1792, so the plan is not new. Readers get an anti-slavery case that better treatment now and freedom in time must keep order, workers, and owners in view all at once.
through-central-borneo-an-account-of-two:
Carl Lumholtz travelled through central Borneo for two years between 1913 and 1917, in what his subtitle calls the land of the head-hunters. His preface recalls camping life with Aboriginal people in Queensland and a long desire to explore New Guinea. Royal and geographical societies in Norway, London, and the Netherlands funded him.

War in 1914 blocked his New Guinea escort, so he turned to unexplored Dutch Borneo instead. He engaged Dayak helpers in the northeast and spent most of two years among native peoples. Readers get an explorer's account rich in photographs, maps, and ethnographic research.
tom-swift-and-his-aerial-warship-or-the-: The Naval Terror of the Seas is the subtitle of the Tom Swift aerial warship story by Victor Appleton, presented through its contents and first line. Twenty-five chapters promise a fire alarm, a desperate battle, a recoil check, stowaways, an ocean flight, and a lightning bolt. The chapter opens with someone asking Tom what is wrong, since he looks rather blue, then stops. The chapter list and that opening exchange are what is on these pages, so Appleton's airship story itself does not appear beyond them.
turkish-prisoners-in-egypt-a-report-by-t:
Delegates of the International Committee of the Red Cross reported on Turkish prisoners of war held in Egypt, in a report published in 1917. Their visit ran from December 1916 into January 1917. The text comes, in translation, from the Red Cross Society's official reports.

The delegates sailed from Marseilles on the liner Morea on December 19 and reached Port Said on December 27. At Cairo, General Murray's staff arranged their programme, with a motor-car, cameras, and free talks with prisoners all permitted. Their first camp, visited on January 2, stood at Heliopolis beside a new city of hotels and villas. The report models neutral inspection of wartime captivity.
who-was-who-5000-b-c-to-date-biographica:
Irwin L. Gordon edited Who Was Who, 5000 B.C. to Date, a comic dictionary of the famous and those who wanted to be. A note at the front sets strict rules with a straight face. Only people who can prove they are dead may enter the book. Press agent praise is barred, and offers to pay for a place will be prosecuted.

The book holds more than five hundred short lives, Gordon says. Errors may slip in, and he invites fixes from the former famous or their foes. Proofs go to subscribers, he adds, and the work is guarded by libel law. No duels will be fought over it. Short, sly entries mock fame old and new.
wild-flowers-an-aid-to-knowledge-of-our-: A Project Gutenberg header alone is present in this record, so Neltje Blanchan's flower guide does not appear. The header names her book Wild Flowers, an aid to knowledge of wild flowers and their insect visitors, in its cut-off title line. It notes the book also came out as Nature's Garden. The header is the older Gutenberg form, with donation appeals by state. No release block is reached in the part shown. Readers see the book's name and second title, but no plant entries.
